story.retell: Before he was king, David and his men protected the flocks of a rich man called Nabal. When David politely asked for food, Nabal sent back insults. Furious, David armed four hundred men to wipe out Nabal's household. Nabal's wife Abigail heard, loaded donkeys with bread, wine and figs, rode out to meet David on the road, and knelt before him, asking him not to stain his hands with blood.
story.verse: Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.

1-samuel-25-the-peacemaker.artLink: Peter Paul Rubens painted the moment they meet on the road, about 1630.
1-samuel-25-the-peacemaker.see: Abigail kneels at the centre in a slate-blue dress and pearls, one hand on her heart, the other pointing to the baskets of bread her servants are carrying. David, in armour with a sword at his hip, bends down to her and holds her elbow, his hand near her cheek, already softened. On the right, his armed men and horses wait. Behind her, her people with bread and a donkey. Two companies meet, and the war does not happen.
1-samuel-25-the-peacemaker.meaning: Abigail did not wait for the men to sort it out. She took food, not weapons, went out on the road, and found the words that let a proud, angry man step back without losing face. David saw it at once: she had saved him from himself. Peacemaking is rarely dramatic. It is usually someone brave enough to go first, with something kind in their hands and the right words.

echo.text: After Achilles has killed Hector, the old king Priam goes alone at night into the enemy camp to beg for his son's body. He kneels and kisses the hands that killed his son. Achilles, thinking of his own old father, weeps with him, and gives the body back.
echo.link: The greatest war poem ends not with a battle but with a peacemaker on his knees, just like Abigail. Both went out alone to an angry, armed man, and both changed his heart.

1-samuel-25-the-peacemaker.question: Is there a quarrel near you, at home, at work or among friends, where you could be the one who goes out with something kind in your hands? What would you take, and what would you say?
1-samuel-25-the-peacemaker.prayer: Lord, blessed are the peacemakers. Give me Abigail's courage to go first, her wisdom to find the right words, and her kindness to bring bread, not blame. Keep me, too, from avenging myself with my own hand. Amen.
1-samuel-25-the-peacemaker.midday: This morning: Abigail on the road with her baskets of bread. Is there a quarrel you could soften this afternoon?
1-samuel-25-the-peacemaker.evening: Today's story was the peacemaker. Did you calm something down today, or stop yourself from making it worse?

music.why: Horatio Spafford wrote it after losing his children at sea: “When peace like a river attendeth my way.” A peace that holds even in loss.

paras: But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying, “Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to Greet our master; and he insulted them.
But the men were very good to us, and we were not harmed, and we didn’t miss anything, as long as we went with them, when we were in the fields.
They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.
Now therefore know and consider what you will do; for evil is determined against our master, and against all his house; for he is such a worthless fellow that one can’t speak to him.”

Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two containers of wine, five sheep ready dressed, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys.
She said to her young men, “Go on before me. Behold, I am coming after you.” But she didn’t tell her husband, Nabal.
As she rode on her donkey, and came down by the covert of the mountain, that behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them.
Now David had said, “Surely in vain I have kept all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that pertained to him. He has returned me evil for good.
God do so to the enemies of David, and more also, if I leave of all that belongs to him by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got off her donkey, and fell before David on her face, and bowed herself to the ground.
She fell at his feet, and said, “On me, my lord, on me be the blame! Please let your servant speak in your ears. Hear the words of your servant.

Please don’t let my lord pay attention to this worthless fellow, Nabal; for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him; but I, your servant, didn’t see my lord’s young men, whom you sent.

Now therefore, my lord, as Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, since Yahweh has withheld you from blood guiltiness, and from avenging yourself with your own hand, now therefore let your enemies, and those who seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal.
Now this present which your servant has brought to my lord, let it be given to the young men who follow my lord.
Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For Yahweh will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord fights Yahweh’s battles. Evil will not be found in you all your days.

Though men may rise up to pursue you, and to seek your soul, yet the soul of my lord will be bound in the bundle of life with Yahweh your God. He will sling out the souls of your enemies, as from the hollow of a sling.
It will come to pass, when Yahweh has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel,

that this shall be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself. When Yahweh has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant.”
David said to Abigail, “Blessed is Yahweh, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me!
Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.

For indeed, as Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, who has withheld me from harming you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, surely there wouldn’t have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
So David received from her hand that which she had brought him. Then he said to her, “Go up in peace to your house. Behold, I have listened to your voice, and have granted your request.”

read.author: Marcus Aurelius
paras: If any have offended against thee, consider first: What is my relation to men, and that we are made for one another; and in another respect I was made to be set over them, as a ram over the flock or a bull over the herd. But examine the matter from first principles, from this. If all things are not mere atoms, it is nature which orders all things: if this is so, the inferior things exist for the sake of the superior, and these for the sake of one another.

Second, consider what kind of men they are at table, in bed, and so forth; and particularly, under what compulsions in respect of opinions they are; and as to their acts, consider with what pride they do what they do.

Third, that if men do rightly what they do, we ought not to be displeased: but if they do not right, it is plain that they do so involuntarily and in ignorance. For as every soul is unwillingly deprived of the truth, so also is it unwillingly deprived of the power of behaving to each man according to his deserts. Accordingly men are pained when they are called unjust, ungrateful, and greedy, and in a word wrong-doers to their neighbors.

Fourth, consider that thou also doest many things wrong, and that thou art a man like others; and even if thou dost abstain from certain faults, still thou hast the disposition to commit them, though either through cowardice, or concern about reputation, or some such mean motive, thou dost abstain from such faults.

Fifth, consider that thou dost not even understand whether men are doing wrong or not, for many things are done with a certain reference to circumstances. And in short, a man must learn a great deal to enable him to pass a correct judgment on another man's acts.
Sixth, consider when thou art much vexed or grieved, that man's life is only a moment, and after a short time we are all laid out dead.

Seventh, that it is not men's acts which disturb us, for those acts have their foundation in men's ruling principles, but it is our own opinions which disturb us. Take away these opinions then, and resolve to dismiss thy judgment about an act as if it were something grievous, and thy anger is gone. How then shall I take away these opinions? By reflecting that no wrongful act of another brings shame on thee: for unless that which is shameful is alone bad, thou also must of necessity do many things wrong, and become a robber and everything else.
Eighth, consider how much more pain is brought on us by the anger and vexation caused by such acts than by the acts themselves, at which we are angry and vexed.

Ninth, consider that a good disposition is invincible if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part. For what will the most violent man do to thee, if thou continuest to be of a kind disposition towards him, and if, as opportunity offers, thou gently admonishest him and calmly correctest his errors at the very time when he is trying to do thee harm, saying, Not so, my child: we are constituted by nature for something else: I shall certainly not be injured, but thou art injuring thyself, my child.—And show him with gentle tact and by general principles that this is so, and that even bees do not do as he does, nor any animals which are formed by nature to be gregarious. And thou must do this neither with any double meaning nor in the way of reproach, but affectionately and without any rancor in thy soul; and not as if thou wert lecturing him, nor yet that any bystander may admire, but either when he is alone, and if others are present …

Remember these nine rules, as if thou hadst received them as a gift from the Muses, and begin at last to be a man while thou livest. But thou must equally avoid flattering men and being vexed at them, for both are unsocial and lead to harm. And let this truth be present to thee in the excitement of anger, that to be moved by passion is not manly, but that mildness and gentleness, as they are more agreeable to human nature, so also are they more manly; and he who possesses these qualities possesses strength, nerves, and courage, and not the man who is subject to fits of passion and discontent. For in the same degree in which a man's mind is nearer to freedom from all passion, in the same degree also is it nearer to strength: and as the sense of pain is a characteristic of weakness, so also is anger. For he who yields to pain and he who yields to anger, both are wounded and both submit.

But if thou wilt, receive also a tenth present from the leader of the Muses [Apollo], and it is this,—that to expect bad men not to do wrong is madness, for he who expects this desires an impossibility. But to allow men to behave so to others, and to expect them not to do thee any wrong, is irrational and tyrannical.
read.who: Marcus Aurelius (121–180), Roman emperor, who wrote these notes to himself and never meant them to be published.
read.when: On campaign by the Danube, about 175
read.why: This part of the road is about holding steady when it's hard. Abigail calmed David's anger. Marcus Aurelius wrote himself these private notes on what to remember when someone has wronged you. Read them slowly: the fourth is the hardest.

daniel-6-as-he-did-before.title: As he did before
daniel-6-as-he-did-before.line: Daniel keeps praying at his open window, even when it is against the law.

story.retell: Daniel was a Jewish exile who rose to high office in Babylon. Jealous rivals persuaded King Darius to sign a law that for thirty days no one could pray to anyone but the king, on pain of being thrown to the lions. Daniel knew the law had been signed.
story.verse: He went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.

daniel-6-as-he-did-before.artLink: Peter Paul Rubens painted Daniel in the lions' den in about 1614–16.
daniel-6-as-he-did-before.see: Daniel sits in the pit with his legs crossed and his hands clasped at his chest, looking up at a small round opening of blue sky. Nine lions surround him, life-size, one roaring with its head thrown back, and there are bones on the ground near your feet. Look at Daniel's face: not terror, but prayer. The light from above falls on him. He is doing in the den exactly what he did at his window.
daniel-6-as-he-did-before.meaning: The most important words in the story are the last three of the verse: as he did before. Daniel didn't make a protest or a speech. He simply kept doing what he had always done, at the same window, at the same times. Character is not built in the moment of crisis; it is revealed there. What we do every ordinary day is what we will do when it costs us.

echo.text: In prison, waiting to be executed, Socrates is visited by his friend Crito, who has bribed the guards and arranged his escape. Socrates calmly refuses. He will not break the principles he has lived by all his life, just because his life is now at stake.
echo.link: Daniel in the lions' den and Socrates in his cell both stay steady when it would be easy to bend, and for the same reason: they had already decided, day by day, who they were.

daniel-6-as-he-did-before.question: What is one small daily practice that keeps you steady? Is there a place where you've been tempted to drop it, because of pressure or embarrassment?
daniel-6-as-he-did-before.prayer: God of Daniel, I want to be faithful in small things, every day, so that I'm faithful when it matters. Keep me at my open window. Give me courage that doesn't need to shout, only to keep going, as I did before. Amen.
daniel-6-as-he-did-before.midday: This morning: Daniel praying at his window, as he did before. Keep your midday moment, as you did yesterday.
daniel-6-as-he-did-before.evening: Today's story was keeping on as before. What steadied you today? Is there a habit you want to keep, whatever happens?

music.why: Tallis's forty voices sing “I have never put my hope in any other but in you”: Daniel's prayer at his window.

paras: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom one hundred twenty local governors, who should be throughout the whole kingdom;
and over them three presidents, of whom Daniel was one; that these local governors might give account to them, and that the king should suffer no loss.
Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the local governors, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.
Then these men said, “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.”
Then these presidents and local governors assembled together to the king, and said this to him, “King Darius, live forever!

All the presidents of the kingdom, the deputies and the local governors, the counselors and the governors, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a strong decree, that whoever asks a petition of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it not be changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which doesn’t alter.”
Therefore king Darius signed the writing and the decree.

When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
Then these men assembled together, and found Daniel making petition and supplication before his God.

Then they came near, and spoke before the king concerning the king’s decree: “Haven’t you signed a decree that every man who makes a petition to any god or man within thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?”
The king answered, “This thing is true, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which doesn’t alter.”

Then they answered and said before the king, “That Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah, doesn’t respect you, O king, nor the decree that you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day.”
Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored until the going down of the sun to rescue him.
Then these men assembled together to the king, and said to the king, “Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians, that no decree nor statute which the king establishes may be changed.”
Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. The king spoke and said to Daniel, “Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you.”
A stone was brought, and laid on the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting. No musical instruments were brought before him; and his sleep fled from him.
Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste to the den of lions.

When he came near to the den to Daniel, he cried with a troubled voice. The king spoke and said to Daniel, “Daniel, servant of the living God, is your God, whom you serve continually, able to deliver you from the lions?”
Then Daniel said to the king, “O king, live forever!
My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm.”

Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

The king commanded, and they brought those men who had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions mauled them, and broke all their bones in pieces, before they came to the bottom of the den.
Then king Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth:
“Peace be multiplied to you.
“I make a decree that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel;

“for he is the living God,
and steadfast forever.
His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed.
His dominion will be even to the end.

He delivers and rescues.
He works signs and wonders in heaven and in earth,
who has delivered Daniel from the power of the lions.”
So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

read.why: Read Daniel's whole story: the plot against him, the night with the lions, the morning after. Notice how little Daniel says. Faithfulness is mostly doing what you did before.

ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.title: Strangers at the door
ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.line: An old couple share their last food with two strangers, who turn out to be gods.

story.retell: The Roman poet Ovid tells how the gods Jupiter and Mercury came to earth disguised as poor travellers. They knocked at a thousand doors and were turned away from every one, until they reached the tiny cottage of an old couple, Philemon and Baucis. The couple had almost nothing, but they lit the fire, washed the strangers' feet and served everything they had. As they ate, they noticed the wine jug kept refilling itself.
story.verse: Don't forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.

ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.artLink: Rembrandt painted the old couple's supper in 1658, when he himself had lost almost everything.
ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.see: The scene glows in warm bronze and gold. On the right, Mercury is lit from behind so his face is almost a silhouette. At the far end sits the old couple: Philemon holds his cap to his chest, Baucis holds a goose in her lap. In Ovid's story she is about to kill their only goose for the meal, and the gods stop her. A small fire burns in the hearth. Everything in the room is poor, and everything is shining.
ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.meaning: This story is not from the Bible, but early Christians loved it, because it says what the Bible says: the stranger at your door may be more than you think. Abraham welcomed three travellers who turned out to bring a message from God. Jesus said that whoever welcomes a stranger welcomes him. Philemon and Baucis had the least and gave the most, and their small house became a temple.

echo.text: Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day, saw three strangers and ran to welcome them, washing their feet and preparing a meal. They brought him the promise of a son. Centuries later the letter to the Hebrews remembered: some have entertained angels without knowing it.
echo.link: Today the story is from Rome and the echo is from the Bible. Ovid and Genesis tell almost the same story: the poor household that opens its door finds it has welcomed heaven.

ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.question: Who is a stranger at your door right now: someone new nearby, at work, at the edge of your circle? What could you offer them today, even if it's very little?
ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.prayer: Lord, you came to us as a stranger and were often turned away. Make my door open and my table generous, even when I have little. Let me welcome others as if I were welcoming you, because I am. Amen.
ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.midday: This morning: Philemon and Baucis open their door. Is there a stranger you could welcome this afternoon?
ovid-metamorphoses-book-8-strangers-at-t.evening: Today's story was the strangers at the door. Did you welcome someone today? Did someone welcome you?

music.why: An ancient chant sung at the washing of feet: “Where charity and love are, God is there.”

paras: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day.
He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth,
and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant.
Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart. After that you may go your way, now that you have come to your servant.”
They said, “Very well, do as you have said.”
Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three seahs of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”
Abraham ran to the herd, and fetched a tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it.
He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
They asked him, “Where is Sarah, your wife?”
He said, “There, in the tent.”
He said, “I will certainly return to you at about this time next year; and behold, Sarah your wife will have a son.”
Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him.
Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing.
Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”
Yahweh said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Will I really bear a child when I am old?’
Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
Then Sarah denied it, saying, “I didn’t laugh,” for she was afraid.
He said, “No, but you did laugh.”

read.why: Read the whole of Abraham's welcome: the running, the hurry, the best food, and Sarah laughing behind the tent door. The welcome is urgent and generous, and the strangers bring a promise.

luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.title: Known in the breaking of bread
luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.line: Two friends walk home in grief with a stranger, and recognise him at supper.

story.ref: Luke 24:13–32 · the feast of St Luke
story.retell: On the evening of the first Easter, two of Jesus's friends walked the seven miles home to Emmaus, heartbroken. A stranger joined them and asked why they were sad, then explained the Scriptures to them as they walked. It was getting dark, so they begged him to stay. At supper he took bread, gave thanks and broke it, and suddenly they knew him. Only Luke, whose feast is today, tells this story.
story.verse: They said to one another, “Weren't our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”

luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.artLink: An unknown American painter of the 1720s painted the three on the road, walking towards us.
luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.see: Three barefoot men walk a dirt path between two stretches of water, past a broken fence, towards us. The one in the middle, with long hair and a pink robe, is turned to the others, talking. They are listening intently. Nothing in the picture says who he is. That is exactly right: on the road, they didn't know. The painter puts us where the two friends were, in the moment before recognition.
luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.meaning: The two friends had all the facts. They had heard about the empty tomb. What they lacked was recognition, and it came not through an argument but at a table, in an ordinary act of hospitality. Looking back, they realised their hearts had been burning all along. Faith often works like that: understood backwards, recognised in hindsight, made real at a shared meal.

echo.from: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, Letter 19, quoting Epicurus
echo.text: Seneca passes on the Greek philosopher Epicurus's advice: think carefully about whom you will eat and drink with, before you think about what you will eat and drink.
echo.link: Two philosophers knew that who sits at a table matters more than what is on it. In Emmaus, a meal with a stranger became the moment everything changed.

luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.question: Looking back over the last few weeks, when did your heart “burn”, even if you didn't notice at the time? Who could you share a meal with this week?
luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.prayer: Stay with us, Lord, for it is evening and the day is almost over. Walk with me when I don't recognise you. Open my eyes at the ordinary table, and let my heart burn again with what is true. Amen.
luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.midday: This morning: two friends on the road to Emmaus. Notice where your heart is stirred this afternoon.
luke-24-known-in-the-breaking-of-bread.evening: Today's story was Emmaus. Looking back on today, where was God, even if you didn't notice at the time?

music.why: The hymn Abide with Me is built on this story: the friends begging the stranger to stay as evening fell (Luke 24:29).

paras: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem.
They talked with each other about all of these things which had happened.
While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them.
But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?”
One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things which have happened there in these days?”
He said to them, “What things?”
They said to him, “The things concerning Jesus, the Nazarene, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people;
and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
Also, certain women of our company amazed us, having arrived early at the tomb;
and when they didn’t find his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive.
Some of us went to the tomb, and found it just like the women had said, but they didn’t see him.”
He said to them, “Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!
Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further.
They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.”
He went in to stay with them.
When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
Their eyes were opened and they recognized him, then he vanished out of their sight.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”
They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them,
saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!”
They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.

read.why: The last day of this stretch is about looking back. Read the whole walk to Emmaus. At the end the two friends ask, “Weren't our hearts burning within us?” Look back over your own fortnight the same way.

elijah-fed-by-ravens.title: Bread for today
elijah-fed-by-ravens.line: Hiding by a stream in the wilderness, Elijah is fed morning and evening, one day at a time.

story.retell: Elijah, a prophet from the hill country of Gilead, told King Ahab to his face that there would be no rain for years. Then God sent him away to hide by a stream called Cherith, east of the Jordan. In hiding, he had no way to feed himself. Every morning and every evening, ravens brought him bread and meat, and he drank from the stream.
story.verse: The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.

elijah-fed-by-ravens.artLink: Giovanni Girolamo Savoldo painted Elijah waiting for the raven in about 1510.
elijah-fed-by-ravens.see: An old man with a long grey beard sits against a tall rock, his head resting in one hand, his bare feet on the dirt. He wears an aquamarine robe with a rose-pink cloth, lined with fleece, tied round his neck. He is looking up and to the right, where a raven leans down from the rock with a bread roll in its beak. Far behind him a river winds through green land, and tiny figures by the water point at the sky, where a man kneeling in a chariot is drawn up into the clouds: the end of Elijah's story, painted into the beginning.
elijah-fed-by-ravens.meaning: Elijah did not get a warehouse. He got two meals a day, brought by the least likely waiters in the world. Each one arrived only when it was needed. Jesus taught his friends to pray the same way: “Give us today our daily bread.” Not this year's bread. Prayer often starts here, with the plain admission that we depend on things we cannot provide for ourselves, and the trust to ask only for today.

echo.text: Horace tells a young woman, Leuconoe, to stop asking astrologers how many years the gods have given them. No one can know. While we talk, time runs away from us. So, he says, cut your long hopes down to size and seize the day, trusting as little as possible to tomorrow.
echo.link: Horace and Elijah both live one day at a time. Horace says grab today, because tomorrow is uncertain. Elijah receives today, because the one who fed him this morning will feed him again this evening.

elijah-fed-by-ravens.question: What are you anxious to have sorted for months ahead that you could simply ask for one day at a time? What do you actually need today?
elijah-fed-by-ravens.prayer: Lord, you fed Elijah morning and evening by a stream in the wilderness. Give me today what I need for today, and teach me to trust you with tomorrow. Amen.
elijah-fed-by-ravens.midday: This morning: Elijah fed by ravens, one meal at a time. What has been given to you today so far?
elijah-fed-by-ravens.evening: Today's story was Elijah by the stream. What did you need today, and was it given? Give thanks for one thing that arrived just in time.

music.why: Mendelssohn's Elijah tells this part of the story early in Part One, as an angel sends the prophet to hide by the brook Cherith.

paras: Elijah the Tishbite, who was one of the settlers of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
Then Yahweh’s word came to him, saying,
“Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan.
You shall drink from the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
So he went and did according to Yahweh’s word; for he went and lived by the brook Cherith that is before the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.
After a while, the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.
Yahweh’s word came to him, saying,
“Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.”

So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. He called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a jar, that I may drink.”
As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of bread in your hand.”

She said, “As Yahweh your God lives, I don’t have a cake, but a handful of meal in a jar, and a little oil in a jar. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and bake it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.”
Elijah said to her, “Don’t be afraid. Go and do as you have said; but make me a little cake from it first, and bring it out to me, and afterward make some for you and for your son.
For Yahweh, the God of Israel says, ‘The jar of meal will not run out, and the jar of oil will not fail, until the day that Yahweh sends rain on the earth.’ ”
She went and did according to the saying of Elijah; and she, and he, and her house, ate many days.
The jar of meal didn’t run out, and the jar of oil didn’t fail, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke by Elijah.

read.why: This week is about learning to pray, and it starts with the simplest prayer there is: asking for what you need. Read on past the ravens. When the stream dries up, Elijah is sent to a poor widow with only a handful of flour, and she is fed day by day as well.

moses-cries-out.title: An honest cry
moses-cries-out.line: Moses is out of his depth, and tells God exactly how he feels.

story.retell: The people of Israel camped at Rephidim in the desert, and there was no water. They turned on Moses: why had he brought them out of Egypt only to let them and their children die of thirst? Moses had nothing to give them, and they were angry enough to stone him. So he took the problem, unpolished, straight to God. He was told to walk ahead with the elders, take his staff and strike a rock at Horeb, and water would come out of it.
story.verse: Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “What shall I do with these people? They are almost ready to stone me.”

moses-cries-out.artLink: Joachim Wtewael painted the water pouring from the rock in Utrecht in 1624.
moses-cries-out.see: Start at the edges. In the shadowy foreground is the whole thirsty camp: a horse, a woman with a small child, a goat, a dog sniffing at a pile of pans, a cat lapping from a dish, a young man drinking from a shell. Beyond them an old bearded man in turquoise, pink and blue taps the rocks with a thin rod, and water runs out in streams into a pool. All round it people bend to fill jugs and pans. In the far distance, dozens more people and wagons are still on their way.
moses-cries-out.meaning: Moses does not pray politely here. He says, in effect: I don't know what to do, and they are about to kill me. The Bible is full of prayers like this, and none of them is told off. Learning to pray does not mean learning the right words. Often it means dropping them and saying what is really going on. God can work with honesty. Pretending gets nowhere.

echo.when: Ancient Israel, traditionally a psalm of David
echo.text: The psalm opens with four questions in a row, each beginning “How long?” How long will you forget me? How long will you hide your face? It is a complaint spoken straight to God, kept in the prayer book of Israel and prayed by Jews and Christians ever since. By the last lines, the same voice is singing.
echo.link: Psalm 13 and Moses at Rephidim both show that complaint can be prayer. Both start with the problem stated plainly, and both end somewhere new: the psalmist singing, and Moses watching water run out of a rock.

moses-cries-out.question: What would you say to God today if you didn't have to be polite? Could you say it, honestly, in one sentence?
moses-cries-out.prayer: Lord, Moses brought you his fear without dressing it up, and you answered him. Here is what is really going on with me today. I don't always know what to do. Show me the next step, and give water to whoever is thirsty around me. Amen.
moses-cries-out.midday: This morning: Moses telling God he was out of his depth. Is there something you've been too polite to pray about?
moses-cries-out.evening: Today's story was an honest cry in the desert. Where were you out of your depth today? Did you tell anyone, or God?

music.why: U2's 40 sets Psalm 40 and ends on the old complaint of the psalms, “how long”, which crowds sang back to the band at the end of their concerts for years.

paras: All the congregation of the children of Israel traveled from the wilderness of Sin, starting according to Yahweh’s commandment, and encamped in Rephidim; but there was no water for the people to drink.
Therefore the people quarreled with Moses, and said, “Give us water to drink.”
Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?”
The people were thirsty for water there; so the people murmured against Moses, and said, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “What shall I do with these people? They are almost ready to stone me.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Walk on before the people, and take the elders of Israel with you, and take the rod in your hand with which you struck the Nile, and go.
Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink.” Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.
He called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because the children of Israel quarreled, and because they tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us, or not?”
Then Amalek came and fought with Israel in Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose men for us, and go out, fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with God’s rod in my hand.”
So Joshua did as Moses had told him, and fought with Amalek; and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

But Moses’ hands were heavy; so they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur held up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side. His hands were steady until sunset.
Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under the sky.”
Moses built an altar, and called its name “Yahweh our Banner”.
He said, “Yah has sworn: ‘Yahweh will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.’ ”

read.why: Read on past the water. Later in the same chapter Moses prays on a hilltop with his hands raised, and grows so tired that his brother Aaron and his friend Hur have to hold his arms up until sunset. Even Moses needed help to keep praying.

joan-hears-a-voice.title: Learning to listen
joan-hears-a-voice.line: A farmer's daughter in a French village hears a voice in her father's garden.

story.ref: The trial of Joan of Arc, Rouen, 22 February 1431
story.retell: Joan was a farmer's daughter from Domrémy, a village in eastern France, who could not read. At her trial she told her judges how it began. When she was about thirteen, at noon one summer's day in her father's garden, she heard a voice from God, usually with a light. She was afraid. Over the following years the voices grew clearer, and she came to name them as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They told her to be good and to go to church, and later sent her to help the king of France.
story.verse: Speak; for your servant hears.
story.verseRef: 1 Samuel 3:10, the prayer the boy Samuel was taught when God called him in the night

joan-hears-a-voice.artLink: Louis-Maurice Boutet de Monvel painted Joan's first vision in about 1907–09, the first of six scenes from her life.
joan-hears-a-voice.see: A young woman kneels on the right, hands together in prayer, lips parted, looking up. She wears a black scarf, a pink jacket and a long beige dress; behind her six white sheep stand and lie in the grass, and a basket at her feet has tipped over. On the left, in an oval of light ringed with small flames, an armoured figure with pale pink and blue wings hovers above the ground, holding up a gold sword: Saint Michael. Two women in white and gold stand on pink clouds beside him, one holding a helmet, one a sword. Grassy hills roll away into the distance.
joan-hears-a-voice.meaning: Most of what we call prayer is talking. Joan's story begins with listening, and with fear. Very few people hear voices, and Christians have always tested such claims carefully; Joan's judges did not believe her, and a later court cleared her name. But the shape of her prayer is open to anyone: stop, be still, and say what the boy Samuel was taught to say. Speak, I'm listening. Then do the next good thing you are given.

echo.text: At his trial, Socrates tells the jury that since childhood he has had a kind of voice, a divine sign, that comes to him. It never tells him what to do; it only holds him back when he is about to do something wrong. He says it is why he kept out of politics, and that it did not stop him coming to court that day.
echo.link: Socrates and Joan both told their judges about a voice they had heard since childhood, and both followed it all the way to a trial and death. Socrates' voice only ever said no. Joan's said go.

joan-hears-a-voice.question: When did you last stop talking long enough to listen, in prayer or to another person? Could you give five minutes today to silence, and then to whatever good thing comes to mind?
joan-hears-a-voice.prayer: Lord, you called Samuel in the night and Joan in a garden. I am not used to listening. Quieten me, and speak; your servant is listening. Then give me courage to do what you ask. Amen.
joan-hears-a-voice.midday: This morning: Joan in her father's garden, listening. Is there a quiet moment this afternoon where you could stop and listen?
joan-hears-a-voice.evening: Today's story was about listening. Did anything nudge you today, a thought, a person, a need? Did you act on it?

music.why: A prayer to the Holy Spirit by Bianco da Siena, a medieval Italian poet, asking God's love to come quietly and kindle the heart.

paras: The child Samuel ministered to Yahweh before Eli. Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.
At that time, when Eli was laid down in his place (now his eyes had begun to grow dim, so that he could not see),
and God’s lamp hadn’t yet gone out, and Samuel had laid down in Yahweh’s temple where God’s ark was,
Yahweh called Samuel. He said, “Here I am.”
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.”
He said, “I didn’t call. Lie down again.”
He went and lay down.
Yahweh called yet again, “Samuel!”
Samuel arose and went to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.”
He answered, “I didn’t call, my son. Lie down again.”
Now Samuel didn’t yet know Yahweh, neither was Yahweh’s word yet revealed to him.
Yahweh called Samuel again the third time. He arose and went to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.”
Eli perceived that Yahweh had called the child.
Therefore Eli said to Samuel, “Go, lie down. It shall be, if he calls you, that you shall say, ‘Speak, Yahweh; for your servant hears.’ ” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
Yahweh came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!”
Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”
Yahweh said to Samuel, “Behold, I will do a thing in Israel at which both the ears of everyone who hears it will tingle.
In that day I will perform against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from the beginning even to the end.
For I have told him that I will judge his house forever for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn’t restrain them.
Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli’s house shall not be removed with sacrifice or offering forever.”
Samuel lay until the morning, and opened the doors of Yahweh’s house. Samuel was afraid to show Eli the vision.
Then Eli called Samuel and said, “Samuel, my son!”
He said, “Here I am.”
He said, “What is the thing that he has spoken to you? Please don’t hide it from me. God do so to you, and more also, if you hide anything from me of all the things that he spoke to you.”
Samuel told him every bit, and hid nothing from him.
He said, “It is Yahweh. Let him do what seems good to him.”
Samuel grew, and Yahweh was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.
All Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of Yahweh.
Yahweh appeared again in Shiloh; for Yahweh revealed himself to Samuel in Shiloh by Yahweh’s word.

read.why: Read the story Joan's has always been compared to: the boy Samuel, sleeping in the temple at a time when, the text says, God's word was rare. He hears his name three times and keeps running to the old priest Eli, until Eli realises who is calling and teaches him how to answer.

gethsemane-not-my-will.title: Not my will
gethsemane-not-my-will.line: On the night before he dies, Jesus prays the hardest prayer there is.

story.retell: After the last supper, Jesus went out, as he often did, to the Mount of Olives. He asked his friends to pray, then went on about a stone's throw, knelt down, and asked his Father to take this cup of suffering away from him. He did not hide what he wanted. But he ended: not my will, but yours. Luke says an angel came to strengthen him. When he got up and went back, his friends were asleep.
story.verse: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.

gethsemane-not-my-will.artLink: The Sienese painter Benvenuto di Giovanni painted this scene in about 1491, one of a series of small panels on the Passion.
gethsemane-not-my-will.see: Jesus kneels in a gloomy, rocky landscape, in a terracotta-red cloak over a sky-blue robe, hands pressed together, looking sharply up. In the upper right corner floats a small angel with white wings, holding out a gold cup. Behind Jesus his friends are asleep on the ground, three close to his bare feet and more beyond a mound. A band of charcoal cloud hangs over the hills. Benvenuto puts in the angel's hand the very thing Jesus has asked to be spared.
gethsemane-not-my-will.meaning: This is the most honest prayer in the Gospels. Jesus asks for what he wants: take this away. He does not pretend to be braver than he is. Then he hands the outcome back. “Not my will, but yours” is not a way of avoiding asking. It is what you say after you have asked with everything you have. It is the place where prayer stops being a request and becomes trust.

echo.text: Seneca quotes a prayer by the Stoic Cleanthes: lead me, Zeus, wherever you have decided, and I will follow without delay; and if I am unwilling, I shall follow anyway. Fate, Seneca adds, leads the willing and drags the unwilling.
echo.link: The Stoic and Jesus both end by accepting what is coming. But Seneca's prayer is addressed to fate, and asks for nothing. Jesus speaks to a Father, tells him exactly what he wants, and only then lets go.

gethsemane-not-my-will.question: Is there something you want so much that you have been afraid to pray “your will be done” about it? Could you ask for it honestly today, and then let go of the outcome?
gethsemane-not-my-will.prayer: Father, Jesus told you what he wanted and then trusted you with the rest. Here is what I want. Take it, and do what is best. Not my will, but yours. And when I am tired, send someone to strengthen me. Amen.
gethsemane-not-my-will.midday: This morning: Jesus in the garden, asking and then letting go. What are you holding on to this afternoon?
gethsemane-not-my-will.evening: Today's story was the garden of Gethsemane. Where did you have to give up your own way today? Who stayed awake for you, or for whom did you?

music.why: In Bach's St Matthew Passion, as the disciples sleep in the garden, a tenor sings “Ich will bei meinem Jesu wachen”: I will keep watch with my Jesus.

paras: The Lord said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat,
but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.”
He said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!”
He said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will by no means crow today until you deny that you know me three times.”
He said to them, “When I sent you out without purse, wallet, and sandals, did you lack anything?”
They said, “Nothing.”
Then he said to them, “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a wallet. Whoever has none, let him sell his cloak, and buy a sword.
For I tell you that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: ‘He was counted with transgressors.’ For that which concerns me has an end.”
They said, “Lord, behold, here are two swords.”
He said to them, “That is enough.”
He came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him.
When he was at the place, he said to them, “Pray that you don’t enter into temptation.”
He was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw, and he knelt down and prayed,
saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.
Being in agony he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.
When he rose up from his prayer, he came to the disciples, and found them sleeping because of grief,
and said to them, “Why do you sleep? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”

read.why: Begin a few verses earlier, where Jesus tells Peter, “I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail.” Before he prays for himself in the garden, he has already prayed for a friend who is about to let him down.

mary-of-egypt.title: A life turned to prayer
mary-of-egypt.line: A woman with a wild past spends the rest of her life in the desert, praying.

story.ref: The Life of Saint Mary of Egypt, attributed to Sophronius of Jerusalem, 7th century
story.retell: Mary lived a wild life in Alexandria for many years. She went to Jerusalem with the pilgrims for the feast of the Cross, but found she could not walk through the church door. Standing outside, she wept and prayed, and when she tried again she went in. She crossed the Jordan and lived in the desert alone for forty-seven years. Near the end, an old monk called Zosimas found her, and at her request came back a year later to the river to bring her communion. The next year he found her dead.
story.verse: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much.
story.verseRef: Luke 7:47, said of another woman with a past

mary-of-egypt.artLink: Sebastiano Ricci painted Mary's last communion in about 1695.
mary-of-egypt.see: A thin woman kneels on the right in profile, leaning towards a wafer held out to her, a tear running down her cheek. Her long chestnut hair falls down her back; she holds a white cloth to her chest and has wrapped herself in cobalt blue. Opposite her, an old balding monk with a thick beard and a patched brown robe offers the wafer with one hand and a gold plate with the other. Angels surround them: one kneels with a torch, one hovers behind her with wide white wings, holding the other end of her cloth, as if to steady her.
mary-of-egypt.meaning: Mary's story is told every Lent in the Orthodox Church, and it is not mainly about what she did wrong. It is about how completely a life can turn. She did not become holy by being careful. She became holy by spending her love on God as freely as she had once spent it elsewhere, for forty-seven years, mostly alone, mostly in prayer. No one is too far gone to begin, and no beginning is too small.

echo.text: People look for retreats in the country, by the sea or in the hills, writes the emperor, and you long for them too. But you can retreat whenever you like, into yourself. Nowhere is quieter or freer from trouble than a person's own mind. So give yourself this retreat often, and renew yourself.
echo.link: Marcus found his retreat inside himself, in the middle of a war. Mary went all the way out into the desert. Both knew that you cannot live well without stepping away; Mary stepped away to someone, not only into herself.

mary-of-egypt.question: What would it look like to turn a small part of your day, ten minutes, entirely towards God? When could you begin, today?
mary-of-egypt.prayer: Lord, Mary came to you with a long past and spent the rest of her life in your company. Whatever I bring, let me begin again today. Turn my love towards you, and keep me praying until the end. Amen.
mary-of-egypt.midday: This morning: Mary of Egypt, whose whole life became prayer. Could you give God one quiet minute this afternoon?
mary-of-egypt.evening: Today's story was Mary of Egypt. Is there something in your past you think puts you out of reach? Hand it over tonight, and begin again tomorrow.

music.why: Allegri set Psalm 51, the great prayer of a heart turning back to God: “Have mercy on me”, the prayer Mary prayed with her whole life.

paras: One of the Pharisees invited him to eat with him. He entered into the Pharisee’s house, and sat at the table.
Behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she knew that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment.
Standing behind at his feet weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment.
Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw it, he said to himself, “This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.”
Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.”
He said, “Teacher, say on.”
“A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.
When they couldn’t pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?”
Simon answered, “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.”
He said to him, “You have judged correctly.”

Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head.
You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet.
You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.”
He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”
Those who sat at the table with him began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?”
He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

read.why: Read the gospel story Mary's life has always been set beside: a woman known for her past comes into a dinner party uninvited, weeps over Jesus' feet and dries them with her hair, while the host looks on, appalled. Jesus tells him a story about two debts.

peter-by-the-lake.title: Breakfast on the beach
peter-by-the-lake.line: Peter, who had denied Jesus three times, hears that it is the Lord and throws himself into the sea.

story.retell: After Easter, Peter went back to fishing on the Sea of Galilee with six others. They caught nothing all night. At dawn a man on the beach told them to cast the net on the right side of the boat, and it filled. One of them said it was the Lord. Peter jumped into the water and made for the shore. Round a charcoal fire, after breakfast, Jesus asked him three times whether he loved him, and three times gave him work to do.
story.verse: That disciple therefore whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!” So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around himself (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea.

peter-by-the-lake.artLink: Alessandro Magnasco, a Genoese painter of wild, flickering landscapes, painted Christ on the shore of Galilee in about 1740.
peter-by-the-lake.see: Two small figures face each other across surging green and turquoise waves in a cove, framed by dark, gnarled trees that curve towards each other like brackets. Jesus stands barefoot on the shore at the lower left, his blue cloak lifting in the wind, one hand held out. Waist-deep in the water, the second man lunges towards him, arms spread wide, his yellow and blue robes whirling. On the beach lie jugs and bits of timber. At the mouth of the cove, barely visible, a pale boat with a man leaning over the side.
peter-by-the-lake.meaning: The last time Peter stood by a charcoal fire, he swore three times that he had never known Jesus. Now, by another fire, he is asked three times whether he loves him. Jesus does not make him grovel. He gives him breakfast and a job. A witness is often someone who has failed in public and been given back their life. Peter spent the rest of his telling people what he had seen, and never hid where he had fallen.

echo.when: Jerusalem, the night of Jesus' arrest
echo.text: While Jesus was being questioned inside the high priest's house, Peter stood in the courtyard warming himself at a charcoal fire. A servant girl asked if he was one of Jesus' disciples. He said he was not. Others asked. Twice more he said no. Then a cock crowed.
echo.link: John uses the same rare word for both fires, a charcoal fire, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Three denials by the first fire; three answers of love by the second. The place of failure becomes the place of healing.

peter-by-the-lake.question: Is there a failure you still carry, something you said or didn't say? What would it be like to let it be met with breakfast, not a lecture?
peter-by-the-lake.prayer: Lord, you met Peter by a fire and asked only whether he loved him. You know everything. You know that I love you, even when I let you down. Give me back my work, and let me feed someone today. Amen.
peter-by-the-lake.midday: This morning: Peter, forgiven over breakfast. Who could you feed or look after this afternoon?
peter-by-the-lake.evening: Today's story was breakfast by the lake. Where did you fall short today? Can you hear the question underneath: do you love me?

music.why: A hymn about the world made new at daybreak, which is exactly when Peter was given his second start.

paras: After these things, Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself this way.
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.”
They told him, “We are also coming with you.” They immediately went out, and entered into the boat. That night, they caught nothing.
But when day had already come, Jesus stood on the beach, yet the disciples didn’t know that it was Jesus.
Jesus therefore said to them, “Children, have you anything to eat?”
They answered him, “No.”
He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.”
They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.
That disciple therefore whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!”
So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around himself (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea.
But the other disciples came in the little boat (for they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish.
So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it.
Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of one hundred fifty-three great fish. Even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn.
Jesus said to them, “Come and eat breakfast!”
None of the disciples dared inquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord.
Then Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise.
This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.
So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?”
He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.”
He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?”
He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.”
He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”
He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?”
Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.”
Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”

read.why: This week is about witnesses: people who saw something and said so, whatever it cost. Read the chapter to verse 19, where Jesus tells Peter how he will one day die, and then says, “Follow me”: the same call Peter first heard by this lake.

paul-in-prison.title: I have kept the faith
paul-in-prison.line: Old, in chains and nearly alone, Paul writes his last letter.

story.retell: Paul had spent thirty years telling the world about Jesus, and now he was in prison again, expecting to die. In the last letter that bears his name, he writes to his young friend Timothy. Most of his companions have gone; only Luke is with him. At his first hearing no one stood by him. He asks Timothy to come quickly and to bring the cloak he left behind, and his books. And he looks back on his life without regret.
story.verse: I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.

paul-in-prison.artLink: Rembrandt, or his workshop, painted Paul at his desk in about 1657, and signed it on the desktop.
paul-in-prison.see: An old man with a long, shaggy beard sits in a heavy wooden armchair in a shadowy room, his head resting in his left hand. In his right hand, lowered to his knee, is a quill. He wears a loose brown robe over rust red, and a cap on the back of his head. On the desk beside him lies a stack of papers. Behind it, leaning against the wall, is the hilt of a long sword, the traditional sign of how Paul died. He is not writing. He is looking off to the right, thinking.
paul-in-prison.meaning: We often imagine witnesses as bold and surrounded by crowds. Paul's last letter is quieter. He is cold, he misses his books, and his friends have left. Yet he can say: I kept the faith. A witness is not someone who never felt abandoned. It is someone who kept going when they did, and who says, as Paul does, that the Lord stood by him when no one else would.

echo.text: Boethius had been one of the most powerful men in Rome. Accused of treason, he was imprisoned and awaiting execution. In his cell he wrote a book in which Philosophy appears to him as a woman, sits by his bed, and teaches him that fortune's gifts were never truly his, and that the highest good cannot be taken away.
echo.link: Two men write in prison as their friends fall away. Boethius is consoled by Philosophy. Paul is consoled by a person: “the Lord stood by me and strengthened me.”

paul-in-prison.question: Who in your life has kept faith over a long time, quietly, when it was hard? Could you write to them this week, a card or a letter, to tell them it mattered?
paul-in-prison.prayer: Lord, you stood by Paul when everyone else had gone. Stand by me, and by anyone who feels alone today. Help me to keep the faith, and to finish what you have given me to do. Amen.
paul-in-prison.midday: This morning: Paul in prison, writing his last letter. Is there someone you could send a short message of encouragement this afternoon?
paul-in-prison.evening: Today's story was Paul's last letter. Did you keep faith today in something small? Who stood by you?

music.why: Brahms chose Paul's words for the sixth movement of his Requiem, where death is “swallowed up in victory”, from 1 Corinthians 15.

paras: I command you therefore before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his Kingdom:
preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort with all patience and teaching.
For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine, but having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers after their own lusts,
and will turn away their ears from the truth, and turn away to fables.
But you be sober in all things, suffer hardship, do the work of an evangelist, and fulfill your ministry.
For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come.
I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.
From now on, the crown of righteousness is stored up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.
Be diligent to come to me soon,
for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; and Titus to Dalmatia.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.
But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.
Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come, and the books, especially the parchments.
Alexander, the coppersmith, did much evil to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds,
of whom you also must beware; for he greatly opposed our words.
At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them.
But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear. So I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me for his heavenly Kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the house of Onesiphorus.
Erastus remained at Corinth, but I left Trophimus at Miletus sick.
Be diligent to come before winter. Eubulus salutes you, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers.
The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.

read.why: Read the whole last chapter, right down to the greetings at the end. Even facing death, Paul is thinking about other people: who is where, who needs help, who should come before winter.

esther-for-such-a-time.title: For such a time
esther-for-such-a-time.line: A young queen must decide whether to speak up, at the risk of her life.

story.retell: Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, had become queen of Persia without anyone at court knowing who her people were. Then a royal decree ordered the killing of every Jew in the empire. Mordecai begged her to plead with the king. But anyone who went to the king without being summoned could be put to death. Mordecai sent back his answer, and Esther made her choice: fast with me for three days, she said, and then I will go.
story.verse: For if you remain silent now, then relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?

esther-for-such-a-time.artLink: Hendrick van Steenwijk the Younger, best known for painting church interiors, set Esther and Mordecai inside a dark church and signed it in 1616.
esther-for-such-a-time.see: A man and a woman stand by a column under a pointed arch in a dark stone church, lit only by the candle he holds. Mordecai, in a red cloak lined with white fur and a tall split cap, has his back half towards us; he leans in and holds her hand. Esther's face is caught in the candlelight, her eyes cast down. She wears a green bodice, a starched lace collar and pink sleeves. Beyond them the vaults vanish into shadow, and the painter has signed the floor as if he had carved it: “H.V.S. 1616.”
esther-for-such-a-time.meaning: Esther had every reason to stay quiet. She was safe as long as no one knew. Mordecai's question cuts through that: perhaps this is why you are where you are. Bearing witness is not always preaching. Sometimes it is simply refusing to stay silent when someone else is in danger, and accepting the cost. And Esther did not go in alone. She asked her people to fast with her first. Courage is easier when it is shared.

echo.text: King Creon forbids anyone to bury the body of Polynices, a rebel, on pain of death. Polynices' sister Antigone buries him anyway. Brought before the king, she tells him that his decree cannot override the unwritten laws of the gods, and accepts her sentence.
echo.link: Two young women stand before kings and break a royal law for the sake of others. Antigone goes to her fate alone. Esther goes in having asked her whole people to fast with her, and says: if I perish, I perish.

esther-for-such-a-time.question: Is there someone who needs you to speak up for them, at work, in your family or on your street? What is one thing you could say this week that you have been keeping quiet?
esther-for-such-a-time.prayer: Lord, you put Esther where she was for such a time as this. Show me why I am where I am. Give me courage to speak for those who cannot, and friends to stand with me when I do. Amen.
esther-for-such-a-time.midday: This morning: Esther deciding to speak. Is there a quiet word that needs saying this afternoon?
esther-for-such-a-time.evening: Today's story was Esther. Was there a moment today when you could have spoken up for someone? What would help you do it next time?

music.why: An ancient prayer to a queen, sung by monks at the close of day, in which those who pray call themselves exiles; Esther was a queen among exiles, and pleaded for them.

paras: Now when Mordecai found out all that was done, Mordecai tore his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, and wailed loudly and bitterly.
He came even before the king’s gate, for no one is allowed inside the king’s gate clothed with sackcloth.
In every province, wherever the king’s commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
Esther’s maidens and her eunuchs came and told her this, and the queen was exceedingly grieved. She sent clothing to Mordecai, to replace his sackcloth; but he didn’t receive it.
Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs, whom he had appointed to attend her, and commanded him to go to Mordecai, to find out what this was, and why it was.
So Hathach went out to Mordecai, to city square which was before the king’s gate.
Mordecai told him of all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of the money that Haman had promised to pay to the king’s treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.

He also gave him the copy of the writing of the decree that was given out in Susa to destroy them, to show it to Esther, and to declare it to her, and to urge her to go in to the king, to make supplication to him, and to make request before him, for her people.
Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach, and gave him a message to Mordecai:

“All the king’s servants, and the people of the king’s provinces, know, that whoever, whether man or woman, comes to the king into the inner court without being called, there is one law for him, that he be put to death, except those to whom the king might hold out the golden scepter, that he may live. I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days.”
They told Esther’s words to Mordecai.
Then Mordecai asked them to return this answer to Esther: “Don’t think to yourself that you will escape in the king’s house any more than all the Jews.

For if you remain silent now, then relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
Then Esther asked them to answer Mordecai,

“Go, gather together all the Jews who are present in Susa, and fast for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day. I and my maidens will also fast the same way. Then I will go in to the king, which is against the law; and if I perish, I perish.”
So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.

read.why: Read the whole chapter, from Mordecai in sackcloth at the palace gate to Esther's decision. The book of Esther never once mentions God by name, yet everything turns on a fast, and on someone being in the right place at the right time.

joan-on-trial.title: Answering the judges
joan-on-trial.line: A nineteen-year-old who cannot read stands alone before a court of learned men.

story.ref: The trial of Joan of Arc, Rouen, 1431
story.retell: Joan had led French soldiers to raise the siege of Orléans and seen the king crowned at Reims. Captured and handed to the English, she was tried for heresy in Rouen in 1431 by a court of churchmen and scholars. She was nineteen, chained, without a lawyer, and could not read. They tried to trap her. Asked whether she knew she was in God's grace, a question with no safe answer, she said: if I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God keep me there. She was burned on 30 May. Twenty-five years later another church court overturned the verdict.
story.verse: But when they deliver you up, don’t be anxious how or what you will say, for it will be given you in that hour what you will say.

joan-on-trial.artLink: Louis-Maurice Boutet de Monvel painted Joan's trial in about 1909–10, the last of his six scenes from her life.
joan-on-trial.see: A young woman with short blond hair stands alone in the middle of a dim, wood-panelled room, facing dozens of men. One hand is clutched to her chest; the other reaches out, fingers curving up, her brow furrowed and lips parted. She wears a blue tunic, grey stockings and black shoes, and from a metal band at her waist hang a chain and a manacle. Around the walls sit rows of men in clerics' robes and hats. In the corner, on a high throne, sits a man in a gold mitre. Behind her, a clerk writes at a green table, and soldiers with halberds wait.
joan-on-trial.meaning: Joan had no education, no advocate and no friends in the room. What she had was the truth as she knew it, and a refusal to say anything else. Jesus told his followers that when they were dragged before courts, they would be given the words. Joan's answers are still read today, and many are simple, even funny. A witness does not need to be clever. She needs to be honest, and to keep standing there.

echo.when: Jerusalem, a few weeks after the first Easter
echo.text: Peter and John, two fishermen, were arrested and brought before the same council that had condemned Jesus. They answered so boldly that the council were astonished, seeing they were uneducated, ordinary men. Ordered to stop speaking about Jesus, they replied that they could not help telling what they had seen and heard.
echo.link: In both courts the learned are baffled by the unlearned. Peter and John, and Joan fourteen centuries later, had no training in argument, only something they had seen and could not deny.

joan-on-trial.question: Is there a question you dread being asked about what you believe? How would you answer it honestly, in one or two plain sentences?
joan-on-trial.prayer: Lord, you gave Joan words when she stood alone. When I am questioned or mocked for what I believe, give me honesty rather than cleverness, and peace rather than fear. If I am not in your grace, put me there; if I am, keep me there. Amen.
joan-on-trial.midday: This morning: Joan before her judges. Is there a plain, honest answer you could give this afternoon?
joan-on-trial.evening: Today's story was Joan's trial. Were you asked about anything that matters to you today? Did you answer honestly?

music.why: William Byrd, a Catholic in Protestant England, wrote this Mass for worship that had to be held in secret: faith kept under hostile questioning.

paras: “Behold, I send you out as sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
But beware of men: for they will deliver you up to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you.
Yes, and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the nations.
But when they deliver you up, don’t be anxious how or what you will say, for it will be given you in that hour what you will say.
For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.
