“Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child. Children will rise up against parents, and cause them to be put to death.
You will be hated by all men for my name’s sake, but he who endures to the end will be saved.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee into the next, for most certainly I tell you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel until the Son of Man has come.
“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord.
It is enough for the disciple that he be like his teacher, and the servant like his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household!
Therefore don’t be afraid of them, for there is nothing covered that will not be revealed; and hidden that will not be known.
What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in the ear, proclaim on the housetops.
Don’t be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul. Rather, fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.
“Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls on the ground apart from your Father’s will,
but the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
Therefore don’t be afraid. You are of more value than many sparrows.
Everyone therefore who confesses me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven.
But whoever denies me before men, I will also deny him before my Father who is in heaven.

read.why: Read Jesus' warning to his first friends before he sent them out: sheep among wolves, dragged before governors and kings. It sounds grim, until the end, where he tells them not to be afraid, because even the sparrows are counted.

centurion-at-the-cross.title: What the soldier saw
centurion-at-the-cross.line: The Roman officer in charge of the execution watches Jesus die, and says what he has seen.

story.retell: At noon a darkness came over the land. At three in the afternoon Jesus cried out in the words of a psalm, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Someone held up sour wine on a sponge. Then, with a loud cry, he died. The centurion, the officer in charge, was standing right in front of the cross. He had surely seen many men die. Watching this one, he said what no one else there would say.
story.verse: When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

centurion-at-the-cross.artLink: Lucas Cranach the Elder, Martin Luther's friend in Wittenberg, painted the soldier's words beside his mouth in 1536.
centurion-at-the-cross.see: Three men hang on rough crosses on a low, stony hill. Jesus, in the centre, wears a crown of thorns; his head has fallen to one side and his loincloth streams in the wind. At the foot of the cross a soldier in grey armour and a red hat ringed with white feathers sits on a rearing grey horse, looking up, mouth open, two fingers raised. Beside his mouth, in pale yellow letters, are his words in Luther's German: truly this man was God's Son. Above the cross is Jesus' last prayer: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit. The sky behind runs from yellow and orange into heavy black cloud.
centurion-at-the-cross.meaning: In Mark's Gospel, the first human being to call Jesus the Son of God is not a disciple. It is the officer who ran his execution. He had no scriptures and no reason to believe. He simply watched how this man died and told the truth about it. That is the heart of witness: not what you were taught to say, but what you saw. Sometimes the clearest witnesses are the people nobody expected to speak.

echo.text: Glaucon challenges Socrates with a thought experiment. Imagine a perfectly just man whom everyone believes to be unjust. He would be whipped, tortured and bound, and at last, after every kind of suffering, impaled or crucified. Would justice still be worth having?
echo.link: Four centuries before Golgotha, Plato imagined the truly good man dying a criminal's death. The centurion saw it happen, and recognised what he was looking at.

centurion-at-the-cross.question: Who around you is easy to overlook, but sees more clearly than you'd expect? And is there something you have seen with your own eyes that you have never said out loud?
centurion-at-the-cross.prayer: Lord Jesus, a soldier watched you die and told the truth about what he saw. Open my eyes at the foot of your cross, and give me the honesty to say what I see. Father, into your hands I commend my spirit. Amen.
centurion-at-the-cross.midday: This morning: a soldier at the cross who said what he saw. What have you seen today that deserves saying?
centurion-at-the-cross.evening: Today's story was the centurion. Where did you see goodness today in an unexpected place? Did you name it?

music.why: The spiritual asks the question the centurion could have answered: were you there when they crucified my Lord?

paras: They compelled one passing by, coming from the country, Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to go with them, that he might bear his cross.
They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.”
They offered him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he didn’t take it.
Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take.
It was the third hour, and they crucified him.
The superscription of his accusation was written over him, “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
With him they crucified two robbers; one on his right hand, and one on his left.
The Scripture was fulfilled, which says, “He was counted with transgressors.”
Those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads, and saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple, and build it in three days,
save yourself, and come down from the cross!”
Likewise, also the chief priests mocking among themselves with the scribes said, “He saved others. He can’t save himself.
Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him.” Those who were crucified with him also insulted him.
When the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.
At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Some of those who stood by, when they heard it, said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.”
One ran, and filling a sponge full of vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”
Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and gave up the spirit.
The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.
When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

read.why: Friday is the day Christians remember the cross. Read Mark's account, from Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross to the centurion's words: short, spare, and seen almost entirely through the eyes of bystanders.

anthony-finds-paul.title: The hidden saint
anthony-finds-paul.line: Anthony, the most famous hermit of his day, walks across the desert to find a holier man no one has heard of.

story.ref: Jerome, The Life of Paul the First Hermit, about AD 375
story.retell: Anthony had lived in the Egyptian desert for decades and was famous across the Christian world. When he was about ninety, Jerome tells us, he began to think no one had served God in the desert longer than he had. Then he learned in a dream of an older man, deeper in the wilderness. He set out walking, found the cave, and met Paul, who had lived there unknown for nearly a century. They embraced, ate the bread a raven brought them, and talked of God. Soon afterwards Paul died, and Anthony buried him.
story.verse: of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and the holes of the earth.

anthony-finds-paul.artLink: The Sienese painter known as the Master of the Osservanza painted Anthony's walk in about 1430–35, as one of a series on his life.
anthony-finds-paul.see: A pebbled path winds up through stylised trees, and Anthony, white-bearded, barefoot, in a black robe with a coral-pink cloak, appears on it three times. In the distance he sets out with a walking stick. Higher up, on a ridge, he meets a centaur holding a palm frond. And closest to us, at the mouth of a dark cave, he embraces a bearded man with long, curly blond hair in white robes, also haloed: Paul. Their two walking sticks lie on the ground at their feet. Above the trees is a sliver of gold sky.
anthony-finds-paul.meaning: Most saints are hidden. The world never hears of them, and they do not mind. Anthony, who had disciples and visitors and fame, needed to meet a man who had none of these, to be reminded that holiness is not the same as being known. Tomorrow is All Saints' Day, and this is its quiet secret: the great company of witnesses is made mostly of people nobody wrote down.

echo.text: Croesus, the richest king in the world, shows the Athenian wise man Solon his treasuries and asks who is the happiest man he has ever seen, expecting to hear his own name. Solon names Tellus, an ordinary Athenian who lived well, saw his grandchildren grow up and died bravely for his city. Croesus has never heard of him.
echo.link: The king and the famous hermit both have to learn the same thing: the best lives are often lived out of sight. Solon's Tellus and Anthony's Paul are known only because someone else went to the trouble of telling.

anthony-finds-paul.question: Who is a hidden saint you have known: someone faithful, kind and largely unnoticed? Could you tell someone about them this weekend, or thank them if they are still alive?
anthony-finds-paul.prayer: Lord, you know the hidden saints the world has never heard of. Thank you for the faithful people who have shaped my life without anyone noticing. Make me content to be faithful unseen. Amen.
anthony-finds-paul.midday: This morning: Anthony walking across the desert to find a forgotten holy man. Who is quietly faithful near you?
anthony-finds-paul.evening: Today's story was the hidden saint. Tomorrow is All Saints' Day. Tonight, name one unknown, faithful person you are grateful for.

music.why: Arvo Pärt's Spiegel im Spiegel is almost nothing, a few notes repeated in stillness, the musical equivalent of a life lived quietly in the desert.

paras: By faith, Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were not afraid of the king’s commandment.
By faith, Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter,
choosing rather to share ill treatment with God’s people than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time,
considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the reward.
By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.
By faith, he kept the Passover, and the sprinkling of the blood, that the destroyer of the firstborn should not touch them.
By faith, they passed through the Red Sea as on dry land. When the Egyptians tried to do so, they were swallowed up.
By faith, the walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been encircled for seven days.
By faith, Rahab the prostitute didn’t perish with those who were disobedient, having received the spies in peace.
What more shall I say? For the time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets,
who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked out righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,
quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, from weakness were made strong, grew mighty in war, and caused foreign armies to flee.
Women received their dead by resurrection. Others were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection.
Others were tried by mocking and scourging, yes, moreover by bonds and imprisonment.
They were stoned. They were sawn apart. They were tempted. They were slain with the sword. They went around in sheep skins and in goat skins; being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated—
of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and the holes of the earth.
These all, having had testimony given to them through their faith, didn’t receive the promise,
God having provided some better thing concerning us, so that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us,
looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.

read.why: Read the end of the great roll call of faith in Hebrews: names you know, then people with no names at all, who lived in caves and deserts. It ends with the image for tomorrow, All Saints: a great cloud of witnesses, surrounding us as we run.

all-saints-great-multitude.title: A great multitude
all-saints-great-multitude.line: All Saints' Day: a man exiled for his witness looks up and sees a crowd that no one could count.

story.retell: A follower of Jesus called John had been exiled to the island of Patmos, he writes, “because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ”. There, one Sunday, he saw visions. In one he looked and saw a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, dressed in white and holding palm branches. An elder told him who they were: people who had come through great suffering. Now God would shelter them, and wipe every tear from their eyes.
story.verse: After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude, which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.

all-saints-great-multitude.artLink: Titian and his workshop painted John's vision on Patmos in about 1553–55 for a ceiling in Venice, which is why we look up at him from below.
all-saints-great-multitude.see: We look up from far below at an old man on a rocky ledge. He half crouches, both hands raised with the palms up, and turns his head back to gaze into the sky. He has a short, curly white beard and wears rose pink, with crimson drapery billowing round him. Beside him lie a book with a red cover and a brown eagle, the old sign of Saint John. Above, in a bank of silvery clouds lit with pale yellow, a white-bearded figure in plum purple raises his hand in blessing, surrounded by six winged children.
all-saints-great-multitude.meaning: Today is All Saints' Day, when Western churches remember all the holy people who have gone before: the famous few and the vast number nobody remembers. (The Orthodox keep their feast of All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost.) John saw them as a crowd too big to count, from every nation and language, and each had come through something hard. Saints are not people who never struggled. They are witnesses who kept going. And the vision says they are not lost. They are home, and every tear is dried.

echo.from: Cicero, On the Republic, Book 6 (The Dream of Scipio)
echo.text: In a dream, the Roman soldier Scipio is taken up among the stars, where he meets his famous grandfather and his own father, long dead. They show him the Milky Way, where those who served justly and loved their country live on in light. From there, Rome looks tiny.
echo.link: Cicero imagined the great and good shining among the stars. John's multitude is wider: no one can count them, and they come from every nation and language, not only the famous and the Roman.

all-saints-great-multitude.question: Who is one ordinary saint you have known, someone whose goodness you still remember? Give thanks for them today, and tell someone about them.
all-saints-great-multitude.prayer: God of every nation, thank you for the great multitude who have gone before us, and for the ones I have known and loved by name. Keep me among your witnesses, bring me home at the last, and wipe away every tear. Amen.
all-saints-great-multitude.midday: This morning: the great multitude, too many to count. Whose faithfulness are you standing on this afternoon?
all-saints-great-multitude.evening: Today was All Saints' Day. Tonight, name before God the people you have loved who have died, and give thanks for each one.

music.why: The hymn of All Saints' Day, by William Walsham How, sung to Ralph Vaughan Williams's tune Sine Nomine.

paras: After this, I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, so that no wind would blow on the earth, or on the sea, or on any tree.
I saw another angel ascend from the sunrise, having the seal of the living God. He cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea,
saying, “Don’t harm the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees, until we have sealed the bondservants of our God on their foreheads!”
I heard the number of those who were sealed, one hundred forty-four thousand, sealed out of every tribe of the children of Israel:

of the tribe of Judah twelve thousand were sealed,
of the tribe of Reuben twelve thousand,
of the tribe of Gad twelve thousand,

of the tribe of Asher twelve thousand,
of the tribe of Naphtali twelve thousand,
of the tribe of Manasseh twelve thousand,

of the tribe of Simeon twelve thousand,
of the tribe of Levi twelve thousand,
of the tribe of Issachar twelve thousand,

of the tribe of Zebulun twelve thousand,
of the tribe of Joseph twelve thousand, and
of the tribe of Benjamin twelve thousand were sealed.

After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude, which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.
They cried with a loud voice, saying, “Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”
All the angels were standing around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell on their faces before his throne, and worshiped God,
saying, “Amen! Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might, be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”
One of the elders answered, saying to me, “These who are arrayed in the white robes, who are they, and where did they come from?”
I told him, “My lord, you know.”
He said to me, “These are those who came out of the great suffering.They washed their robes, and made them white in the Lamb’s blood.
Therefore they are before the throne of God, they serve him day and night in his temple. He who sits on the throne will spread his tabernacle over them.
They will never be hungry or thirsty any more. The sun won’t beat on them, nor any heat;
for the Lamb who is in the middle of the throne shepherds them and leads them to springs of life-giving waters. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

read.why: Read the whole chapter. First John hears a number, a hundred and forty-four thousand from the tribes of Israel. Then he looks, and sees a crowd that no one could count. It ends a week of witnesses with their homecoming.

all-souls-the-burial.title: Two men and a burial
all-souls-the-burial.line: On All Souls' Day, two quiet followers ask for a body and bury it with care.

story.retell: When Jesus had died, two men who had followed him in secret came out into the open. Joseph of Arimathea went to Pilate and asked for the body. Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night, brought a huge weight of myrrh and aloes. Together they wrapped him in linen and laid him in a new tomb in a garden. Today is All Souls' Day, when Catholics, many Anglicans and Lutherans remember everyone who has died; the Orthodox keep several Saturdays of the dead through the year instead.
story.verse: So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury.

all-souls-the-burial.artLink: A painter close to Fra Angelico, perhaps Angelico himself, painted the burial in about 1450.
all-souls-the-burial.see: Two old men carry the body of Jesus on a yellow cloth towards the opening of a stone tomb. Just beyond, his mother bends to look at his face, held up by two other women, and a young man in pink stands with his head lowered and his hands clasped. On our side, one woman kneels and wipes his feet; another sits with her robe pulled over her head and her face in her hands. On the grass between them lie a hammer, the crown of thorns and a nail puller. Far off, on a green hill, three crosses still stand. Everyone here is doing something small and careful.
all-souls-the-burial.meaning: Joseph and Nicodemus could do nothing to save Jesus. They could only do the last thing: take his body down, wash it, wrap it and lay it somewhere decent. It cost them; until then they had kept their faith hidden. Caring for the dead is one of the oldest signs of being human, and on All Souls' Day Christians do a version of it, saying aloud the names of those they have lost and placing them in God's hands. Remembering is not a way of holding on. It is a way of handing over, with love.

echo.text: King Creon orders that the body of Polynices, who died attacking the city, be left unburied for the dogs and birds. His sister Antigone buries him anyway, scattering dust over him with her own hands. When she is caught, she says she obeyed laws older than any king's: the unwritten laws of the gods, which no one can overrule.
echo.link: Antigone and the two secret disciples all risk something to give a dead man a burial. In both stories, care for the dead is a duty love will not leave undone.

all-souls-the-burial.question: Who have you lost whom you would like to remember today? Could you say their name aloud, light a candle for them, or tell someone one thing about them?
all-souls-the-burial.prayer: Lord, Joseph and Nicodemus gave you the last kindness they could. I bring you the names of those I have lost. Keep them in your care, give rest to the dead and comfort to those who miss them, and hold us all until we meet again. Amen.
all-souls-the-burial.midday: This morning: two men burying their friend with care. Hold one name in mind this afternoon, and give thanks for them.
all-souls-the-burial.evening: Today's story was a burial in a garden. Whom did you remember today? Did you tell anyone about them?

music.why: Fauré's Requiem is a Mass for the dead, the music of days like All Souls'; it ends with “In Paradisum”, the prayer sung as a body is carried from church to the grave.

paras: Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation Day, so that the bodies wouldn’t remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a special one), asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away.
Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him;
but when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they didn’t break his legs.
However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe.
For these things happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled, “A bone of him will not be broken.”
Again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.”

After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gave him permission. He came therefore and took away his body.
Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, also came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds.
So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid.
Then because of the Jews’ Preparation Day (for the tomb was near at hand) they laid Jesus there.
Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb.
Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”
Therefore Peter and the other disciple went out, and they went toward the tomb.
They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first.
Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in.
Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying,
and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.
So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed.
For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.

read.why: We begin a week about death and hope where every Christian funeral begins: with a body, grief, and people doing what love asks. Read on past the burial into the next chapter, to the empty grave clothes, because for Christians that is where All Souls' Day points.

widow-of-zarephath.title: The last handful
widow-of-zarephath.line: A widow gathers sticks to cook her last meal, and a stranger asks her to share it.

story.retell: In a long drought, the prophet Elijah was sent to the town of Zarephath, outside Israel. At the gate he met a widow gathering sticks and asked her for water and a little bread. She told him she had only a handful of flour and a drop of oil left: enough for one last meal for herself and her son, and then they expected to die. Elijah told her not to be afraid, to make him a small loaf first, and promised that her jar would not run out. She did, and it did not.
story.verse: Behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and bake it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.

widow-of-zarephath.artLink: Cornelis van Poelenburch, a Dutch painter who had worked in Rome, painted the meeting at the gate in about 1630.
widow-of-zarephath.see: In a landscape of crumbling ruins, an old man with a grey beard and a scarlet cloak holds out his hand towards a young woman kneeling at his feet. Her arms are spread wide as she looks at his hand. Beside her, a boy hugs a bundle of sticks: the firewood for their last meal. Behind them, ordinary people go about their day across the fields, one woman carrying a load on her head. Nobody else notices that anything is happening.
widow-of-zarephath.meaning: The widow is not grieving yet, but she is preparing to. She has done the sums and they come out at zero. Then a stranger asks her for the very thing she cannot spare. The story does not say her fear was foolish; it says she was met inside it. Hope here is not a feeling that things will be fine. It is being given enough for today, and then enough again tomorrow. Later in the chapter, when her son falls ill and dies, Elijah carries him upstairs, prays, and brings him back to her alive.

echo.when: Nazareth, about AD 30; written about AD 80
echo.text: Preaching in his home town, Jesus reminded his neighbours of this very widow. There were many widows in Israel in the famine, he said, but Elijah was sent to none of them, only to a foreign woman in Zarephath. The congregation was so angry that they drove him out of town to the edge of a cliff.
echo.link: Jesus chose this widow as his example of whom God goes looking for: someone outside, at the end of her resources, expecting nothing. His hearers did not like it any more than we like to be told who God's favourites are.

widow-of-zarephath.question: Is there somewhere in your life where you have done the sums and they come out at zero? What would it look like to give a little from it anyway, today?
widow-of-zarephath.prayer: God of the widow at the gate, you know what I have left and how little it looks. Meet me in my fear. Give me enough for today, and the courage to share it, and teach me to trust you for tomorrow. Amen.
widow-of-zarephath.midday: This morning: a widow with one handful of flour, asked to share it. What could you give this afternoon from what feels like too little?
widow-of-zarephath.evening: Today's story was the last handful. Where did you find there was enough today, when you had expected not?

music.why: Mendelssohn's Elijah sets this chapter: in Part One the widow pleads with Elijah over her son, he prays, and the child revives.

paras: Elijah the Tishbite, who was one of the settlers of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
Then Yahweh’s word came to him, saying,
“Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan.
You shall drink from the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
So he went and did according to Yahweh’s word; for he went and lived by the brook Cherith that is before the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.
After a while, the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.
Yahweh’s word came to him, saying,
“Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.”

So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. He called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a jar, that I may drink.”
As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of bread in your hand.”

She said, “As Yahweh your God lives, I don’t have a cake, but a handful of meal in a jar, and a little oil in a jar. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and bake it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.”
Elijah said to her, “Don’t be afraid. Go and do as you have said; but make me a little cake from it first, and bring it out to me, and afterward make some for you and for your son.
For Yahweh, the God of Israel says, ‘The jar of meal will not run out, and the jar of oil will not fail, until the day that Yahweh sends rain on the earth.’ ”
She went and did according to the saying of Elijah; and she, and he, and her house, ate many days.
The jar of meal didn’t run out, and the jar of oil didn’t fail, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke by Elijah.
After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became sick; and his sickness was so severe that there was no breath left in him.
She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!”
He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed.
He cried to Yahweh, and said, “Yahweh my God, have you also brought evil on the widow with whom I am staying, by killing her son?”
He stretched himself on the child three times, and cried to Yahweh, and said, “Yahweh my God, please let this child’s soul come into him again.”
Yahweh listened to the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.
Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
The woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that Yahweh’s word in your mouth is truth.”

read.why: Yesterday we began with a burial. Today's chapter goes from a woman expecting to die to a mother handed her living son. Read all of it, and notice that hope comes in small daily portions before it comes as a miracle.

lazarus-unbound.title: Unbind him
lazarus-unbound.line: Jesus weeps at his friend's grave, then calls him out and tells the others to set him free.

story.retell: Jesus's friend Lazarus had been dead four days when Jesus reached Bethany. His sisters, Martha and Mary, each said the same thing to him: if you had been here, he would not have died. Seeing Mary and her friends weeping, Jesus was deeply moved, and he wept too. Then he had the stone rolled away and called, “Lazarus, come out!” The dead man came out still wrapped in his grave clothes.
story.verse: He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”

lazarus-unbound.artLink: Benozzo Gozzoli painted this in the mid 1490s, near the end of his long working life.
lazarus-unbound.see: A crowd in rich robes of pink, teal and gold presses round the mouth of a cave in a hilly landscape. In the opening stands a man wrapped in off-white strips of cloth, looking out at them, while two men beside him are unwinding his wrappings. Facing him, in blue and gold, Jesus raises one arm, a golden book in his other hand, with his friends gathered behind him. Beyond them is a city of white houses with red roofs, palm trees and a pink-clouded sky. The miracle has happened; now there is work for other hands.
lazarus-unbound.meaning: Two things in this story are easy to miss. The first is that Jesus wept, even though he knew what he was about to do. Christian hope does not skip grief or tell people not to cry. The second is that Jesus did not unwrap Lazarus himself. He gave that job to the people standing round: free him, let him go. Hope for the dead belongs to God, but there is a part for us, here and now, in helping each other out of whatever still binds us.

echo.when: Athens, 399 BC; written some years later
echo.text: On the day of his execution, Socrates drinks the hemlock calmly. His friends break down: one covers his face and weeps, another howls aloud. Socrates scolds them gently. He had sent the women away, he says, precisely to avoid this. A man should die in peace; be quiet and bear up.
echo.link: The greatest death in Greek philosophy asks the mourners to stop crying. At Lazarus's tomb, Jesus does the opposite: he weeps with the mourners, and only then speaks the word of life.

lazarus-unbound.question: Is there someone grieving near you whom you could simply sit with, without trying to fix it? And is there something that still binds you, that you need someone else's help to take off?
lazarus-unbound.prayer: Lord Jesus, you wept at your friend's grave. Weep with me for those I have lost, and with those I know who are grieving. Call us out of what binds us, and give us the patience to unwrap one another, one strip at a time. Amen.
lazarus-unbound.midday: This morning: Jesus wept, then said “Free him, and let him go.” Whom could you help set free this afternoon?
lazarus-unbound.evening: Today's story was Lazarus unbound. Did you stay with anyone's sadness today, or let someone help you with yours?

music.why: Brahms wrote his Requiem not for the dead but to comfort the living, and it opens with “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted”: the mourners at Bethany.

paras: So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already.
Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away.
Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother.
Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house.
Therefore Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.
Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”
Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”
Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.”
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.
Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”
She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.”
When she had said this, she went away and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here and is calling you.”
When she heard this, she arose quickly and went to him.
Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him.
Then the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.”
Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.”
When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,
and said, “Where have you laid him?”
They told him, “Lord, come and see.”
Jesus wept.
The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!”
Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?”
Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.”
Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.”
Jesus said to her, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?”
So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me.
I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me.”
When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”
He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth.
Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”

read.why: Read the whole scene at Bethany: two sisters, the same grief said twice, Martha's hard-won faith, and the tears. In the middle is one of the boldest things Jesus ever said: “I am the resurrection and the life.”

behold-your-mother.title: Behold your mother
behold-your-mother.line: From the cross, Jesus gives his grieving mother and his friend to each other.

story.retell: At the foot of the cross stood a small group: Jesus's mother, two other Marys, and the friend John's Gospel calls the disciple whom Jesus loved. Dying, Jesus looked down at his mother and his friend. He said to her, “Woman, behold, your son!” and to him, “Behold, your mother!”
story.verse: Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.

behold-your-mother.artLink: Pietro Perugino painted this as the centre of a three-part altarpiece, in about 1482–85.
behold-your-mother.see: Jesus hangs on the cross high in the picture, head bowed, a small paper above him lettered INRI. Below, on the left, his mother stands with her head bowed and hands folded in prayer. On the right, a fair young man in pink over blue looks up at the cross, his fingers knotted together. Between them and behind them opens a calm landscape: a river winding past a town, boats, a man fishing off a bridge, blue mountains. The two mourners stand apart, each alone with their grief, in the moment before they are given to each other.
behold-your-mother.meaning: Even dying, Jesus thinks about who will look after the people left behind. He does not give his mother a reason for her loss, or his friend an explanation. He gives them each other. Grief is very often like that: what helps most is not an answer but a person, someone who takes us home. The Church began here, in a sense, with two mourners told to belong to each other.

echo.text: Plutarch was away from home when his two-year-old daughter Timoxena died. He wrote to his wife. He remembers how the little girl used to ask her nurse to feed not only other babies but even her toys, sharing what she loved. He thanks his wife for keeping the funeral simple and their house calm, and asks her to grieve without letting grief swallow the love they had.
echo.link: Plutarch's letter and the words from the cross do the same thing: they turn two people towards each other in a loss neither could carry alone.

behold-your-mother.question: Who in your life is grieving, or alone, and might need someone to “take them home”, even for an evening? Could you be that person this week?
behold-your-mother.prayer: Lord Jesus, even on the cross you cared for those you were leaving. Give me eyes for those who are alone in their grief. Make me someone who takes others home, and let me be taken home when it is my turn. Amen.
behold-your-mother.midday: This morning: a mother and a friend given to each other at the cross. Who could you belong to a little more this afternoon?
behold-your-mother.evening: Today's story was at the foot of the cross. Did anyone stand with you today, or did you stand with someone?

music.why: The spiritual asks one quiet question, “Were you there when they crucified my Lord?”, and puts you where Mary and the beloved disciple stood.

paras: So then he delivered him to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus and led him away.
He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”,
where they crucified him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle.
Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, “I am King of the Jews.” ’ ”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the coat. Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
Then they said to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says,

“They parted my garments among them.
For my cloak they cast lots.”
Therefore the soldiers did these things.
But standing by Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.
After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty.”
Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.

read.why: It is Friday, the day Christians remember the cross. Read John's account of the crucifixion, and notice how, in the middle of it, Jesus stops to look after two people.

job-and-his-daughters.title: After everything
job-and-his-daughters.line: Job, who lost everything, sits with the daughters born afterwards and gives them an inheritance.

story.retell: Job lost his wealth, his health and all ten of his children in a single season. His friends sat with him in silence for seven days, then spent many chapters arguing he must have deserved it. God said they were wrong. Job prayed for them anyway, and afterwards his life was rebuilt. He had seven sons and three daughters, and the book names the daughters, Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and says their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers.
story.verse: In all the land were no women found so beautiful as the daughters of Job. Their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.

job-and-his-daughters.artLink: William Blake painted Job and his daughters in 1799–1800; years later he made it the last-but-one of his engravings of the Book of Job.
job-and-his-daughters.see: An old man with a long white beard sits in a golden room, his arms held out wide to either side, fingers pointing, as if telling a story. Three young women lean in close: one on each side, one with her face resting on his knees and her back to us. Behind them, on the wall, are a round panel and two square ones, with figures we can barely make out. Job is not looking at the future here. He is telling his daughters what happened.
job-and-his-daughters.meaning: The end of Job is not tidy, and it is not meant to say that new children replaced the ones he lost. Nothing does. What it says is quieter: that life can grow again after devastation, and that a person who has been through the worst can still be generous. Job names his daughters, beautiful names, and gives them what daughters in his world did not usually get. The man who lost everything becomes a giver. Hope after grief is often like that: not forgetting, but telling the story to someone, and handing something on.

echo.from: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2
echo.text: Boethius had been one of the most powerful men in Rome. Accused of treason, he wrote this book in prison while awaiting execution. In it, Lady Philosophy visits him and reminds him that Fortune turns her wheel: whatever she gives, she can take away, and only what is truly ours cannot be taken.
echo.link: Job and Boethius both lost everything and both asked why. Neither got a neat answer, but each was visited in his darkness, and each found something no loss could take.

job-and-his-daughters.question: Is there a loss in your past that you have never told anyone the story of? Is there someone you could tell, or someone whose story you could ask to hear?
job-and-his-daughters.prayer: God of Job, you do not explain every sorrow, but you stay. For those who have lost much, bring life again in its time. Make me generous after loss, as Job was, and give me people to tell my story to. Amen.
job-and-his-daughters.midday: This morning: Job telling his story to his daughters. Whose story could you listen to this afternoon?
job-and-his-daughters.evening: Today's story was Job after everything. What has grown again in your life after something you lost?

music.why: Horatio Spafford wrote it after his four daughters drowned in a shipwreck: a man who, like Job, lost his children and still found words of faith.

paras: Then Job answered Yahweh,

“I know that you can do all things,
and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.

You asked, ‘Who is this who hides counsel without knowledge?’
therefore I have uttered that which I didn’t understand,
things too wonderful for me, which I didn’t know.

You said, ‘Listen, now, and I will speak;
I will question you, and you will answer me.’

I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear,
but now my eye sees you.

Therefore I abhor myself,
and repent in dust and ashes.”

It was so, that after Yahweh had spoken these words to Job, Yahweh said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.

Now therefore, take to yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept him, that I not deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.”
So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did what Yahweh commanded them, and Yahweh accepted Job.
Yahweh turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends. Yahweh gave Job twice as much as he had before.

Then came there to him all his brothers, and all his sisters, and all those who had been of his acquaintance before, and ate bread with him in his house. They comforted him, and consoled him concerning all the evil that Yahweh had brought on him. Everyone also gave him a piece of money, and everyone a ring of gold.
So Yahweh blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.
He had also seven sons and three daughters.
He called the name of the first, Jemimah; and the name of the second, Keziah; and the name of the third, Keren Happuch.
In all the land were no women found so beautiful as the daughters of Job. Their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
After this Job lived one hundred forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, to four generations.
So Job died, being old and full of days.

read.why: Job's book is mostly argument; this last chapter is where it finally comes to rest. Read Job's last words to God, God's verdict on the friends, and the life that follows. Tomorrow the week ends at an empty tomb.

the-guards-at-the-tomb.title: He is not here
the-guards-at-the-tomb.line: Soldiers lie like dead men at the tomb, and the women are told: he is not here.

story.retell: Soldiers had been posted to guard the tomb of Jesus and the stone sealed. At dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the grave. There was an earthquake; an angel rolled back the stone and sat on it, and the guards shook with fear and became like dead men. The angel told the women not to be afraid. Today, in Britain and across the Commonwealth, is Remembrance Sunday, when the dead of war are remembered.
story.verse: He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was lying.

the-guards-at-the-tomb.artLink: Benvenuto di Giovanni of Siena painted it, probably in 1491, as one of a series of scenes from the Passion.
the-guards-at-the-tomb.see: Jesus stands on top of a stone tomb in front of a doorway cut into the rock, his right hand raised in blessing, holding a white banner with a red cross. A heavy white slab lies on the ground. Under and around it sprawl six soldiers in armour of yellow, pink, blue, violet and orange, arms and legs flung out like the fallen. Only one, on the right, has propped himself up on an elbow and is looking at Jesus. Behind them, rivers wind away to a town and pale mountains.
the-guards-at-the-tomb.meaning: On Remembrance Sunday it is hard to look at a picture of soldiers lying like the dead without thinking of the ones who did not get up. This painting does not make war beautiful. It puts the soldiers at the foot of the one who has come through death, and one of them is beginning to look up. That is the Christian hope for the dead: not only that we remember them, though we must, but that death itself is not the last word. “He is not here” is the most hopeful thing ever said at a grave.

echo.from: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 2
echo.text: At the public funeral for the first Athenians killed in the war, the statesman Pericles gave the city's most famous speech. The bravest, he said, have the whole earth as their tomb. They are remembered not only by inscriptions on stone at home, but by an unwritten memory carried in the hearts of people far away.
echo.link: Pericles promised the dead a memory that would outlast their graves. The angel at the tomb says something more: not that the dead man is remembered, but that he is not there.

the-guards-at-the-tomb.question: Whom will you remember today: someone lost in war, or someone from your own family? Could you take two minutes of silence for them, and pray for those who still live with war?
the-guards-at-the-tomb.prayer: Risen Lord, today we remember those who have died in war, and those who grieve them. Give rest to the dead and peace to the living. Where there is fear, say again, “Don't be afraid.” Bring us all at last to the place where death has no more power. Amen.
the-guards-at-the-tomb.midday: This morning: an empty tomb and soldiers like the dead. Keep a moment's silence this afternoon for those lost in war.
the-guards-at-the-tomb.evening: Today's story was the empty tomb. Whom did you remember today? What hope do you hold for them?

music.why: William Walsham How's hymn of 1864, sung to Vaughan Williams's tune, gives thanks for all who have died in faith and looks forward to the morning when the saints rise.

paras: Now on the next day, which was the day after the Preparation Day, the chief priests and the Pharisees were gathered together to Pilate,
saying, “Sir, we remember what that deceiver said while he was still alive: ‘After three days I will rise again.’

Command therefore that the tomb be made secure until the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come at night and steal him away, and tell the people, ‘He is risen from the dead;’ and the last deception will be worse than the first.”
Pilate said to them, “You have a guard. Go, make it as secure as you can.”
So they went with the guard and made the tomb secure, sealing the stone.
Now after the Sabbath, as it began to dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.
Behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from the sky, and came and rolled away the stone from the door, and sat on it.
His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow.
For fear of him, the guards shook, and became like dead men.
The angel answered the women, “Don’t be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus, who has been crucified.
He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was lying.
Go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has risen from the dead, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him.’ Behold, I have told you.”
They departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to bring his disciples word.
As they went to tell his disciples, behold, Jesus met them, saying, “Rejoice!”
They came and took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.
Then Jesus said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Go tell my brothers that they should go into Galilee, and there they will see me.”

read.why: The week of death and hope ends here. Read how the tomb was sealed and guarded, and how the guarding came to nothing. Every story this week has looked towards this morning.

adam-and-eve-blame.title: It wasn't me
adam-and-eve-blame.line: Asked what they have done, the man blames the woman, and the woman blames the snake.

story.retell: After eating the fruit they had been told not to eat, the man and the woman hid among the trees. God came walking in the garden in the cool of the day and called, “Where are you?” Asked what had happened, the man blamed the woman, and the woman blamed the serpent. There were consequences, spelled out plainly. But before they left the garden, God made clothes of skins and dressed them.
story.verse: The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”

adam-and-eve-blame.artLink: Domenichino painted the scene of verse 12 in 1626.
adam-and-eve-blame.see: On the left, Adam and Eve, wearing only leaves, stand under fruit trees. Adam's knees are bent and he holds both hands, palms up, towards Eve, while looking up at God. Eve, kneeling, looks back at Adam and points down at a striped snake on the ground. On the right, God sweeps in through the air in a blue robe, carried by small angels in a billowing red cloth, reaching towards Adam. Below him lie a lamb and a lion. Follow the gestures: God reaches to the man, the man points to the woman, the woman points to the snake.
adam-and-eve-blame.meaning: This is the first conversation about wrongdoing in the Bible, and it goes the way most of ours do. Nobody says “I did it.” Each person passes the blame along, and the man even manages to blame God: the woman you gave me. Justice begins with something very simple and very hard: owning what we have done. But notice the end of the story. The consequences are real, and then God makes them clothes. Judgement and mercy come from the same hands.

echo.text: After his quarrel with Achilles has cost the Greeks thousands of lives, King Agamemnon finally makes peace. But even then he will not quite take the blame. It was not me, he says: it was Zeus, and Fate, and the Fury who walks in darkness, who blinded my mind that day.
echo.link: The oldest story of the Greeks and the oldest story of the Bible both catch the same reflex: when we do wrong, we point somewhere else. Only one of them ends with someone stooping to clothe the guilty.

adam-and-eve-blame.question: Is there something you have done this week that you have quietly blamed on someone or something else? Could you own it, out loud, to the person it affected?
adam-and-eve-blame.prayer: Lord, you call me as you called Adam: where are you? Give me the courage to answer honestly, without pointing at anyone else. Thank you that your judgement is never without mercy, and that you clothe those who have nowhere to hide. Amen.
adam-and-eve-blame.midday: This morning: the man blamed the woman, the woman blamed the snake. Notice this afternoon when you want to say “it wasn't me”.
adam-and-eve-blame.evening: Today's story was the first blame. Did you own up to anything today, however small? How did it feel?

music.why: Allegri sets Psalm 51, the prayer of someone who stops blaming and says, “I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.”

paras: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’ ”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.
Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?”
The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”
Yahweh God said to the serpent,

“Because you have done this,
you are cursed above all livestock,
and above every animal of the field.
You shall go on your belly
and you shall eat dust all the days of your life.

I will put hostility between you and the woman,
and between your offspring and her offspring.
He will bruise your head,
and you will bruise his heel.”
To the woman he said,

“I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth.
You will bear children in pain.
Your desire will be for your husband,
and he will rule over you.”
To Adam he said,

“Because you have listened to your wife’s voice,
and ate from the tree,
about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’
the ground is cursed for your sake.
You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life.

It will yield thorns and thistles to you;
and you will eat the herb of the field.

You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground,
for you were taken out of it.
For you are dust,
and you shall return to dust.”
The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.
Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.

read.why: A week about justice and mercy starts at the very beginning, with the first wrong and the first reckoning. Read the whole chapter, and look for the mercy hidden in it: the question “Where are you?”, and the clothes.

joseph-accused.title: Falsely accused
joseph-accused.line: Joseph does the right thing, is accused of the wrong one, and goes to prison.

story.retell: Joseph, sold as a slave into Egypt, became the trusted steward of Potiphar's household. Potiphar's wife pressed him day after day to sleep with her, and he refused: his master trusted him, and it would be a sin against God. One day she caught hold of his cloak, and he fled, leaving it in her hand. She kept the cloak and told her husband that Joseph had attacked her. Potiphar believed her and threw Joseph into prison.
story.verse: When his master heard the words of his wife, which she spoke to him, saying, “This is what your servant did to me,” his wrath was kindled.

joseph-accused.artLink: Rembrandt's workshop painted the accusation in 1655; Rembrandt's own version of the same year is in Berlin.
joseph-accused.see: In a pool of light, a woman in a fur-trimmed pink robe sits by a bed, pointing to it with one hand and holding her chemise closed at the neck with the other. Her mouth is open: she is telling her story. Her husband, in a turban and patterned cloak with a sword at his belt, stoops over her chair and listens, his hand on her shoulder. On the far side of the bed, half in shadow, stands a young man with keys at his belt and his hands quietly clasped. A red garment hangs over the bedpost. Joseph says nothing.
joseph-accused.meaning: Joseph did everything right and it made no difference. The person with power told the story, and the person without power went to prison. That still happens every day, in families, offices and courts. Two things are worth noticing. The first is that the story does not pretend: it lets the injustice stand. The second is the next line: “But the Lord was with Joseph,” even there. Justice matters precisely because people like Joseph exist. And being wronged does not mean being abandoned.

echo.text: Queen Phaedra falls in love with her stepson Hippolytus, and he rejects her. Ashamed and afraid, she dies, leaving a written note accusing him of assaulting her. His father, Theseus, believes the note without hearing his son out, curses him, and Hippolytus is killed. Only afterwards is the truth revealed.
echo.link: The Greeks told the same story of a false accusation, and in their version it ends in ruin. Joseph's story is just as unjust, but it does not end in the prison: someone is with him there.

joseph-accused.question: Do you know someone who has been blamed for something they didn't do? Is there a way you could stand up for them, or at least tell them you believe them?
joseph-accused.prayer: God of Joseph, you see what happens in the dark and who is telling the truth. Be with all who are falsely accused and in prison tonight. Make me slow to believe the first story I hear, and brave enough to speak for those who cannot. Amen.
joseph-accused.midday: This morning: Joseph accused, and silent. This afternoon, before you believe a story about someone, ask whether you have heard their side.
joseph-accused.evening: Today's story was Joseph falsely accused. Did you hear a story about someone today? Did you hear their side too?

music.why: Messiaen composed it in a prisoner-of-war camp and first played it there to prisoners and guards in 1941: music made in a prison, like Joseph's faith.

paras: Joseph was brought down to Egypt. Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites that had brought him down there.
Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
His master saw that Yahweh was with him, and that Yahweh made all that he did prosper in his hand.
Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and Potiphar made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Yahweh’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field.
He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he ate.
Joseph was well-built and handsome.
After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, “Lie with me.”
But he refused, and said to his master’s wife, “Behold, my master doesn’t know what is with me in the house, and he has put all that he has into my hand.
No one is greater in this house than I am, and he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
As she spoke to Joseph day by day, he didn’t listen to her, to lie by her, or to be with her.
About this time, he went into the house to do his work, and there were none of the men of the house inside.
She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!”
He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand, and had run outside,
she called to the men of her house, and spoke to them, saying, “Behold, he has brought a Hebrew in to us to mock us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice.
When he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment by me, and ran outside.”
She laid up his garment by her, until his master came home.
She spoke to him according to these words, saying, “The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought to us, came in to me to mock me,
and as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment by me, and ran outside.”
When his master heard the words of his wife, which she spoke to him, saying, “This is what your servant did to me,” his wrath was kindled.
Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound, and he was there in custody.
But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
The keeper of the prison committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever they did there, he was responsible for it.
The keeper of the prison didn’t look after anything that was under his hand, because Yahweh was with him; and that which he did, Yahweh made it prosper.

read.why: Justice begins with seeing what injustice looks like. Read the whole chapter: Joseph rising, Joseph refusing, Joseph wronged. It opens and closes with the same sentence: the Lord was with Joseph.

st-martin-cloak.title: Half a cloak
st-martin-cloak.line: A young soldier cuts his cloak in two for a freezing beggar, and later lays down his arms.

story.ref: The life of St Martin, by Sulpicius Severus · St Martin's Day
story.retell: Martin was a young soldier in the Roman army in the 4th century. One bitterly cold winter at the gate of Amiens, he met a poor man with almost nothing on, whom everyone else was passing by. Martin had nothing with him but his weapons and his soldier's cloak, so he cut the cloak in two with his sword and gave the man half. That night he dreamed of Christ wearing the half cloak. Later he asked to leave the army, saying he was Christ's soldier and could not fight. He became bishop of Tours, and today, 11 November, is his feast in the Western Church. The Armistice that ended the First World War was signed on St Martin's Day, 1918.
story.verse: The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’
story.verseRef: Matthew 25:40, the words Martin's dream recalled

st-martin-cloak.artLink: El Greco painted Martin and the beggar in 1597–99 for a chapel in Toledo.
st-martin-cloak.see: A young man in gold-trimmed armour sits on a tall white horse, looking down. In one hand he holds a sword; with the other he gathers a great swath of green cloak. The other end of it already wraps the hips of the nearly naked man standing beside him, who holds the cloth and looks up at him. There is a bandage round the beggar's shin. Behind them the land drops away under a wide blue sky. The two are almost the same height: the horse lifts the rider, but the cloak joins them.
st-martin-cloak.meaning: Martin did not solve poverty in Amiens. He did the thing in front of him with what he had, and it cost him half of what he needed to keep warm. People laughed at him for it. Mercy is usually like that: concrete, partial, a little foolish-looking. The story's deepest claim comes from Jesus himself: that what we do for the person no one else sees, we do for him. On Armistice Day it is worth remembering, too, that the soldier who is the patron of mercy is also the soldier who laid down his sword.

echo.text: Cicero quotes the old poet Ennius: a man who kindly shows a lost traveller the way is like someone lighting another's lamp from his own; his own shines no less for it. From this, Cicero says, comes a rule: whatever we can give without loss to ourselves, we should give even to a stranger.
echo.link: Cicero asked us to share what costs us nothing. Martin gave away half of what kept him warm. Mercy starts where Cicero's rule leaves off.

st-martin-cloak.question: Who is at your gate this week, someone in need whom others walk past? What could you give them that would actually cost you something, even a little?
st-martin-cloak.prayer: Lord, you met Martin in a freezing beggar and wore the cloak he gave. Open my eyes to you in those I would rather pass by. Give me Martin's quick generosity, and his courage to choose peace. Amen.
st-martin-cloak.midday: This morning: Martin cutting his cloak in two. Today is also Armistice Day: at eleven, many keep two minutes' silence for those who died in war.
st-martin-cloak.evening: Today's story was half a cloak. Did you share anything today that cost you something? Whom did you see that others missed?

music.why: Neale's carol tells a story much like Martin's, a ruler going out in the winter cold to help a poor man, and ends: “Ye who now will bless the poor shall yourselves find blessing.”

paras: “But I tell you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you.
To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other; and from him who takes away your cloak, don’t withhold your coat also.
Give to everyone who asks you, and don’t ask him who takes away your goods to give them back again.
“As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.
If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.
If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same.
If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive back as much.
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil.

“Therefore be merciful,
even as your Father is also merciful.

Don’t judge,
and you won’t be judged.
Don’t condemn,
and you won’t be condemned.
Set free,
and you will be set free.
“Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you. For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you.”
He spoke a parable to them. “Can the blind guide the blind? Won’t they both fall into a pit?
A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
Why do you see the speck of chaff that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?

Or how can you tell your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck of chaff that is in your eye,’ when you yourself don’t see the beam that is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck of chaff that is in your brother’s eye.
For there is no good tree that produces rotten fruit; nor again a rotten tree that produces good fruit.
For each tree is known by its own fruit. For people don’t gather figs from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble bush.

The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.
“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?
Everyone who comes to me, and hears my words, and does them, I will show you who he is like.

He is like a man building a house, who dug and went deep, and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house, and could not shake it, because it was founded on the rock.
But he who hears, and doesn’t do, is like a man who built a house on the earth without a foundation, against which the stream broke, and immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

read.why: Martin took Jesus at his word. Read the words he would have known: love your enemies, give to everyone who asks, and from anyone who takes your cloak do not hold back your coat. “Be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.”

through-the-roof-forgiven.title: Forgiven first
through-the-roof-forgiven.line: Four friends lower a paralysed man through a roof, and Jesus forgives him before he heals him.

story.retell: The house in Capernaum was so crowded that nobody could get near the door. So four people carrying a paralysed man on a mat climbed onto the roof, broke a hole in it, and lowered him down in front of Jesus. Jesus saw their faith and said something no one expected: “Son, your sins are forgiven.” Some religious teachers sitting there thought this was blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins. So Jesus told the man to get up, pick up his mat and go home, and he did, in front of them all.
story.verse: Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.”

through-the-roof-forgiven.artLink: An unknown Netherlandish painter of the later 1500s painted the story's ending, with its beginning far behind.
through-the-roof-forgiven.see: A man with a brown beard strides towards us, bent almost double under a huge bundle on his back: his bedding, tied up in a green cloth. His feet are bare and his eyes are down. Now look behind him, along the path, to the arched doorway of a building. There, tiny, a crowd surrounds someone standing with an arm stretched out over a man lying on a cloth, which hangs from four ropes let down from the roof. The painter shows the end and the beginning at once: the man carried in, and the man carrying his own bed out.
through-the-roof-forgiven.meaning: The man came for his legs and was given something else first. Jesus seems to say that what he most needed was not to walk but to be forgiven. That is a strange kind of justice: not getting what we deserve, but being set free from it. And it came through his friends. It was their faith Jesus saw, their effort that tore the roof open. Some of us need to be carried to mercy. Some of us are the ones on the roof.

echo.text: Seneca wrote this book for the young emperor Nero, early in his reign. Mercy, he argued, suits no one so well as a ruler: the more power someone has to punish, the more their mercy means. A cruel king is feared, he wrote, but a merciful one is loved and kept safe by his own people.
echo.link: Seneca hoped an emperor would learn mercy; Nero did not. In Capernaum, someone with real authority uses it first to forgive, and the critics in the room are exactly the people who see what a claim that is.

through-the-roof-forgiven.question: Is there someone you could “carry” to help this week, someone who can't get there on their own? Or is there a forgiveness you need, more than the thing you are asking for?
through-the-roof-forgiven.prayer: Lord, you saw the faith of four friends and forgave the man they carried. Forgive me, and set me on my feet. Make me a friend who will climb a roof for someone, and humble enough to be carried when I can't walk. Amen.
through-the-roof-forgiven.midday: This morning: four friends and a hole in the roof. Who could you carry this afternoon: a call, a lift, a favour?
through-the-roof-forgiven.evening: Today's story was the man forgiven first. Did anyone carry you today, or did you carry someone? Is there anything you need forgiving for tonight?

music.why: Recorded live in a Los Angeles Baptist church in 1972: an album about undeserved grace, sung by a congregation carrying the singer as much as she carries them.

paras: When he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was in the house.
Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even around the door; and he spoke the word to them.
Four people came, carrying a paralytic to him.
When they could not come near to him for the crowd, they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on.
Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.”
But there were some of the scribes sitting there, and reasoning in their hearts,
“Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you reason these things in your hearts?
Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk?’
But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—
“I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.”
He arose, and immediately took up the mat, and went out in front of them all; so that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!”
He went out again by the seaside. All the multitude came to him, and he taught them.
As he passed by, he saw Levi, the son of Alphaeus, sitting at the tax office, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he arose and followed him.
He was reclining at the table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners sat down with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many, and they followed him.
The scribes and the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with the sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why is it that he eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?”
