When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

read.why: Read on past the healing to the dinner that follows at Levi's house, where Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners. It ends with the reason for the whole week: he came not for the righteous, but for sinners.

manna-enough-for-all.title: Enough for everyone
manna-enough-for-all.line: In the wilderness, those who gathered much had nothing over, and those who gathered little had no lack.

story.retell: In the desert after leaving Egypt, the people of Israel were hungry and complaining. One morning they found the ground covered with something fine and white, like frost. “What is it?” they asked; it was manna, bread from God. Everyone was to gather what their household needed. Some gathered more and some less, but when they measured it, everyone had exactly enough. Those who tried to keep extra overnight found it had gone bad by morning.
story.verse: When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They each gathered according to his eating.

manna-enough-for-all.artLink: Bachiacca, a Florentine painter who loved animals, painted the gathering of manna between about 1540 and 1555.
manna-enough-for-all.see: Dozens of people in pink, orange, sky blue and green spread across a hilly landscape, gathering. Some bend to the ground, some fill barrel-sized jars, some sit and rest. A man at the lower left points the way with a stick. And the painter cannot resist animals: a porcupine, a white rabbit, a black bear, a cow, spotted big cats, even a giraffe. A path winds away to a town on a rocky coast. Nobody is guarding a pile; everyone is gathering.
manna-enough-for-all.meaning: The manna came with a rule: take what you need, and don't hoard. It is one of the Bible's first pictures of a just economy, and it is not about everyone having the same skills or working the same hours. It is about everyone having enough, and trusting that there will be enough tomorrow. Paul later quoted this verse when asking rich churches to share with poor ones. Hoarded manna rotted. Shared manna fed everyone.

echo.text: Aristotle disagreed with his teacher Plato, who wanted the rulers of his ideal city to own everything in common. Better, Aristotle said, for property to be owned privately but used generously, as the old saying goes: friends share what they have. Good habits of giving, not laws, make that possible.
echo.link: Aristotle hoped generous people would make sure everyone had enough. The manna built it into each morning: gather your own share, keep nothing over, and trust that tomorrow there will be more.

manna-enough-for-all.question: Is there something you are keeping “in case” that someone else needs now? What would it mean to have enough, and share the rest?
manna-enough-for-all.prayer: God who fed your people in the desert, thank you for this day's bread. Free me from the fear that makes me hoard. Teach me to take what I need, to share what I don't, and to trust you for tomorrow. Amen.
manna-enough-for-all.midday: This morning: manna in the desert, enough for everyone. Notice this afternoon what “enough” looks like for you.
manna-enough-for-all.evening: Today's story was the manna. Did you have enough today? Did you share anything you might have kept?

music.why: Chisholm's hymn is built on Lamentations 3, God's mercies new every morning: the manna's lesson that there is fresh provision each day.

paras: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,

“I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel. Speak to them, saying, ‘At evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am Yahweh your God.’ ”
In the evening, quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning the dew lay around the camp.
When the dew that lay had gone, behold, on the surface of the wilderness was a small round thing, small as the frost on the ground.
When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, “What is it?” For they didn’t know what it was. Moses said to them, “It is the bread which Yahweh has given you to eat.

“This is the thing which Yahweh has commanded: ‘Gather of it everyone according to his eating; an omer a head, according to the number of your persons, you shall take it, every man for those who are in his tent.’ ”
The children of Israel did so, and some gathered more, some less.
When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They each gathered according to his eating.
Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.”
Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, so it bred worms and became foul; and Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it morning by morning, everyone according to his eating. When the sun grew hot, it melted.
On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much bread, two omers for each one; and all the rulers of the congregation came and told Moses.

He said to them, “This is that which Yahweh has spoken, ‘Tomorrow is a solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to Yahweh. Bake that which you want to bake, and boil that which you want to boil; and all that remains over lay up for yourselves to be kept until the morning.’ ”
They laid it up until the morning, as Moses ordered, and it didn’t become foul, and there were no worms in it.
Moses said, “Eat that today, for today is a Sabbath to Yahweh. Today you shall not find it in the field.
Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath. In it there shall be none.”
On the seventh day, some of the people went out to gather, and they found none.
Yahweh said to Moses, “How long do you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?
Behold, because Yahweh has given you the Sabbath, therefore he gives you on the sixth day the bread of two days. Everyone stay in his place. Let no one go out of his place on the seventh day.”
So the people rested on the seventh day.
The house of Israel called its name “Manna”, and it was like coriander seed, white; and its taste was like wafers with honey.

read.why: Justice is not only about courts; it is about bread. Read how the manna came, the rule that went with it, and the Sabbath rest built into it. It is the first lesson Israel learned in freedom.

woman-at-the-well.title: Known and not condemned
woman-at-the-well.line: At a well at noon, Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, and tells her everything she ever did.

story.retell: Tired from walking, Jesus sat down by a well in Samaria at about midday. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, and he asked her for a drink. She was astonished: Jews and Samaritans did not mix, and a Jewish teacher did not talk to a woman alone. They talked about water, worship and her life; he knew she had had five husbands, and he did not turn away. She left her water jar and ran into town.
story.verse: “Come, see a man who told me everything that I did. Can this be the Christ?”

woman-at-the-well.artLink: An unknown American painter of the early 1700s painted the conversation at the well.
woman-at-the-well.see: A woman in a golden yellow dress with a blue underskirt and red shoes stands by a well, a jug in her right hand. Sitting on the edge of the well in a light blue robe is a bearded man with long dark hair, turned towards her. Above them hangs a pulley with its rope. Trees stand on either side, and far behind are houses and rolling hills under a soft blue sky. It is a plain, quiet picture of two people talking, which is exactly what the story is.
woman-at-the-well.meaning: Two kinds of contempt meet at this well: between Jews and Samaritans, and towards a woman with a complicated past. Jesus crosses both by asking her for something. He does not pretend her life is other than it is; he tells her everything she ever did. But being fully known by him does not end in condemnation. It ends with her running into town to tell the very people she may have avoided. Mercy is not being overlooked. It is being seen completely, and welcomed anyway.

echo.text: Terence, a playwright said to have come to Rome from Carthage as a slave, wrote a line for a nosy old neighbour who is told to mind his own business. He answers: “I am human; I think nothing human is foreign to me.” It became one of the most quoted sentences in Latin.
echo.link: Terence's line is a joke that became a creed. At the well, Jesus lives it: no boundary of nation, sex or reputation makes this woman a stranger to him.

woman-at-the-well.question: Is there someone you have quietly written off because of where they come from or what they have done? Could you ask them for something, or simply talk to them, this week?
woman-at-the-well.prayer: Lord, you know everything I have ever done, and you still ask to share my day. Thank you for seeing me and not turning away. Help me to cross the lines I draw between myself and others, and to offer them the welcome you gave her. Amen.
woman-at-the-well.midday: This morning: a conversation at a well that crossed every line. Whom could you speak to this afternoon whom you usually wouldn't?
woman-at-the-well.evening: Today's story was the woman at the well. Did you cross a line today, to talk to someone or to let yourself be known?

music.why: Bach's chorale moves like running water over its gentle triplets: a fitting sound for the promise of living water.

paras: So he came to a city of Samaria, called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son, Joseph.
Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being tired from his journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour.
A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.
The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. So where do you get that living water?
Are you greater than our father, Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his children and his livestock?”
Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw.”
Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”
The woman answered, “I have no husband.”
Jesus said to her, “You said well, ‘I have no husband,’
for you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have is not your husband. This you have said truly.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.
Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour comes, when neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, will you worship the Father.
You worship that which you don’t know. We worship that which we know; for salvation is from the Jews.
But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”
The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.”
Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”
At this, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?”
So the woman left her water pot, went away into the city, and said to the people,
“Come, see a man who told me everything that I did. Can this be the Christ?”
They went out of the city, and were coming to him.
In the meanwhile, the disciples urged him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”
But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.”
The disciples therefore said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”
Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.
Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest?’ Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.
He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit to eternal life; that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.
For in this the saying is true, ‘One sows, and another reaps.’
I sent you to reap that for which you haven’t labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”
From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything that I did.”
So when the Samaritans came to him, they begged him to stay with them. He stayed there two days.
Many more believed because of his word.
They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.”

read.why: The fortnight ends with the longest conversation Jesus has with anyone in the Gospels. Read it all, including what happens when the whole town comes out. Justice and mercy meet here: a woman told the truth about her life and given a welcome.

the-kingdoms-refused.title: The kingdoms refused
the-kingdoms-refused.line: Hungry and alone in the desert, Jesus is offered the whole world, and says no.

story.retell: Before he began to teach, Jesus went out alone into the wilderness and fasted for forty days. At the end, hungry and weak, he was tempted three times: to turn stones into bread, to throw himself from the top of the Temple so that angels would catch him, and last of all to take every kingdom in the world and its glory, if only he would bow down to the one offering them.
story.verse: Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’ ”

the-kingdoms-refused.artLink: Juan de Flandes painted all three temptations in one small panel, about 1500–1504, for Queen Isabella of Castile.
the-kingdoms-refused.see: In front, the tempter has come disguised as a monk in a brown habit, with a string of beads at his belt and a stone in his hand: turn this into bread. But look closer. Two little horns curl back from his head, and a webbed claw pokes out under his robe. Jesus sits on a rock and raises one hand, palm out: no. Now look into the distance. Two tiny figures stand on top of the cliff, high above the world, and on a tower in the city the two of them appear again. The whole story is there, one temptation behind another.
the-kingdoms-refused.meaning: Every temptation in the story is a shortcut to something good. Bread for a hungry man. Proof that God is with him. The kingdoms of the world, which he could surely have ruled well. The price was simply to bow to the wrong thing. Jesus refused, not because power is evil, but because his kingdom would come another way: by serving, not seizing. Most of our temptations are like this. They rarely ask us to want bad things, only to get good things the wrong way.

echo.text: Xenophon passes on an old story told by the teacher Prodicus. As a young man, Heracles sat alone at a place where the road divided. Two women came to him. One, whose friends called her Happiness and whose enemies called her Vice, promised him the easy road: every pleasure, no effort. The other, Virtue, promised nothing easy, only a hard road to the things truly worth having.
echo.link: Both stories put a young man alone where the road divides, offered an easy way and a hard one. Heracles chose the hard road to win glory. Jesus chose it knowing it would lead to a cross.

the-kingdoms-refused.question: Where are you being offered a shortcut at the moment: a way to get something good by doing something you know isn't right? What would the longer road look like, and could you take one step on it today?
the-kingdoms-refused.prayer: Lord Jesus, you were hungry and alone, and still you said no. When I am tired and the shortcut looks easy, give me your steadiness. Let me worship God alone, and bow to nothing that would make me less than I am meant to be. Amen.
the-kingdoms-refused.midday: This morning: Jesus in the desert, offered every kingdom in the world. Notice any shortcut that tempts you this afternoon.
the-kingdoms-refused.evening: Today's story was the kingdoms refused. Was there a moment today when you were offered the easy road? Which way did you go?

music.why: The old Irish prayer turns down the world's prizes, “riches I heed not, nor man's empty praise”, and calls God the “High King of Heaven”.

paras: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward.
The tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.”
But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’ ”
Then the devil took him into the holy city. He set him on the pinnacle of the temple,
and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and,

‘On their hands they will bear you up,
so that you don’t dash your foot against a stone.’ ”
Jesus said to him, “Again, it is written, ‘You shall not test the Lord, your God.’ ”
Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world, and their glory.
He said to him, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.”
Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’ ”
Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him.
Now when Jesus heard that John was delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee.
Leaving Nazareth, he came and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea, in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali,
that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying,

“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali,
toward the sea, beyond the Jordan,
Galilee of the Gentiles,

the people who sat in darkness saw a great light,
to those who sat in the region and shadow of death,
to them light has dawned.”
From that time, Jesus began to preach, and to say, “Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.”

read.why: This part of the road is about the kingdom, which Jesus talked about more than anything else. It begins with the kingdoms he turned down. Read on to the end of the passage: straight after the desert, his first words in public are “The Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.”

melchizedek-bread-and-wine.title: The king with bread
melchizedek-bread-and-wine.line: After a battle, a mysterious king comes out to meet Abraham, carrying bread and wine.

story.retell: Abram, later called Abraham, was coming home from a battle he had fought to rescue his nephew Lot, who had been carried off as a captive. Two kings came out to meet him. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought bread and wine for the tired men, and blessed him. The king of Sodom came to bargain over the spoils, and Abraham refused to take anything from him.
story.verse: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High.

melchizedek-bread-and-wine.artLink: Peter Paul Rubens painted the meeting in about 1626 as a design for a tapestry, in a series on the Eucharist.
melchizedek-bread-and-wine.see: Rubens paints a tapestry being hung, with small winged children lifting its corners. On it, Abraham, in armour and a swirling red cloak, leans forward to take two loaves of bread. Facing him is the old king Melchizedek, white-bearded, in a heavy golden cloak with a white fur collar and a wreath of leaves round his cap. Behind the king a man carries a basket of bread on his shoulders, and in the corner men hold huge silver and gold jars. The soldiers stand on Abraham's side; the bread comes from the king's.
melchizedek-bread-and-wine.meaning: Melchizedek appears for three verses and vanishes. But the Bible never forgot him. His name means “king of righteousness”, and Salem means peace. A psalm promised a king who would be “a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek”, and the first Christians saw Jesus in him: a king whose first act is to feed tired people and bless them. Notice the other king in the story, the one who comes to bargain. Abraham takes the bread and refuses the bargain. There are two ways to rule, and both are still on offer.

echo.text: Plutarch tells of Numa, the second king of Rome, chosen not for his courage in war but for his wisdom and his reverence for the gods. He gave Rome its priests and its prayers. The gates of the temple of Janus, which stood open whenever Rome was at war, stayed shut for the whole of his forty-three-year reign.
echo.link: Rome remembered one king of peace who was also a kind of priest. Genesis remembers Melchizedek. Both hold up the same rare thing: a ruler whose power is spent on blessing.

melchizedek-bread-and-wine.question: Who around you is worn out after a long struggle, at work, at home or in their family? What is your “bread and wine”: something simple you could bring them today?
melchizedek-bread-and-wine.prayer: Lord, you are the king who comes out to meet us with bread. Thank you for the times I have been fed and blessed when I was worn out. Make me generous like Melchizedek, and wise like Abraham, to take the gift and refuse the bargain. Amen.
melchizedek-bread-and-wine.midday: This morning: a king who came out with bread. Who could you bring something to this afternoon?
melchizedek-bread-and-wine.evening: Today's story was Melchizedek's bread and wine. Did you bless someone today, or were you blessed? Did you turn down a bargain you should have?

music.why: Christians have long seen Melchizedek's bread and wine as a picture of Communion. Mozart wrote this short motet for the feast of Corpus Christi in 1791, greeting Christ present in the bread.

paras: In the days of Amraphel, king of Shinar; Arioch, king of Ellasar; Chedorlaomer, king of Elam; and Tidal, king of Goiim,
they made war with Bera, king of Sodom; Birsha, king of Gomorrah; Shinab, king of Admah; Shemeber, king of Zeboiim; and the king of Bela (also called Zoar).
All these joined together in the valley of Siddim (also called the Salt Sea).
They served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled.
In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who were with him, and struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth Karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh Kiriathaim,
and the Horites in their Mount Seir, to El Paran, which is by the wilderness.
They returned, and came to En Mishpat (also called Kadesh), and struck all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites, that lived in Hazazon Tamar.

The king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (also called Zoar) went out; and they set the battle in array against them in the valley of Siddim
against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings against the five.
Now the valley of Siddim was full of tar pits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and some fell there. Those who remained fled to the hills.
They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and went their way.
They took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, who lived in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.
One who had escaped came and told Abram, the Hebrew. At that time, he lived by the oaks of Mamre, the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner. They were allies of Abram.
When Abram heard that his relative was taken captive, he led out his three hundred eighteen trained men, born in his house, and pursued as far as Dan.
He divided himself against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them, and pursued them to Hobah, which is on the left hand of Damascus.
He brought back all the goods, and also brought back his relative Lot and his goods, and the women also, and the other people.
The king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, at the valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley).
Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High.
He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth.
Blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.”
Abram gave him a tenth of all.
The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself.”
Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth,
that I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap nor anything that is yours, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’
I will accept nothing from you except that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their portion.”

read.why: Read the whole episode, battle and all. Then watch the two kings who come out to meet Abraham, and the two very different things they offer him.

the-king-with-a-towel.title: The king with a towel
the-king-with-a-towel.line: On the night before he dies, Jesus kneels down and washes his friends' feet.

story.retell: On his last evening with his friends, during supper, Jesus got up from the table, took off his outer clothes and tied a towel round his waist. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash their feet, a servant's job. Peter was appalled and refused. Jesus told him that unless he let him do it, he could have no part with him.
story.verse: If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

the-king-with-a-towel.artLink: Garofalo, a painter from Ferrara, painted the moment with Peter in about 1520–25.
the-king-with-a-towel.see: The twelve friends sit along a curved white bench. In the middle, Jesus kneels in a red robe, holding an old man's bare leg over a golden basin. That is Peter, white-haired, one hand flat on his chest, looking down at him: “Lord, do you wash my feet?” Every head has a faint gold halo except one. Bottom right, a man with a money pouch at his belt looks straight out at us and points at Jesus. It is almost certainly Judas, who kept the common purse, and Jesus will wash his feet too.
the-king-with-a-towel.meaning: Kings do not wash feet. In Jesus's world it was work for the lowest servant, and Peter's horror is completely understandable. But John says Jesus did it knowing that the Father had put all things into his hands. That is the point: this is not a king pretending to be humble for an evening. This is what his kingship is. He even washes the feet of the friend who will betray him that night. And being served can be harder than serving. Peter had to let himself be loved first.

echo.text: Herodotus tells of Amasis, a commoner who became king of Egypt. Unsure of his people's respect, he had a golden footbath, in which he and his guests washed their feet, melted down and made into the statue of a god. When the people began to worship it, he told them what it had been. So it was with him, he said: once a common man, now their king, and to be honoured.
echo.link: Amasis turned a footbath into a god to prove that a king must be honoured. Jesus, whom his friends rightly called Lord, picked up a basin to show what honour really looks like.

the-king-with-a-towel.question: Whose “feet” could you wash today: a humble, unseen job you could do for someone, perhaps someone you find difficult? And is there someone you need to let help you?
the-king-with-a-towel.prayer: Lord Jesus, you knelt with a towel and a basin, even for the friend who would betray you. Wash me, though I would rather manage on my own. Then give me a servant's hands, and make me glad to do the jobs nobody notices. Amen.
the-king-with-a-towel.midday: This morning: the king with a towel. Is there an unglamorous job you could quietly do for someone this afternoon?
the-king-with-a-towel.evening: Today's story was the washing of feet. Did you serve someone today in a way that cost you a little pride? Did you let anyone serve you?

music.why: This ancient chant, “Where charity and love are, God is there”, is sung while feet are washed in church on the Thursday before Easter. Duruflé set it in 1960.

paras: Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,
Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”
Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.”
Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!”
Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.”
For he knew him who would betray him, therefore he said, “You are not all clean.”
So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.
Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

read.why: Read the whole scene, and especially what Jesus says afterwards. His question, “Do you know what I have done to you?”, is the question for this whole part of the road: what kind of king is this?

not-of-this-world.title: Not of this world
not-of-this-world.line: Pilate asks Jesus if he is a king. The answer changes what a kingdom is.

story.retell: Early on the morning of his death, Jesus was handed over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate asked him the only question that mattered to Rome: are you the King of the Jews? Jesus said his kingdom was of a different kind, and that he had come into the world to tell the truth. Pilate answered, “What is truth?”, found no case against him, and had him flogged anyway.
story.verse: Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.”

not-of-this-world.artLink: Bachiacca painted what Pilate ordered next, the flogging, in about 1512–15.
not-of-this-world.see: Jesus stands tied to a column in a bright, elegant courtyard, wearing only a blue cloth. Two men lean away from him with their whips raised, like mirror images: one facing us, one with his back to us, both in fancy caps. Beyond the arches, green hills roll away to blue mountains under a calm sky, and nothing out there seems to notice. Jesus does not struggle. He turns his head towards one of the men.
not-of-this-world.meaning: Pilate had all the power in the room: soldiers, law, the authority of Rome. Jesus had none. Yet in John's telling, it is Pilate who is anxious and Jesus who is free. “My Kingdom is not of this world” does not mean it has nothing to do with this world. It means it doesn't come from here, and doesn't work like the kingdoms here. It won't fight to save itself. It rules by truth, not force. Pilate asked what truth was, and walked out before he heard the answer.

echo.text: Epictetus, who had been born a slave, taught his students what to say to a tyrant. “I will put you in chains.” You will chain my leg; not even Zeus can conquer my will. “I will throw you into prison.” My body, you mean. “I will cut off your head.” Did I ever tell you mine was the one neck that couldn't be cut?
echo.link: A former slave and a prisoner before a governor both knew something the powerful forget: there is a freedom no one can take from you. Jesus called it a kingdom.

not-of-this-world.question: Where do you feel powerless at the moment? Is there one true thing you have been afraid to say there, which you could say kindly today?
not-of-this-world.prayer: King of truth, you stood before Pilate with nothing but the truth, and you were free. When I feel powerless, keep me honest. Let me listen for your voice, and not walk away before the answer, as Pilate did. Amen.
not-of-this-world.midday: This morning: Jesus before Pilate. “My Kingdom is not of this world.” Where do you need to be free and truthful this afternoon?
not-of-this-world.evening: Today's story was Jesus before Pilate. Did you tell the truth today when it was easier not to? Where did you feel free, or not?

music.why: A medieval meditation on the thorn-crowned head that the soldiers mocked as a king's. Bach loved its melody so much that he set it five times in the St Matthew Passion.

paras: They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. It was early, and they themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.
Pilate therefore went out to them, and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man weren’t an evildoer, we wouldn’t have delivered him up to you.”
Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law.”
Therefore the Jews said to him, “It is illegal for us to put anyone to death,”
that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
Pilate therefore entered again into the Praetorium, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”
Jesus answered him, “Do you say this by yourself, or did others tell you about me?”
Pilate answered, “I’m not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests delivered you to me. What have you done?”
Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.”
Pilate therefore said to him, “Are you a king then?”

Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?”
When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him.
But you have a custom, that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Therefore, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
Then they all shouted again, saying, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
So Pilate then took Jesus, and flogged him.
The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment.
They kept saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and they kept slapping him.
Then Pilate went out again, and said to them, “Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.”
Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, “Behold, the man!”

read.why: Read the whole trial. Notice how often Pilate goes in and out of the building, and how still Jesus is. It ends with Pilate's own words, “Behold, the man!” He meant it as mockery. Christians have read it ever since as the truth.

clovis-bows-his-head.title: A king bows his head
clovis-bows-his-head.line: A warrior king steps into the font with his crown on, and is told to bow.

story.ref: The baptism of Clovis, from Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 2
story.retell: Clovis was the fierce young king of the Franks, the people who gave France its name. His wife Clotilde was a Christian and had long urged him to believe. In a battle he was losing, he prayed to her God and promised to be baptised if he won. He won. At Reims, around the year 500, he came to the font, and Bishop Remigius said to him: “Bow your head, proud Sicambrian. Worship what you have burned, and burn what you have worshipped.”
story.verse: Yes, all kings shall fall down before him. All nations shall serve him.

clovis-bows-his-head.artLink: The Master of Saint Giles, a painter working in Paris, painted the baptism in about 1500, a thousand years after it happened.
clovis-bows-his-head.see: Clovis stands naked in a stone font with his hands together in prayer, and still wearing his jewelled crown. The bishop, in a red and gold cloak, pours water on his head from a golden bowl. Behind the king a woman in a gold veil looks on: probably Clotilde, who had prayed for this for years. Lords in fur-trimmed cloaks touch his arms, a monk holds a great book, and through the doorway a crowd watches from the courtyard. High on an archway outside sits a peacock, an old Christian sign of eternal life.
clovis-bows-his-head.meaning: The painter leaves the crown on Clovis's head, and that is the whole story. He was still a king, and would stay one. But in the water, a king had to bow to another King. The Christian claim that Jesus is Lord was always a shock: it means no ruler, government, boss or self has the final word. Clovis's later life was not gentle, and baptism did not make him a saint. But that day, at least, the most powerful man in the room bowed his head. Each of us wears some crown we would rather keep on.

echo.when: On campaign by the Danube, about AD 175
echo.text: The most powerful man in the world wrote a private warning to himself: take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, not dyed in the purple of power, because it happens. Keep yourself simple, good and honest, he told himself, and remember that life is short.
echo.link: Marcus Aurelius knew that a crown can swallow the person wearing it. Clovis was told, in the water, to bow his head. Both knew that even a ruler needs something above him.

clovis-bows-his-head.question: What “crown” do you wear: a role, a reputation, the habit of being in charge? Is there one place today where you could bow your head, by admitting you were wrong or letting someone else lead?
clovis-bows-his-head.prayer: King of kings, every crown is smaller than yours. Where I like to be in charge, teach me to bow my head. Where I have burned what was good, teach me to love it again. Amen.
clovis-bows-his-head.midday: This morning: a king with his crown on, bowing his head in the font. Where could you let go of being in charge this afternoon?
clovis-bows-his-head.evening: Today's story was the baptism of Clovis. Did you bow your head anywhere today, in an apology, or by letting someone else lead?

music.why: Handel wrote it for the coronation of George II in 1727, on the words of a priest anointing a king (1 Kings 1). It has been sung at every British coronation since: a king made by someone else's hands.

paras: If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion,
make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
So then, my beloved, even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.
For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.
Do all things without complaining and arguing,
that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world,
holding up the word of life, that I may have something to boast in the day of Christ, that I didn’t run in vain nor labor in vain.
Yes, and if I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice, and rejoice with you all.
In the same way, you also rejoice, and rejoice with me.

read.why: Many scholars think these verses are one of the earliest Christian hymns. They say what Clovis was bowing to: a king who emptied himself and became a servant, and to whom, one day, every knee will bow.

remember-me-christ-the-king.title: Remember me
remember-me-christ-the-king.line: On the feast of Christ the King, a dying criminal sees a king where everyone else sees a failure.

story.ref: Luke 23:33–43 · the feast of Christ the King
story.retell: Today is the feast of Christ the King, kept on the Sunday before Advent by Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and many other churches; the Orthodox do not keep it. Jesus was crucified between two criminals, under a sign that mocked him: “This is the King of the Jews.” The crowd jeered, and one of the criminals joined in. The other told him to stop, and turned to Jesus.
story.verse: He said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.” Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”

remember-me-christ-the-king.artLink: A painter from Münster in Westphalia, known only as the Master of the Death of Saint Nicholas, painted Calvary in about 1470–80.
remember-me-christ-the-king.see: Three crosses stand against a gold sky. Tiny angels catch Christ's blood in golden cups, and blood runs down his face from the ring of thorns. Now look at the two criminals. Beside the one on our left, an angel holds up a little figure like a doll: his soul, being carried away. The one on our right turns his head from a demon holding out his. And far behind, so small you might miss it, a crowd greets a man riding into the city on a donkey: the same king, cheered there only days before.
remember-me-christ-the-king.meaning: Everything in the scene says Jesus has lost. The sign over his head is a joke, the soldiers are laughing, and most of his followers have fled. One person sees it differently: a man dying beside him, with nothing to offer and no time left to put things right. He asks only to be remembered, and is promised paradise that very day. This is the king Christians celebrate today: not one who saves himself, but one whose kingdom opens first to a thief. No one is too late for it.

echo.text: Seneca wrote this short book for the young emperor Nero, his former pupil. Of all people, he told him, mercy suits no one better than a king. Anyone can take a life; saving one is the mark of true greatness.
echo.link: Seneca told an emperor that mercy is a king's true crown, and Nero did not listen. On the cross, a king crowned with thorns spent his last strength being merciful to a thief.

remember-me-christ-the-king.question: Who have you quietly written off as too far gone? Could you remember them today, with a message or a prayer, as the king remembered the thief?
remember-me-christ-the-king.prayer: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. You are the king who was mocked and did not save himself, so that you could save others. Rule in me with your mercy, and let me never think anyone, myself included, is too late for you. Amen.
remember-me-christ-the-king.midday: This morning: the thief who asked to be remembered. Who could you remember this afternoon?
remember-me-christ-the-king.evening: Today was the feast of Christ the King. Where did you see his kind of power today: mercy rather than force? Who did you remember?

music.why: The Hallelujah Chorus sings Revelation's words about this king: “The kingdom of this world is become the kingdom of our Lord”, and “King of Kings, and Lord of Lords”.

paras: When they led him away, they grabbed one Simon of Cyrene, coming from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it after Jesus.
A great multitude of the people followed him, including women who also mourned and lamented him.
But Jesus, turning to them, said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, don’t weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
For behold, the days are coming in which they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed.’
Then they will begin to tell the mountains, ‘Fall on us!’ and tell the hills, ‘Cover us.’
For if they do these things in the green tree, what will be done in the dry?”
There were also others, two criminals, led with him to be put to death.
When they came to the place that is called “The Skull”, they crucified him there with the criminals, one on the right and the other on the left.
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.”
Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots.
The people stood watching. The rulers with them also scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others. Let him save himself, if this is the Christ of God, his chosen one!”
The soldiers also mocked him, coming to him and offering him vinegar,
and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!”
An inscription was also written over him in letters of Greek, Latin, and Hebrew: “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
One of the criminals who was hanged insulted him, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!”
But the other answered, and rebuking him said, “Don’t you even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation?
And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward for our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong.”
He said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.”
Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”
It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.
The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn in two.
Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” Having said this, he breathed his last.
When the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying, “Certainly this was a righteous man.”
All the multitudes that came together to see this, when they saw the things that were done, returned home beating their breasts.
All his acquaintances and the women who followed with him from Galilee stood at a distance, watching these things.

read.why: This part of the road ends at the strangest throne in history. Read the whole crucifixion in Luke: the women on the road, the prayer for his killers, the thief, and the soldier at the end. Every king in this week's stories is measured against this one.

noah-shut-in.title: Shut in the ark
noah-shut-in.line: Noah, his family and the animals go into the ark, and the door is closed behind them.

story.retell: God told Noah that a great flood was coming, and that the rain would begin in seven days. Noah did everything he was told. He went into the ark he had built with his family and pairs of every kind of animal, and God himself shut them in. Then they waited: first for the rain, and afterwards, for many months, for the waters to go down.
story.verse: Those who went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God commanded him; then Yahweh shut him in.

noah-shut-in.artLink: J. M. W. Turner painted the evening before the flood in about 1843, late in his life.
noah-shut-in.see: Turner paints almost nothing solid. A pale sun hangs in a swirling yellow sky that darkens to rust and wine red at the top. A long, curving stream of birds, tiny blue marks, sweeps round the sun and away into the distance. Below, in the haze, is a dark, arched shape: the ark. Look hard at the cloudy green and gold around it and you may make out ghostly animals: a bear, a crocodile, a giraffe. It is the last calm evening, and the sky is already changing.
noah-shut-in.meaning: The hardest part of Noah's story is not the building. It is the waiting. The door is shut, by God, not by Noah, and for a long time nothing happens. There is nothing left to do but sit in the dark and trust that the one who closed the door will open it again. Many waits are like this: the work is done, the decision made, and all we can do is wait. But being shut in is not the same as being forgotten. A chapter later, the Bible says, “God remembered Noah”.

echo.text: Ovid tells the Greek flood story. When Jupiter drowned the wicked world, only an old couple, Deucalion and Pyrrha, survived, drifting in a small boat until it came to rest on Mount Parnassus. Alone in an empty world, they waited for the waters to fall, then prayed for help to begin again. They were told to throw stones over their shoulders, and the stones became people.
echo.link: The Greeks and the Hebrews both remembered a flood, and a small boat of the faithful waiting it out. In both stories the waiting ends with a new beginning for the whole world.

noah-shut-in.question: What are you waiting for at the moment, with the door shut and nothing more you can do? Is there someone else waiting through something hard whom you could ring or visit this week?
noah-shut-in.prayer: God who shuts the door and opens it again, I am waiting for things I cannot hurry. Keep me safe while I wait. Remember me, as you remembered Noah, and teach me to trust you in the dark until the rain is over. Amen.
noah-shut-in.midday: This morning: Noah shut in the ark, waiting. Is there something you could stop trying to hurry this afternoon?
noah-shut-in.evening: Today's story was Noah waiting in the ark. What did you wait for today? Was it easier to trust, or harder?

music.why: U2's song sets Psalm 40, which begins with waiting patiently for the Lord and goes on to being lifted out of the pit and set on a rock.

paras: Yahweh said to Noah, “Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation.
You shall take seven pairs of every clean animal with you, the male and his female. Of the animals that are not clean, take two, the male and his female.
Also of the birds of the sky, seven and seven, male and female, to keep seed alive on the surface of all the earth.
In seven days, I will cause it to rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights. I will destroy every living thing that I have made from the surface of the ground.”
Noah did everything that Yahweh commanded him.
Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came on the earth.
Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives, because of the floodwaters.
Clean animals, unclean animals, birds, and everything that creeps on the ground
went by pairs to Noah into the ship, male and female, as God commanded Noah.
After the seven days, the floodwaters came on the earth.
In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the sky’s windows opened.
It rained on the earth forty days and forty nights.
In the same day Noah, and Shem, Ham, and Japheth—the sons of Noah—and Noah’s wife and the three wives of his sons with them, entered into the ship—
they, and every animal after its kind, all the livestock after their kind, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth after its kind, and every bird after its kind, every bird of every sort.
Pairs from all flesh with the breath of life in them went into the ship to Noah.
Those who went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God commanded him; then Yahweh shut him in.
The flood was forty days on the earth. The waters increased, and lifted up the ship, and it was lifted up above the earth.
The waters rose, and increased greatly on the earth; and the ship floated on the surface of the waters.
The waters rose very high on the earth. All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered.
The waters rose fifteen cubits higher, and the mountains were covered.
All flesh died that moved on the earth, including birds, livestock, animals, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, and every man.
All on the dry land, in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, died.

Every living thing was destroyed that was on the surface of the ground, including man, livestock, creeping things, and birds of the sky. They were destroyed from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship.
The waters flooded the earth one hundred fifty days.
God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship; and God made a wind to pass over the earth. The waters subsided.
The deep’s fountains and the sky’s windows were also stopped, and the rain from the sky was restrained.
The waters continually receded from the earth. After the end of one hundred fifty days the waters receded.
The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat’s mountains.
The waters receded continually until the tenth month. In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were visible.
At the end of forty days, Noah opened the window of the ship which he had made,
and he sent out a raven. It went back and forth, until the waters were dried up from the earth.
He himself sent out a dove to see if the waters were abated from the surface of the ground,

but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned into the ship to him, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship.
He waited yet another seven days; and again he sent the dove out of the ship.
The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters were abated from the earth.
He waited yet another seven days, and sent out the dove; and she didn’t return to him any more.

read.why: This last part of the road before Advent is about waiting: the long waits in the Bible, and what people found in them. Read on past the flood to the raven and the dove, and notice how often the story simply says Noah waited.

simeon-and-anna.title: Worth the wait
simeon-and-anna.line: Two old people have waited all their lives in the Temple. Then a young couple walk in with a baby.

story.retell: About six weeks after Jesus was born, Mary and Joseph brought him to the Temple in Jerusalem, as the law required, with the offering of the poor: two doves. An old man called Simeon had been promised that he would not die before he saw the Messiah. He took the baby in his arms and thanked God that he could now die in peace. Then Anna, a widow of great age who had spent her life praying in the Temple, came up and began telling everyone about the child.
story.verse: It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

simeon-and-anna.artLink: A Netherlandish painter known only as the Master of the Prado Adoration of the Magi painted this scene in about 1470–80.
simeon-and-anna.see: In a church full of columns, pointed arches and stained glass, a young woman in blue and an old man in a purple robe hold a baby over an altar between them. The old man is Simeon: bald, deeply wrinkled, gazing down at the child. Right behind the baby stands an old woman in green with a white headdress, her palm turned up towards him: Anna. To the left, an old man with a cane, probably Joseph, holds a wicker cage with a blue-grey bird inside: the offering of a family who could not afford a lamb.
simeon-and-anna.meaning: Simeon and Anna had waited their whole lives, and when the moment came it was a young couple with a six-week-old baby and a bird in a cage. Nothing that looked like the answer to a nation's prayers. But they had spent so long looking that they recognised it. Waiting had trained their eyes. Tomorrow Advent begins, the season of waiting for Christ. These two old people show how it is done: faithfully, for a long time, with eyes open for something small.

echo.text: Cicero's old Cato says that a farmer who plants trees he will never sit under is not foolish. Ask him who they are for, Cato says, and he will answer: for the gods, who wanted me not only to receive these things from those before me but to hand them on to those who come after.
echo.link: Cicero's old farmer and Simeon both lived for a future they would barely see. Simeon held it in his arms for a moment, and it was enough.

simeon-and-anna.question: What have you waited for so long that you might have stopped looking? And is there an older person whose patience and faith you could thank this week?
simeon-and-anna.prayer: Lord, now let your servant go in peace, for my eyes have seen. As Advent begins, give me the patience of Simeon and Anna: to wait faithfully, to keep looking, and to know you when you come small and unannounced. Amen.
simeon-and-anna.midday: This morning: Simeon and Anna, who waited all their lives. Keep your eyes open this afternoon for something small and good.
simeon-and-anna.evening: Today's story was Simeon and Anna in the Temple. What are you waiting for as Advent begins tomorrow? Did you notice anything small today that was an answer?

music.why: The fifth movement is Simeon's song, “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace”, ending with the basses' famous descent; Rachmaninoff asked for it to be sung at his funeral.

paras: When the days of their purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him up to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord
(as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”),
and to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, “A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.”
Behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, looking for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was on him.
It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.
He came in the Spirit into the temple. When the parents brought in the child, Jesus, that they might do concerning him according to the custom of the law,
then he received him into his arms, and blessed God, and said,

“Now you are releasing your servant, Master,
according to your word, in peace;
for my eyes have seen your salvation,
which you have prepared before the face of all peoples;

a light for revelation to the nations,
and the glory of your people Israel.”
Joseph and his mother were marveling at the things which were spoken concerning him,
and Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary, his mother, “Behold, this child is set for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which is spoken against.
Yes, a sword will pierce through your own soul, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”
There was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher (she was of a great age, having lived with a husband seven years from her virginity,
and she had been a widow for about eighty-four years), who didn’t depart from the temple, worshiping with fastings and petitions night and day.
Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of him to all those who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem.
When they had accomplished all things that were according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth.
The child was growing, and was becoming strong in spirit, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.

read.why: This part of the road ends where Advent begins: with a long wait rewarded. Read the whole visit to the Temple. Simeon's song has been sung at evening prayer for centuries, the last words of the day for people still waiting.

john-in-the-desert.title: Into the wilderness
john-in-the-desert.line: Advent Sunday: a young man puts down his fine clothes and goes into the desert to listen.

story.retell: John was the son of an elderly priest, Zechariah, and his birth had been a wonder. Luke says almost nothing about his growing up, except that he grew strong and lived in the desert. There, years later, the word of God came to him, and he went out to the Jordan calling people to get ready. Luke heard in him the voice Isaiah had promised, calling in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord.
story.verse: The child was growing and becoming strong in spirit, and was in the desert until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

john-in-the-desert.artLink: Domenico Veneziano painted the young John going into the desert in Florence, about 1445 to 1450, as a small panel beneath a large altarpiece.
john-in-the-desert.see: A young man stands alone among bare, ridged mountains. Nothing grows but a few dark bushes, and a thin blue stream curves along the right. He has a gold halo and wears nothing at all. He is letting a coral-red cloth drop onto a white one already on the ground, and over his shoulder he holds a rough brown animal skin. He is not looking at the mountains. He is looking down at what he is leaving behind.
john-in-the-desert.meaning: Advent begins in the wilderness, not on a lit-up high street. Before anyone can prepare a way for someone else, they have to clear a space in themselves, and that usually means putting something down. John swaps fine cloth for a rough skin, not because comfort is wicked but because he wants to hear. Advent is four weeks of the same choice in a small form: a little less noise, a little less stuff, a little more room for whatever God might say.

echo.text: Writing in December, while the whole city feasted for the Saturnalia, Seneca advised his friend to set aside a few days to live on the plainest food and in the roughest clothes. Then ask yourself, he said: is this what I was so afraid of? Someone who has practised going without is free, because they no longer fear losing what they have.
echo.link: Seneca practised going without in December, while Rome celebrated; John went into the desert before he spoke a word. Both knew that what we can do without no longer has a hold on us. Advent asks for the same small freedom, in the same month.

john-in-the-desert.question: What is one thing you could put down for the four weeks of Advent, to make a little room? And what would you like to hear in the quiet it leaves?
john-in-the-desert.prayer: Lord, at the start of Advent, lead me a little way into the wilderness. Help me put down what crowds you out, and give me ears to hear your word when it comes. Prepare in me a way for you. Amen.
john-in-the-desert.midday: This morning: John laying down his fine clothes in the desert. What could you leave on the ground this afternoon?
john-in-the-desert.evening: Today's story was John going into the wilderness. Did you make any room today, even a little? What filled it?

music.why: Handel's Messiah begins with Isaiah 40, the chapter John lived by: “Comfort ye my people”, then “Every valley shall be exalted”.

paras: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
“Speak comfortably to Jerusalem; and call out to her that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received of Yahweh’s hand double for all her sins.”

The voice of one who calls out,
“Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness!
Make a level highway in the desert for our God.

Every valley shall be exalted,
and every mountain and hill shall be made low.
The uneven shall be made level,
and the rough places a plain.

The voice of one saying, “Cry!”
One said, “What shall I cry?”
“All flesh is like grass,
and all its glory is like the flower of the field.

The grass withers,
the flower fades,
because Yahweh’s breath blows on it.
Surely the people are like grass.

You who tell good news to Zion, go up on a high mountain.
You who tell good news to Jerusalem, lift up your voice with strength!
Lift it up! Don’t be afraid!
Say to the cities of Judah, “Behold, your God!”

Behold, the Lord Yahweh will come as a mighty one,
and his arm will rule for him.
Behold, his reward is with him,
and his recompense before him.

He will feed his flock like a shepherd.
He will gather the lambs in his arm,
and carry them in his bosom.
He will gently lead those who have their young.

Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand,
and marked off the sky with his span,
and calculated the dust of the earth in a measuring basket,
and weighed the mountains in scales,
and the hills in a balance?

Who has directed Yahweh’s Spirit,
or has taught him as his counselor?

Who did he take counsel with,
and who instructed him,
and taught him in the path of justice,
and taught him knowledge,
and showed him the way of understanding?

Behold, the nations are like a drop in a bucket,
and are regarded as a speck of dust on a balance.
Behold, he lifts up the islands like a very little thing.

Lebanon is not sufficient to burn,
nor its animals sufficient for a burnt offering.

All the nations are like nothing before him.
They are regarded by him as less than nothing, and vanity.

To whom then will you liken God?
Or what likeness will you compare to him?

A workman has cast an image,
and the goldsmith overlays it with gold,
and casts silver chains for it.

He who is too impoverished for such an offering chooses a tree that will not rot.
He seeks a skillful workman to set up a carved image for him that will not be moved.

Haven’t you known?
Haven’t you heard?
Haven’t you been told from the beginning?
Haven’t you understood from the foundations of the earth?

It is he who sits above the circle of the earth,
and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers;
who stretches out the heavens like a curtain,
and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in,

who brings princes to nothing,
who makes the judges of the earth meaningless.

They are planted scarcely.
They are sown scarcely.
Their stock has scarcely taken root in the ground.
He merely blows on them, and they wither,
and the whirlwind takes them away as stubble.

“To whom then will you liken me?
Who is my equal?” says the Holy One.

Lift up your eyes on high,
and see who has created these,
who brings out their army by number.
He calls them all by name.
by the greatness of his might,
and because he is strong in power,
not one is lacking.

Why do you say, Jacob,
and speak, Israel,
“My way is hidden from Yahweh,
and the justice due me is disregarded by my God?”

Haven’t you known?
Haven’t you heard?
The everlasting God, Yahweh,
the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint.
He isn’t weary.
His understanding is unsearchable.

He gives power to the weak.
He increases the strength of him who has no might.

Even the youths faint and get weary,
and the young men utterly fall;

but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength.
They will mount up with wings like eagles.
They will run, and not be weary.
They will walk, and not faint.

read.why: Advent starts here. Luke heard in John the voice this chapter promised: “Prepare the way of the Lord in the wilderness!” Read it slowly as the season opens. It begins with comfort, and it ends with strength for the tired.

andrew-brings-his-brother.title: He brought his brother
andrew-brings-his-brother.line: St Andrew's Day: the first thing Andrew did was go and find his brother.

story.ref: John 1:35–42, and the tradition of his death at Patras
story.retell: Andrew was a fisherman and a follower of John the Baptist. One day John pointed to Jesus walking past, and Andrew and a friend followed him and spent the rest of the day with him. Before doing anything else, Andrew went to find his brother Simon and brought him to Jesus, who gave Simon a new name: Peter. Tradition says Andrew later took the good news to Greece, and died on a cross at Patras.
story.verse: He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ). He brought him to Jesus.

andrew-brings-his-brother.artLink: The Florentine painter Agnolo Gaddi painted Andrew on the wing of an altarpiece, shortly before 1387.
andrew-brings-his-brother.see: Andrew stands on the left under a pointed gold arch: an old man with wild grey hair, in a green cloak over a pink robe. Leaning on his shoulder is a wooden cross taller than he is, and in the same hand he holds a coil of white rope. Beside him, under his own arch, stands St Benedict with an open book. Gaddi does not paint the afternoon by the lake. He paints the whole life it led to, right to the end.
andrew-brings-his-brother.meaning: Andrew is the disciple who keeps bringing people. He brings his brother Simon; later he brings the boy with five loaves, and some Greeks who want to meet Jesus. He never becomes the famous one: Peter does. Andrew seems not to mind. Most faith is passed on like this, not by preachers but by a brother, a friend, a neighbour who says, “Come and see.” You don't need to have all the answers to do it. Andrew had spent one afternoon with Jesus.

echo.text: Plutarch wrote a whole essay on how brothers should treat each other. Nature, he said, made most of our useful parts in pairs, two hands, two feet, two eyes, so that each could help the other. Brothers are meant to work the same way. He urged a brother who is less honoured not to envy the other, but to share in his success as his own.
echo.link: Andrew lived it. He brought his brother to Jesus, then watched Simon become Peter, the leader, the rock. There is no sign of envy. He was glad to be the one who brought him.

andrew-brings-his-brother.question: Who is one person you could say “come and see” to, about something good you've found? Is there a brother, sister or old friend you could simply get back in touch with this week?
andrew-brings-his-brother.prayer: Lord, Andrew spent one afternoon with you and went straight to find his brother. Make me glad to bring others, and glad when they go further than me. Bless my family today, especially the ones I find hardest. Amen.
andrew-brings-his-brother.midday: This morning: Andrew, who went to find his brother. Who could you get in touch with this afternoon?
andrew-brings-his-brother.evening: Today's story was St Andrew. Did you bring anyone anything good today? Is there someone in your family you'd like to be closer to?

music.why: Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland, and this is Scotland's best-loved psalm, sung to a tune named after a village in Aberdeenshire.

paras: This is John’s testimony, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”
He declared, and didn’t deny, but he declared, “I am not the Christ.”
They asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?”
He said, “I am not.”
“Are you the prophet?”
He answered, “No.”
They said therefore to him, “Who are you? Give us an answer to take back to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”
He said, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.”
The ones who had been sent were from the Pharisees.
They asked him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”
John answered them, “I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you don’t know.
He is the one who comes after me, who is preferred before me, whose sandal strap I’m not worthy to loosen.”
These things were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
This is he of whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who is preferred before me, for he was before me.’
I didn’t know him, but for this reason I came baptizing in water: that he would be revealed to Israel.”
John testified, saying, “I have seen the Spirit descending like a dove out of heaven, and it remained on him.
I didn’t recognize him, but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘On whomever you will see the Spirit descending and remaining on him is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’
I have seen, and have testified that this is the Son of God.”
Again, the next day, John was standing with two of his disciples,
and he looked at Jesus as he walked, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”
The two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?”
They said to him, “Rabbi” (which is to say, being interpreted, Teacher), “where are you staying?”
He said to them, “Come, and see.”
They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.
One of the two who heard John and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him, and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).
On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, of the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?”
Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!”
Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?”
Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!”
Jesus answered him, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you underneath the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these!”
He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

read.why: On St Andrew's Day, read the chapter where he first appears. Watch how it spreads: John points to Jesus, Andrew finds Simon, Philip finds Nathanael. Each person brings one other.

what-should-we-do.title: What should we do?
what-should-we-do.line: The crowds ask John how to get ready, and his answer is surprisingly ordinary.

story.retell: Crowds walked out from the towns to hear John by the Jordan. He told them bluntly that being descended from Abraham was not enough: they needed to change. So they asked him what to do. His answer was not a ritual or a pilgrimage but everyday fairness. Share your spare coat and your food. Tax collectors, take no more than you are owed. Soldiers, bully no one, and be content with your pay.
story.verse: The multitudes asked him, “What then must we do?” He answered them, “He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none. He who has food, let him do likewise.”

what-should-we-do.artLink: Willem Reuter, a Flemish painter who worked in Rome, painted John preaching in the wilderness about 1665.
what-should-we-do.see: The crowd sits and stands among tall trees: men, women and children in cloaks and headscarves, a few on horseback, many holding tall staffs, as if they have walked a long way. John sits on the left, one hand raised as he speaks, the other holding a small cross wrapped in cloth. A sheep rests beside him. Some of his listeners turn to talk to one another. Beyond them the land opens out to distant hills, with more people and animals in the fields.
what-should-we-do.meaning: When people asked John how to get ready for God, he did not send them to the Temple or into the desert. He sent them home, to their own coats, their own cupboards, their own jobs. Getting ready for God, it turns out, looks a lot like being fair and generous where you already are. The question “what should I do?” usually has an answer close at hand. Quite often it is in the wardrobe.

echo.text: Marcus Aurelius noticed three kinds of people who do good. One expects a return. One doesn't ask, but privately counts the other as in his debt. The third is like a vine that bears its grapes, asks nothing more, and simply goes on to bear again next season. Be like the vine, he told himself.
echo.link: John's answers are vine-like: give the coat, take only what is fair, and move on. No speech, no reward. Marcus wrote it as an emperor; John said it to soldiers and tax collectors. The advice is the same.

what-should-we-do.question: Look in your wardrobe or cupboard today. What do you have two of that someone else has none of? Who could you give it to this week?
what-should-we-do.prayer: Lord, when I ask what I should do, show me the coat I don't need and the person who needs it. Make me fair in my work and content with what I have. Let my getting ready for you be practical. Amen.
what-should-we-do.midday: This morning: John's answer to the crowd: share your spare coat. Is there something you could give away by the end of the day?
what-should-we-do.evening: Today's story was John's plain advice. Were you fair today, in your work and your dealings? Did you share anything?

music.why: Bach's cantata opens with the watchmen's voice calling a sleeping city to wake up and get ready: the call of Advent, and of John.

paras: Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
in the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness.
He came into all the region around the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for remission of sins.
As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet,

“The voice of one crying in the wilderness,
‘Make ready the way of the Lord.
Make his paths straight.

Every valley will be filled.
