Every mountain and hill will be brought low.
The crooked will become straight,
and the rough ways smooth.
All flesh will see God’s salvation.’ ”
He said therefore to the multitudes who went out to be baptized by him, “You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?

Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance, and don’t begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father;’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones!
Even now the ax also lies at the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down, and thrown into the fire.”
The multitudes asked him, “What then must we do?”
He answered them, “He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none. He who has food, let him do likewise.”
Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what must we do?”
He said to them, “Collect no more than that which is appointed to you.”
Soldiers also asked him, saying, “What about us? What must we do?”
He said to them, “Extort from no one by violence, neither accuse anyone wrongfully. Be content with your wages.”
As the people were in expectation, and all men reasoned in their hearts concerning John, whether perhaps he was the Christ,
John answered them all, “I indeed baptize you with water, but he comes who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to loosen. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire,
whose fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, and will gather the wheat into his barn; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”
Then with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people,
but Herod the tetrarch, being reproved by him for Herodias, his brother’s wife, and for all the evil things which Herod had done,
added this also to them all, that he shut up John in prison.
Now when all the people were baptized, Jesus also had been baptized, and was praying. The sky was opened,
and the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form like a dove on him; and a voice came out of the sky, saying “You are my beloved Son. In you I am well pleased.”

read.why: Read John's whole preaching, from the voice in the wilderness to the day Jesus comes to be baptised. Notice how fierce his words are at first, and how ordinary his advice turns out to be.

elijahs-mantle.title: The falling cloak
elijahs-mantle.line: Elijah is taken up in fire, and his cloak falls to the one who stayed with him.

story.retell: Elijah knew his time was ending. Three times he told his young follower Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha refused: “I will not leave you.” By the Jordan, Elijah asked what he could do for him, and Elisha asked for a double share of his spirit. Then a chariot of fire came between them and Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind. Elisha cried out, picked up the cloak that had fallen from him, and struck the river with it, as his master had done.
story.verse: As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha saw it, and he cried, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”

elijahs-mantle.artLink: Giuseppe Angeli, a Venetian painter, painted Elijah going up some time between about 1740 and 1755.
elijahs-mantle.see: Elijah sits in a chariot made of flames, pulled by two white horses climbing a bank of brown clouds. One hand grips his white cloak; the other is flung out wide, and he looks up into the light. On the rock below, Elisha kneels, half turned away from us, arms spread, head tipped back, mouth open. You can see the bare sole of one foot, his toes dug into the rock. Below them the rock slopes down to a blue-green sea.
elijahs-mantle.meaning: Elisha's faithfulness is stubborn. Three times he is told to stay behind, and three times he goes on. He stays to the very end, and so he is there when the cloak falls. Much of what we are given in life comes like this, from people we stayed close to: a parent, a teacher, someone older who showed us how. In Advent, Christians remember that the prophet Malachi promised Elijah would come again before the Lord, and that Jesus said John the Baptist was that Elijah. The cloak keeps being passed on.

echo.text: As Troy burns, Aeneas's old father Anchises refuses to leave. In the end Aeneas lifts him onto his shoulders and carries him out of the city, holding his little son by the hand, while his father holds the sacred images of their household gods. He loses almost everything that night, but he carries his father, and what his father carries, into a new life.
echo.link: Both stories are about receiving from those who went before. Aeneas carries his father out of the fire; Elisha watches his father in faith go up in fire, and picks up his cloak. Neither of them starts from nothing.

elijahs-mantle.question: Whose cloak have you picked up? Who taught you something you still carry? Could you thank them this week, or pass it on to someone younger?
elijahs-mantle.prayer: Lord, thank you for those who went before me and left me something good. Make me faithful like Elisha, who would not leave. And let me pass on what I was given. Amen.
elijahs-mantle.midday: This morning: Elisha picking up Elijah's cloak. Think of one person whose example you still carry.
elijahs-mantle.evening: Today's story was Elijah's falling cloak. Who did you think of today? Did you pass anything on?

music.why: Mendelssohn's oratorio tells Elijah's whole story, and near the end the choir sings of the fiery chariot and horses that took him to heaven in a whirlwind.

paras: When Yahweh was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
Elijah said to Elisha, “Please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me as far as Bethel.”
Elisha said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they went down to Bethel.
The sons of the prophets who were at Bethel came out to Elisha, and said to him, “Do you know that Yahweh will take away your master from your head today?”
He said, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.”
Elijah said to him, “Elisha, please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me to Jericho.”
He said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So they came to Jericho.
The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho came near to Elisha, and said to him, “Do you know that Yahweh will take away your master from your head today?”
He answered, “Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.”
Elijah said to him, “Please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me to the Jordan.”
He said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” Then they both went on.
Fifty men of the sons of the prophets went, and stood opposite them at a distance; and they both stood by the Jordan.
Elijah took his mantle, and rolled it up, and struck the waters, and they were divided here and there, so that they both went over on dry ground.
When they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.”
Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.”
He said, “You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be so for you; but if not, it will not be so.”
As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
Elisha saw it, and he cried, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”
He saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes, and tore them in two pieces.
He also took up Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and went back, and stood by the bank of the Jordan.
He took Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and struck the waters, and said, “Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah?” When he also had struck the waters, they were divided apart, and Elisha went over.
When the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho facing him saw him, they said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.” They came to meet him, and bowed themselves to the ground before him.

They said to him, “See now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. Perhaps Yahweh’s Spirit has taken him up, and put him on some mountain, or into some valley.”
He said, “Don’t send them.”
When they urged him until he was ashamed, he said, “Send them.”
Therefore they sent fifty men; and they searched for three days, but didn’t find him.
They came back to him, while he stayed at Jericho; and he said to them, “Didn’t I tell you, ‘Don’t go?’ ”

read.why: Read the whole of Elijah's last walk. Notice the three times Elisha is told to wait, and his answer each time. The last words of the Old Testament, in Malachi, promise that Elijah will come again to prepare the way; the Gospels see him in John.

john-tells-the-truth.title: It is not lawful
john-tells-the-truth.line: John tells a king the truth, and it costs him his life.

story.retell: John told King Herod plainly that he had no right to marry his brother's wife, Herodias, and Herod had him thrown into prison. Yet Herod also respected John, and liked to listen to him. At his birthday feast, delighted by a girl's dance, Herod swore to give her anything she asked. Prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head, and Herod, unwilling to break his oath in front of his guests, gave the order.
story.verse: For John said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”

john-tells-the-truth.artLink: Benozzo Gozzoli painted the feast and the beheading together on one small panel, in Florence, in 1461 and 1462.
john-tells-the-truth.see: Gozzoli paints the whole story in one room. In the middle, a fair-haired girl in blue and yellow dances, one foot kicked up behind her. At the long table the bearded king in red watches her, a hand on his chest and a knife in the other. On the left, in a small stone cell, John kneels in prayer while a soldier in armour raises his sword. And at the back, in an alcove, the girl kneels again before her mother, with John's head on a silver plate.
john-tells-the-truth.meaning: Herod is the most human person in the room. He knows John is good. He likes hearing him. But he has made a promise in front of important people, and he cannot bear to lose face. So he does what he knows is wrong. John, meanwhile, has nothing left but his integrity, and he keeps it. Preparing the way can mean telling the truth to someone powerful, kindly and plainly, and accepting what it costs.

echo.text: King Creon forbids anyone to bury the rebel Polynices. His sister Antigone buries him anyway, and when she is caught she tells the king that his order cannot override the unwritten, unchanging laws of the gods. Creon, unwilling to back down in public, has her shut up alive in a rocky tomb. By the time he changes his mind, it is too late.
echo.link: Two rulers who would not lose face, and two people who would not stay silent. Antigone and John both answered to a law higher than a king's word, and both paid for it. Herod, like Creon, was sorry, and did it anyway.

john-tells-the-truth.question: Is there a truth you've been avoiding saying, kindly, to someone who needs to hear it? Or a promise you're keeping only to save face?
john-tells-the-truth.prayer: Lord, give me John's courage to say what is true, and the kindness to say it well. Free me from caring too much what the guests will think. And strengthen all who suffer today for telling the truth. Amen.
john-tells-the-truth.midday: This morning: John, who told a king the truth. Is there anything you're saying, or not saying, just to save face?
john-tells-the-truth.evening: Today's story was John's courage before Herod. Did you tell the truth today when it would have been easier not to? Did you do anything just to save face?

music.why: William Byrd wrote this Mass for Catholics worshipping in secret in Elizabethan England: music by a man who would not pretend to be other than he was, whatever it cost.

paras: King Herod heard this, for his name had become known, and he said, “John the Baptizer has risen from the dead, and therefore these powers are at work in him.”
But others said, “He is Elijah.” Others said, “He is a prophet, or like one of the prophets.”
But Herod, when he heard this, said, “This is John, whom I beheaded. He has risen from the dead.”
For Herod himself had sent out and arrested John, and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, for he had married her.
For John said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
Herodias set herself against him, and desired to kill him, but she couldn’t,
for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe. When he heard him, he did many things, and he heard him gladly.
Then a convenient day came, that Herod on his birthday made a supper for his nobles, the high officers, and the chief men of Galilee.
When the daughter of Herodias herself came in and danced, she pleased Herod and those sitting with him. The king said to the young lady, “Ask me whatever you want, and I will give it to you.”
He swore to her, “Whatever you shall ask of me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.”
She went out, and said to her mother, “What shall I ask?”
She said, “The head of John the Baptizer.”
She came in immediately with haste to the king, and asked, “I want you to give me right now the head of John the Baptizer on a platter.”
The king was exceedingly sorry, but for the sake of his oaths, and of his dinner guests, he didn’t wish to refuse her.
Immediately the king sent out a soldier of his guard, and commanded to bring John’s head, and he went and beheaded him in the prison,
and brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the young lady; and the young lady gave it to her mother.
When his disciples heard this, they came and took up his corpse, and laid it in a tomb.

read.why: Read the whole story, starting with Herod's guilty fear that Jesus is John come back to life. Mark tells it in the middle of the disciples' first mission, as a warning of what faithfulness can cost.

walking-on-the-water.title: It is I
walking-on-the-water.line: The Second Sunday of Advent, and St Nicholas's Day: in the darkest hours of the night, Jesus comes to his friends across the water.

story.retell: Jesus sent the disciples across the lake by boat while he went up a mountain to pray alone. In the night a wind rose against them, and they spent hours fighting the waves. Before dawn Jesus came to them, walking on the water, and they cried out in terror, thinking he was a ghost. “It is I,” he said. Peter asked to come to him, stepped out, began to sink, and cried, “Lord, save me!” At once Jesus reached out and caught him.
story.verse: But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.”

walking-on-the-water.artLink: This storm was painted in Venice in the 1570s by an artist close to Tintoretto, probably Lambert Sustris.
walking-on-the-water.see: Sea and sky take up almost everything: choppy waves and swirling clouds in every blue from topaz to navy. Near us, Jesus stands at the water's edge with his back to us, one arm raised towards the boat; you cannot quite tell whether his bare feet are on land or water. In the boat seven men are each doing something different. One leans over to grab a net, one pulls a rope for the sail. At the back, one looks far into the distance. And one is beginning to step out onto the water.
walking-on-the-water.meaning: The disciples spent most of the night rowing against the wind, and Jesus came in the fourth watch, the darkest hours before dawn. He didn't calm the storm first. He came into it, and his first words were, “It is I. Don't be afraid.” Peter's courage lasted a few steps; then he looked at the wind and sank. What saved him was not his faith but a hand. Advent is for people in the middle of the night, still rowing. The light doesn't always come as morning. Sometimes it comes as someone walking towards you across the dark. Today is also St Nicholas's Day: among much else, he is the patron saint of sailors.

echo.text: Odysseus is alone on a raft when the sea god raises a storm and smashes it to pieces. As he clings to a single beam, the sea goddess Ino rises from the waves like a seabird and takes pity on him. She gives him her veil and tells him to tie it round himself and swim. Two days and nights later, half dead, he reaches land.
echo.link: Two men alone in a storm, both saved by someone who comes to them over the water. Ino gives Odysseus a veil and tells him to swim. Jesus doesn't send anything: he comes himself, and takes Peter by the hand.

walking-on-the-water.question: Where in your life are you rowing against the wind at the moment? And who is someone else in the dark that you could reach a hand out to this week?
walking-on-the-water.prayer: Lord Jesus, you came to your friends in the darkest hours of the night. When I am rowing against the wind, come to me. When I start to sink, catch me. And make my hand ready for someone else who is going under. Amen.
walking-on-the-water.midday: This morning: Jesus walking across the dark water: “It is I.” Whose hand could you take this afternoon?
walking-on-the-water.evening: Today's story was the night on the lake. Where did you feel the wind against you today? Did a hand reach you, or did you reach out to someone?

music.why: U2 set Psalm 40, the prayer of someone lifted out of the pit and set on a rock, as Peter was lifted out of the waves.

paras: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat, to a deserted place apart. When the multitudes heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities.
Jesus went out, and he saw a great multitude. He had compassion on them, and healed their sick.

When evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, “This place is deserted, and the hour is already late. Send the multitudes away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves food.”
But Jesus said to them, “They don’t need to go away. You give them something to eat.”
They told him, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.”
He said, “Bring them here to me.”

He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave to the multitudes.
They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces.
Those who ate were about five thousand men, in addition to women and children.
Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away.
After he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray. When evening had come, he was there alone.
But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, distressed by the waves, for the wind was contrary.
In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea.
When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It’s a ghost!” and they cried out for fear.
But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.”
Peter answered him and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.”
He said, “Come!”
Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus.
But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!”
Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
When they got up into the boat, the wind ceased.
Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “You are truly the Son of God!”

read.why: The second week of Advent is about light in the dark. Read the long day that led to this night: Jesus feeds five thousand people, sends everyone away, prays alone, and then walks out to his friends on the water.

drawn-from-the-water.title: Drawn from the water
drawn-from-the-water.line: In a cruel time, the king's own daughter hears a baby crying, and is kind.

story.retell: Pharaoh had ordered every newborn Hebrew boy to be thrown into the Nile. One mother hid her son for three months, then laid him in a basket of reeds coated with tar and set it among the rushes by the river, while his sister watched. Pharaoh's own daughter came down to bathe, found the basket, and saw the baby crying. She knew whose child he was, and she took pity on him. She named him Moses, because she had drawn him out of the water.
story.verse: She opened it, and saw the child, and behold, the baby cried. She had compassion on him, and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”

drawn-from-the-water.artLink: Paolo Veronese painted the princess finding Moses in Venice, about 1581 to 1582, and dressed her as a great Venetian lady.
drawn-from-the-water.see: The princess stands at the centre in a dress of silver and gold brocade, pearls in her blond hair, leaning to speak to the woman beside her. Her ladies gather round, and one kneels at the lower left holding the naked baby, while an older woman holds up a cloth to wrap him. A jester in navy and crimson stands with a recorder. Down in the riverbed a man holds a basket. Beyond them, a bridge crosses the river to a town under blue hills.
drawn-from-the-water.meaning: It was a dark time: a king had decided that some babies didn't count. Into that darkness came small lights. A mother who hid her son. A sister who kept watch, and spoke up at the right moment. And a princess who saw a crying baby and could not look away. She was the daughter of the man who gave the order, and she broke it anyway. Light in the dark is often like this: not a blaze, but one person's compassion at the right moment, refusing the cruelty of their own side.

echo.from: Livy, The History of Rome, Book 1
echo.text: When the twins Romulus and Remus were born, the king who had seized their grandfather's throne ordered them to be thrown into the Tiber. But the river was in flood, and the men left the babies in the shallows. As the water went down, a she-wolf found them and fed them, and a shepherd took them home to his wife to bring up.
echo.link: Rome and Israel both remembered their founders as babies left by a river under a king's sentence of death. In Livy, a wolf takes pity. In Exodus, it is the king's own daughter: compassion found in the house of the enemy.

drawn-from-the-water.question: Who in your world is easy to treat as not counting? Is there one small thing you could do this week to notice them, as the princess noticed the crying baby?
drawn-from-the-water.prayer: Lord, thank you for the small lights in dark times: the mother, the sister, the princess. Give me eyes to see the one who is crying, and the courage to be kind even when my own side isn't. Amen.
drawn-from-the-water.midday: This morning: a princess who heard a baby crying and chose to be kind. Who might be crying, quietly, near you this afternoon?
drawn-from-the-water.evening: Today's story was Moses drawn from the water. Did you notice anyone today whom others overlook? Were you a small light for anyone?

music.why: Vivaldi wrote his Gloria for the girls of the Pietà in Venice, a home for abandoned children: foundlings, like Moses, who were taken in and given a voice.

paras: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who didn’t know Joseph.
He said to his people, “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we.
Come, let’s deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it happen that when any war breaks out, they also join themselves to our enemies and fight against us, and escape out of the land.”
Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens. They built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Raamses.
But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and the more they spread out. They started to dread the children of Israel.
The Egyptians ruthlessly made the children of Israel serve,
and they made their lives bitter with hard service in mortar and in brick, and in all kinds of service in the field, all their service, in which they ruthlessly made them serve.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, of whom the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah,
and he said, “When you perform the duty of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them on the birth stool, if it is a son, then you shall kill him; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.”
But the midwives feared God, and didn’t do what the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the baby boys alive.
The king of Egypt called for the midwives, and said to them, “Why have you done this thing and saved the boys alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “Because the Hebrew women aren’t like the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them.”
God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied, and grew very mighty.
Because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.
Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “You shall cast every son who is born into the river, and every daughter you shall save alive.”
A man of the house of Levi went and took a daughter of Levi as his wife.
The woman conceived and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
When she could no longer hide him, she took a papyrus basket for him, and coated it with tar and with pitch. She put the child in it, and laid it in the reeds by the river’s bank.
His sister stood far off, to see what would be done to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe at the river. Her maidens walked along by the riverside. She saw the basket among the reeds, and sent her servant to get it.
She opened it, and saw the child, and behold, the baby cried. She had compassion on him, and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Should I go and call a nurse for you from the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Go.”
The young woman went and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child away, and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.”
The woman took the child, and nursed it.
The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, and said, “Because I drew him out of the water.”

read.why: Read how the darkness grew before the light came: a new king who feared the Hebrews, the brave midwives who refused his order, and then the basket in the reeds. Notice how many women save the day.

light-on-the-road.title: Light on the road
light-on-the-road.line: A light from heaven throws a persecutor to the ground, and a frightened man is sent to open his eyes.

story.retell: Saul was on his way to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus when a light from the sky flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He got up blind, and was led by the hand into the city, where for three days he neither ate nor drank. Then God sent a disciple called Ananias, who was afraid of Saul, to lay his hands on him. Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see.
story.verse: As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him. He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”

light-on-the-road.artLink: The young Jacopo Tintoretto painted Saul thrown to the ground in Venice, about 1544.
light-on-the-road.see: Chaos on a riverbank: about two dozen men and more than a dozen horses tumbling in every direction. At the bottom centre Saul lies sprawled across some stone steps in a teal tunic and pink cape, arms raised, palms out, looking back and up. His helmet, shield and armour lie scattered in the grass. A rider on a rearing white horse clutches his head with both hands. Men and horses flail in the river. And at the top left, from a bank of white clouds, a bearded figure in pink and blue leans out over it all with an open hand.
light-on-the-road.meaning: The light that stopped Saul didn't make everything clear at once. It made him blind. For three days he sat in the dark, eating nothing, the man who had been so sure. Real change often feels like that: one blinding moment, then a long dark wait. And the light came back to him through someone else. Ananias was frightened of him and went anyway, put his hands on his old enemy, and called him “Brother Saul”. Sometimes we are Saul, waiting in the dark. Sometimes we are Ananias, sent to someone we would rather avoid.

echo.text: Plato imagines prisoners chained in a cave who have only ever seen shadows on a wall. If one were freed and dragged up into the sunlight, he says, the light would at first hurt his eyes so much that he could see nothing. Only slowly, looking first at shadows and reflections, would he learn to see things as they are, and at last the sun itself.
echo.link: Plato knew that the first effect of real light can be blindness. Saul found it so: the light that showed him the truth left him in the dark for three days. In both, learning to see takes time. In Acts, it also takes a friend.

light-on-the-road.question: Is there someone you've written off, as Ananias had written off Saul? What would it take to treat them as a brother or sister this week?
light-on-the-road.prayer: Lord Jesus, you stopped Saul with your light and opened his eyes through a frightened friend. When your light dazzles me, stay with me in the dark until I see. And send me, like Ananias, to someone I would rather avoid. Amen.
light-on-the-road.midday: This morning: Saul blinded on the road, and Ananias sent to him. Who might you be sent to this afternoon?
light-on-the-road.evening: Today's story was the light on the Damascus road. Did anything stop you in your tracks today? Who did you find hard to treat as a brother or sister?

music.why: John Newton, a former captain of slave ships, wrote of being blind and then seeing: a turning round as complete as Saul's.

paras: But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.
He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
He said, “Who are you, Lord?”
The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do.”
The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one.
Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus.
He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.
Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!”
He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.”
The Lord said to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying,
and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem.
Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”
But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel.
For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”

Ananias departed and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.
He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.
Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God.
All who heard him were amazed, and said, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!”
But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ.

read.why: Read the whole of Saul's turning round, including the part people forget: Ananias's fear, and his courage. The man who came to arrest Christians is speaking for Jesus in Damascus within days.

a-great-light.title: A great light
a-great-light.line: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light: an old picture of Christ reaching into the deepest dark.

story.retell: Isaiah promised a day when the people who walked in darkness would see a great light, even in the land of the shadow of death. The first letter of Peter says that after his death Christ went and preached to the spirits in prison. From these lines grew one of the oldest Christian pictures: Christ going down into the place of the dead, breaking down its doors, and leading out by the hand all who had waited there, beginning with Adam and Eve. The creeds say it simply: he descended to the dead.
story.verse: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. The light has shined on those who lived in the land of the shadow of death.

a-great-light.artLink: Benvenuto di Giovanni of Siena painted this, probably in 1491, as one of a series of small panels of Christ’s death and rising.
a-great-light.see: Jesus, seen from behind, wrapped in a white cloth and carrying a white banner with a red cross, steps barefoot onto a door that has fallen flat. Pinned underneath it is a small red demon. In front of him, more than two dozen men and women are crowded into a box-like prison set in the rock, every face turned up to him. He has taken the wrist of an old man with a long white beard, in a fur garment, with a hoe hooked over his knee. A second man, in yellow, grips Jesus' wrist with both hands.
a-great-light.meaning: Isaiah's light shines on those in “the land of the shadow of death”. The early Christians took that further than we might dare: there is no darkness so deep that Christ has not gone down into it. In the old pictures of this scene, the first person he takes by the hand is Adam, the one we met hiding in the garden, and here the old man with the hoe, the first gardener, seems to be him. Benvenuto paints it as a rescue: a door broken in and a hand round a wrist. Whatever dark you are in, or someone you love is in, this is Advent's boldest claim: the light comes all the way down.

echo.text: When his wife Eurydice dies, the singer Orpheus goes down to the underworld and sings so beautifully that its rulers let her go, on one condition: he must not look back until they reach the light. Just short of the edge, afraid she isn't following, he turns. She slips back into the dark, and he loses her a second time.
echo.link: The ancient world told of a descent to the dead that failed at the last step. The Christian picture is the reverse: Christ goes down, comes back up holding them by the hand, and does not let go.

a-great-light.question: Who do you know who is in a dark place at the moment? What would it look like to go a little way into it with them this week: a visit, a letter, a meal?
a-great-light.prayer: Lord Jesus, there is no darkness you have not entered. Reach into the dark places in me, and into the lives of those I love who cannot see the way out. Take us by the hand, and lead us into your light. Amen.
a-great-light.midday: This morning: Christ reaching into the darkest place and taking hold of a hand. Whose hand could you hold this afternoon?
a-great-light.evening: Today's story was the light that went all the way down. Where was it dark today? Did you go towards anyone in their darkness?

music.why: MacMillan sets the ancient Advent prayer to Christ the dawn, which asks him to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death: Isaiah's own words.

paras: When they tell you, “Consult with those who have familiar spirits and with the wizards, who chirp and who mutter,” shouldn’t a people consult with their God? Should they consult the dead on behalf of the living?
Turn to the law and to the covenant! If they don’t speak according to this word, surely there is no morning for them.
They will pass through it, very distressed and hungry. It will happen that when they are hungry, they will worry, and curse by their king and by their God. They will turn their faces upward,
and look to the earth, and see distress, darkness, and the gloom of anguish. They will be driven into thick darkness.

But there shall be no more gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time, he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali; but in the latter time he has made it glorious, by the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.
The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.
The light has shined on those who lived in the land of the shadow of death.

You have multiplied the nation.
You have increased their joy.
They rejoice before you according to the joy in harvest, as men rejoice when they divide the plunder.
For the yoke of his burden, and the staff of his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as in the day of Midian.
For all the armor of the armed man in the noisy battle, and the garments rolled in blood, will be for burning, fuel for the fire.
For a child is born to us. A son is given to us; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on David’s throne, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will perform this.

read.why: This is the prophecy at the heart of the week. Read how Isaiah describes the darkness first, distress and gloom with nowhere to turn, before the light breaks and a child is born.

immanuel-god-with-us.title: God with us
immanuel-god-with-us.line: A frightened king refuses to ask for a sign, and is given one anyway: a child called God-with-us.

story.retell: About seven hundred years before Jesus, two neighbouring kings marched on Jerusalem, and the young king Ahaz and his people shook like trees in the wind. The prophet Isaiah went out to meet him and told him to stay calm and trust God, and even to ask for a sign. Ahaz refused, piously, because he had already made his own plans. Isaiah answered that God would give a sign anyway.
story.verse: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

immanuel-god-with-us.artLink: Duccio painted Isaiah holding this very promise beside the Nativity, for the great altarpiece of Siena Cathedral, between 1308 and 1311.
immanuel-god-with-us.see: On the left panel stands Isaiah, grey-bearded, in a lilac cloak over coral orange. He holds out an unrolled scroll and points one finger upward. The words on it are Latin for “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Immanuel.” In the centre, his promise has come true: Mary rests in a blue robe beside a swaddled baby in a manger, an ox and a donkey looking on, a star sending thin gold rays down onto the roof. To the right, an angel holds out a scroll to two shepherds and their dog: “I bring you tidings of great joy.”
immanuel-god-with-us.meaning: Ahaz didn't want a sign, because a sign might ask him to trust instead of scheme. God gave him one anyway, and its name is the whole of Advent in two words: God with us. Not God above us, watching, or God against us, keeping score, but with us, in the middle of our fear and our plans. Today is Gaudete Sunday, the Sunday of “rejoice”, when many churches light a rose-pink Advent candle. It is also St Lucy's day, whose name means light; in the old calendar her feast fell on what was reckoned the shortest day of the year. The joy is not that the danger has gone. It is that someone has come to be in it with us.

echo.text: Seneca told his young friend that there was no need to lift his hands to the sky or ask a temple keeper to let him near a statue's ear, as if that would help his prayers be heard. God is near you, he wrote; he is with you; he is within you.
echo.link: A Roman philosopher reached the edge of the idea Isaiah announced: that God is not far off. Isaiah's promise goes further than Seneca's: God would not only be near us, he would be born as one of us.

immanuel-god-with-us.question: Where are you making your own plans in a hurry, like Ahaz, because you don't quite trust anyone else to be with you in it? Who could you let in today?
immanuel-god-with-us.prayer: God with us, you came close when we were afraid and busy with our own schemes. Come close to me now, in the thing I am most anxious about. Give me the joy that doesn't wait for the danger to pass, because you are already here. Amen.
immanuel-god-with-us.midday: This morning: a promise to a frightened king, a child called God-with-us. Whatever this afternoon holds, you are not in it alone.
immanuel-god-with-us.evening: Today's story was the sign of Immanuel. Where did you notice that you were not alone today? Was there someone you were with, when they needed it?

music.why: The Advent hymn takes its name and its longing straight from this verse: Emmanuel, God with us, the child Isaiah promised.

paras: In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.
David’s house was told, “Syria is allied with Ephraim.” His heart trembled, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the forest tremble with the wind.
Then Yahweh said to Isaiah, “Go out now to meet Ahaz, you, and Shearjashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller’s field.

Tell him, ‘Be careful, and keep calm. Don’t be afraid, neither let your heart be faint because of these two tails of smoking torches, for the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria, and of the son of Remaliah.
Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have plotted evil against you, saying,
“Let’s go up against Judah, and tear it apart, and let’s divide it among ourselves, and set up a king within it, even the son of Tabeel.”
This is what the Lord Yahweh says: “It shall not stand, neither shall it happen.”
For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. Within sixty-five years Ephraim shall be broken in pieces, so that it shall not be a people.
The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.’ ”
Yahweh spoke again to Ahaz, saying,
“Ask a sign of Yahweh your God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.”
But Ahaz said, “I won’t ask. I won’t tempt Yahweh.”
He said, “Listen now, house of David. Is it not enough for you to try the patience of men, that you will try the patience of my God also?
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
He shall eat butter and honey when he knows to refuse the evil and choose the good.
For before the child knows to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you abhor shall be forsaken.

read.why: Read the whole scene, from the king's fear to the promise. Notice Ahaz's polite refusal, “I won't tempt the Lord”, which is really a way of keeping God at arm's length. Advent begins to turn from waiting to arriving here.

joseph-quietly.title: A quiet decency
joseph-quietly.line: Joseph learns that Mary is expecting a child that isn't his, and decides not to shame her.

story.retell: Joseph, a builder in Nazareth, was engaged to Mary. In their world an engagement was as binding as a marriage. Then he found out that she was pregnant, and he knew the child was not his. The law gave him the right to accuse her publicly. He decided instead to end the engagement quietly, so that she would not be disgraced.
story.verse: Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly.

joseph-quietly.artLink: An unknown French painter showed Mary expecting her child, with Joseph close behind her, in about 1425–50.
joseph-quietly.see: Mary kneels in a dark blue cloak lined with green, one hand resting on her belly. A small angel at her shoulder holds one of her fingers and looks up at her face. Behind a red and gold curtain stands Joseph, grey-haired under a white cloth, in a red robe. He clutches a crutch and a green book to his chest. He is very close to her, but the curtain is between them. Above, two red angels hold a crown in the dark blue sky.
joseph-quietly.meaning: Matthew calls Joseph “righteous”, and then shows what that means. He had been hurt, and the law was on his side. He could have protected his own name at the cost of hers. Instead he chose the course that cost him and spared her, and he chose it before any angel had explained anything. Real goodness often looks like this: not a public stand, but a private decision not to humiliate someone, even when you could, even when you're in the right.

echo.text: Cicero quoted a saying that was already a proverb in his day: “the more law, the more injustice”. He meant that people often do wrong by sticking to the letter of their rights, using the law to its last inch against someone else.
echo.link: Joseph had the law on his side, and refused to use it to the full. Cicero saw that strict rights can become cruelty. Joseph saw a frightened young woman, and chose mercy over his rights.

joseph-quietly.question: Is there someone you could shame or embarrass, perhaps with good reason? What would it look like to protect their dignity today instead, quietly, without anyone knowing?
joseph-quietly.prayer: Lord, Joseph was hurt, and still chose not to hurt. Give me his quiet decency. When I am in the right, keep me from using it as a weapon. Teach me to guard other people's dignity, as you guard mine. Amen.
joseph-quietly.midday: This morning: Joseph, deciding quietly not to shame Mary. Whose dignity could you protect this afternoon?
joseph-quietly.evening: Today's story was Joseph's quiet decency. Did you have a chance today to embarrass someone, and let it go? Did someone spare you?

music.why: A hymn about faithfulness shown not in grand moments but “morning by morning”: the plain, steady goodness Joseph lived.

paras: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
Abraham became the father of Isaac. Isaac became the father of Jacob. Jacob became the father of Judah and his brothers.
Judah became the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Perez became the father of Hezron. Hezron became the father of Ram.
Ram became the father of Amminadab. Amminadab became the father of Nahshon. Nahshon became the father of Salmon.
Salmon became the father of Boaz by Rahab. Boaz became the father of Obed by Ruth. Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of King David. David became the father of Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s wife.
Solomon became the father of Rehoboam. Rehoboam became the father of Abijah. Abijah became the father of Asa.
Asa became the father of Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat became the father of Joram. Joram became the father of Uzziah.
Uzziah became the father of Jotham. Jotham became the father of Ahaz. Ahaz became the father of Hezekiah.
Hezekiah became the father of Manasseh. Manasseh became the father of Amon. Amon became the father of Josiah.
Josiah became the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the exile to Babylon.
After the exile to Babylon, Jechoniah became the father of Shealtiel. Shealtiel became the father of Zerubbabel.
Zerubbabel became the father of Abiud. Abiud became the father of Eliakim. Eliakim became the father of Azor.
Azor became the father of Zadok. Zadok became the father of Achim. Achim became the father of Eliud.
Eliud became the father of Eleazar. Eleazar became the father of Matthan. Matthan became the father of Jacob.
Jacob became the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.

So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the exile to Babylon fourteen generations; and from the carrying away to Babylon to the Christ, fourteen generations.
Now the birth of Jesus Christ was like this: After his mother, Mary, was engaged to Joseph, before they came together, she was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit.
Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly.

read.why: Matthew opens with Jesus's family tree before he reaches Joseph. Read it slowly: among the kings are four women with complicated stories, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba. Then comes Joseph, facing a complicated story of his own.

joseph-takes-mary-home.title: Don't be afraid
joseph-takes-mary-home.line: An angel tells Joseph in a dream not to be afraid. He wakes up and takes Mary home.

story.retell: Joseph had made up his mind to end the engagement quietly. While he was still thinking it over, an angel came to him in a dream and told him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife, because her child was from God, and he was to name him Jesus. Joseph woke up, and did it. He married her, and the child would grow up as his son.
story.verse: Joseph arose from his sleep, and did as the angel of the Lord commanded him, and took his wife to himself.

joseph-takes-mary-home.artLink: Luca Signorelli painted Joseph and Mary's wedding in about 1490–91. Matthew says only that Joseph “took his wife”; painters filled in the scene from later legend.
joseph-takes-mary-home.see: In a long room full of people, an old priest in white robes and a tall mitre holds the hands of the couple in front of him. Joseph is balding and bearded; Mary is young, with honey-blond hair, and they reach towards each other. On the left a man plays a lute, and others are breaking sticks: in the old legend, the other suitors broke their rods in disappointment. At the far right an old woman in black screws up her eyes and holds up a hand. Few of the guests are looking at the couple at all.
joseph-takes-mary-home.meaning: “Don't be afraid” is one of the most repeated commands in the Bible, and Joseph needed it. Marrying Mary meant raising a child who was not his, and living with what the neighbours would say. What strikes you about Joseph is that he never says a word in the Gospels. He simply wakes up and does it. Sometimes faith is not a feeling or an argument, just getting up in the morning and doing the brave, kind thing you were told in the night.

echo.text: In Genesis, Jacob's son Joseph was a dreamer. His brothers sold him into Egypt, but he trusted his dreams, rose to power there, and saved his whole family from famine. Matthew tells us that the father of Mary's Joseph was also called Jacob.
echo.link: Matthew sets the two Josephs side by side: each a son of Jacob, each guided by dreams, each bringing his family into Egypt to keep them alive. The first Joseph saved a family. The second makes a home for the one who will save everyone.

joseph-takes-mary-home.question: What are you afraid to take on, though you sense it is the right thing: a commitment, a person, a responsibility? What would it look like to wake up and simply do it?
joseph-takes-mary-home.prayer: Lord, you told Joseph not to be afraid, and he got up and did what you asked. When I am afraid of what the right thing will cost, speak to me again. Give me his silence, his courage and his faithfulness. Amen.
joseph-takes-mary-home.midday: This morning: Joseph woke and did what he had been told in the night. Is there something brave and kind you could just do this afternoon?
joseph-takes-mary-home.evening: Today's story was Joseph's dream. Did fear hold you back from anything today? What would you do tomorrow if you weren't afraid?

music.why: “Sleepers, wake”: Bach's cantata is about waking up ready to go and meet what God is bringing, which is exactly what Joseph did.

paras: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was like this: After his mother, Mary, was engaged to Joseph, before they came together, she was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit.
Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly.

But when he thought about these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, don’t be afraid to take to yourself Mary, your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit.
She shall give birth to a son. You shall name him Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.”
Now all this has happened that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying,

“Behold, the virgin shall be with child,
and shall give birth to a son.
They shall call his name Immanuel;”
which is, being interpreted, “God with us.”
Joseph arose from his sleep, and did as the angel of the Lord commanded him, and took his wife to himself;
and didn’t know her sexually until she had given birth to her firstborn son. He named him Jesus.

read.why: Read the whole of Matthew's account of Jesus's birth. It is told entirely from Joseph's side. He is the one who doubts, dreams, wakes and names the child, and Matthew stops to say what it all means: Immanuel, God with us.

zechariah-his-name-is-john.title: After the silence
zechariah-his-name-is-john.line: An old priest who could not speak for nine months writes four words, and his voice comes back as a song.

story.retell: Zechariah, an old priest, had doubted an angel's promise that his elderly wife Elizabeth would have a son, and he had been unable to speak ever since. When the baby was born, the relatives wanted to name him after his father. Elizabeth said no, he would be called John. They turned to Zechariah, who asked for a writing tablet.
story.verse: He asked for a writing tablet, and wrote, “His name is John.” They all marveled. His mouth was opened immediately and his tongue freed, and he spoke, blessing God.

zechariah-his-name-is-john.artLink: Giovanni Baronzio, a painter from Rimini, painted the birth and naming in about 1335.
zechariah-his-name-is-john.see: On the left, Elizabeth lies in bed under a bright red cover, while two women look after the swaddled baby. In front, on a bench, sits Zechariah, balding and grey-bearded, brows furrowed, writing on a sheet braced on his knee. The Latin words on it mean “His name is John.” A man beside him gestures at him with both hands. To the right, the same baby is held by a man in green for the ceremony of the eighth day, with others crowding round.
zechariah-his-name-is-john.meaning: Zechariah's nine months of silence were a consequence of his doubt, but they turned into something else: a long time to listen. When his voice came back, his first words were not a complaint but a blessing, and then a song about a dawn coming to people sitting in darkness. Silence is not wasted time. It can be where our doubts are slowly turned into praise. And sometimes the first step out of it is small and practical: a name written down, a promise kept.

echo.text: Plutarch wrote a whole essay against chatter. He observed that we learn to speak from other people, but we learn silence from the gods, and that the person who cannot hold his tongue never really listens.
echo.link: Zechariah learned silence the hard way, from God. Plutarch would have recognised what it did: when Zechariah spoke again, he had something worth saying.

zechariah-his-name-is-john.question: Is there a silence you could keep today: a complaint, a criticism, an opinion nobody needs? And is there a word of blessing you've been holding back that you could finally say?
zechariah-his-name-is-john.prayer: Blessed be the Lord, who comes to visit his people. Lord, teach me the silence that listens, and then open my mouth to bless. Let the dawn from on high shine on all who sit in darkness tonight. Amen.
zechariah-his-name-is-john.midday: This morning: Zechariah, silent for nine months, wrote four words and began to sing. Keep a small silence this afternoon, and notice what you hear.
zechariah-his-name-is-john.evening: Today's story was Zechariah's song. Did you keep a silence today, or speak a blessing? Which was harder?

music.why: Arvo Pärt fell silent as a composer for years, and came back with this slow, simple music. Like Zechariah's song, it was made out of a long silence.

paras: Now the time that Elizabeth should give birth was fulfilled, and she gave birth to a son.
Her neighbors and her relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.
On the eighth day, they came to circumcise the child; and they would have called him Zacharias, after the name of his father.
His mother answered, “Not so; but he will be called John.”
They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who is called by this name.”
They made signs to his father, what he would have him called.
He asked for a writing tablet, and wrote, “His name is John.”
They all marveled.
His mouth was opened immediately and his tongue freed, and he spoke, blessing God.
Fear came on all who lived around them, and all these sayings were talked about throughout all the hill country of Judea.
All who heard them laid them up in their heart, saying, “What then will this child be?” The hand of the Lord was with him.
His father Zacharias was filled with the Holy Spirit, and prophesied, saying,

“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,
for he has visited and redeemed his people;
and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David
(as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old),
salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;

to show mercy toward our fathers,
to remember his holy covenant,
the oath which he swore to Abraham our father,

to grant to us that we, being delivered out of the hand of our enemies,
should serve him without fear,
in holiness and righteousness before him all the days of our life.

And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High;
for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways,
to give knowledge of salvation to his people by the remission of their sins,

because of the tender mercy of our God,
by which the dawn from on high will visit us,

to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death;
to guide our feet into the way of peace.”
The child was growing and becoming strong in spirit, and was in the desert until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

read.why: Read the naming and then Zechariah's song, the Benedictus, which Christians have sung at morning prayer for many centuries. Notice how it ends: a dawn breaking over people in darkness, guiding their feet into peace.

the-road-to-bethlehem.title: The long road
the-road-to-bethlehem.line: An emperor orders a census, and a pregnant woman has to make a hard journey.

story.retell: Far away in Rome, the emperor Augustus ordered a count of everyone in his empire. So Joseph had to go to Bethlehem, his family's town, some eighty or ninety miles south of Nazareth, with Mary, who was heavily pregnant. Nobody asked whether it was a good time. While they were there, the baby came.
story.verse: Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David; to enroll himself with Mary, who was pledged to be married to him as wife, being pregnant.

the-road-to-bethlehem.artLink: Fra Filippo Lippi and his workshop painted the journey's end in about 1445: Joseph, worn out, still has his travelling bag on his shoulder.
the-road-to-bethlehem.see: On the left, Joseph sits on the grass at the foot of steep green hills, his knee drawn up, his head resting on his hand, his eyes closed. A staff leans against his shoulder with a sack tied to the end: he hasn't even put his luggage down. Behind him a path winds back through the hills to distant towns, the way they came. On the right, in a pink stone stable, Mary kneels with her hands crossed over her chest before the baby, who is tucked up in a fold of her blue cloak against the hay. An ox and a donkey look in.
the-road-to-bethlehem.meaning: Mary and Joseph did not choose this road. An order from a man they would never meet sent them on a long walk at the worst possible time. Much of life is like that: we are moved around by decisions made far above us. Luke's quiet point is that God was working through it all along. Bethlehem was where the prophets said the king would be born. The emperor thought he was counting his subjects. He was really moving a family into place.

echo.from: Augustus, The Deeds of the Divine Augustus, chapter 8
echo.text: Near the end of his life Augustus wrote a list of his achievements, to be set up in bronze outside his tomb. Among them he records that he took a census of Roman citizens three times, and gives the totals, more than four million each time.
echo.link: The most powerful man in the world proudly counted his millions. He never knew about one family on the road to Bethlehem. Two thousand years later, it is their child whose birth the world keeps.

the-road-to-bethlehem.question: Where are you being moved around by things you didn't choose: a deadline, a decision from above, a family need? Could you look for what might be being made ready in it?
the-road-to-bethlehem.prayer: Lord, Mary and Joseph walked the road they were given, and you were with them on it. When my life is pushed about by things I can't control, keep me walking. Show me what you are making ready, and give rest to everyone who is tired tonight. Amen.
the-road-to-bethlehem.midday: This morning: the long road to Bethlehem, and Joseph too tired to put his bag down. Be gentle this afternoon with anyone who's worn out.
the-road-to-bethlehem.evening: Today's story was the road to Bethlehem. Was there something today you had to do but didn't choose? Did any good come of it?

music.why: Bach's Christmas Oratorio begins its story with these very verses: the emperor's decree, and Joseph and Mary setting out for Bethlehem.

paras:
But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah,
being small among the clans of Judah,
out of you one will come out to me that is to be ruler in Israel;
whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.

Therefore he will abandon them until the time that she who is in labor gives birth.
Then the rest of his brothers will return to the children of Israel.

He shall stand, and shall shepherd in the strength of Yahweh,
in the majesty of the name of Yahweh his God:
and they will live, for then he will be great to the ends of the earth.

He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land,
and when he marches through our fortresses,
then we will raise against him seven shepherds,
and eight leaders of men.

classic.author: Augustus
classic.work: The Deeds of the Divine Augustus

read.why: Why Bethlehem? Seven hundred years before the census, the prophet Micah named this small town as the place a ruler would come from, one who would shepherd his people and be their peace. Read it, then think of Joseph asleep at the end of the road.

the-peaceable-kingdom.title: A little child will lead them
the-peaceable-kingdom.line: Isaiah sees a world where the wolf lies down with the lamb, and a child leads them.

story.retell: Isaiah promised that a new shoot would grow from the cut-down stump of King David's family, the line of David's father Jesse. On this coming king God's Spirit would rest: he would judge the poor fairly and stand up for the humble. And in his time even nature would be at peace: predators and prey lying down together, with a small child in charge of them all.
story.verse: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat, the calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them.

the-peaceable-kingdom.artLink: Edward Hicks, a Quaker preacher in Pennsylvania, painted Isaiah's vision dozens of times; this version dates from about 1834.
the-peaceable-kingdom.see: On a grassy bank, three small blond children sit and stand among the animals. A big brown bull stands beside a pale lion; around them rest a tiger, a wolf, sheep, goats, cows, bears and a jaguar, all at ease. One child puts an arm round the tiger's shoulders. Another reaches out and touches the jaguar's nose. Across the river on the left, in the distance, a group of Native American people meet men in three-cornered hats, one lifting a roll of cloth out of a chest. The animals are painted simply, almost like a child's picture.
the-peaceable-kingdom.meaning: Today's old Advent prayer is “O Root of Jesse”, from this passage. Isaiah's vision sounds impossible, and it is meant to: the world as it is runs on fear, the strong eating the weak. The promise is not that the wolf will be killed but that it will be changed. Hicks painted it again and again through quarrels that split his own Quaker community, as if he needed to keep looking at it. Peace, in this vision, is led by a child, someone weak enough to have no need to win.

echo.text: Virgil wrote a poem about a child soon to be born who would bring back a golden age. In his time the goats would come home with full udders, the herds would not fear great lions, and the snake would die out. Later Christians read it as a pagan prophecy of Christ.
echo.link: A Roman poet and a Hebrew prophet, seven centuries apart, both pinned the world's hope of peace on a child, and both imagined lions that no longer frighten anyone. Medieval Christians, Dante among them, honoured Virgil almost as a prophet because of it.

the-peaceable-kingdom.question: Who are you “wolf and lamb” with at the moment: someone you instinctively defend yourself against? What is one small step of peace you could take towards them?
the-peaceable-kingdom.prayer: Root of Jesse, come and change what is fierce in the world, and in me. Where I bite, make me gentle; where I fear, make me safe. Let a child lead me into your peace. Amen.
the-peaceable-kingdom.midday: This morning: the wolf and the lamb, and a little child leading them. Is there a quarrel you could quieten this afternoon?
the-peaceable-kingdom.evening: Today's story was the peaceable kingdom. Was there a moment today when you chose not to bite back? Who made peace easier for you?

music.why: Handel's Messiah opens with Isaiah's promises of comfort and a coming king, sung first in Dublin in 1742 as a concert for charity.

paras:
A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse,
and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.

Yahweh’s Spirit will rest on him:
the spirit of wisdom and understanding,
the spirit of counsel and might,
the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.

but he will judge the poor with righteousness,
and decide with equity for the humble of the earth.
He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth;
and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.

Righteousness will be the belt of his waist,
and faithfulness the belt of his waist.

The wolf will live with the lamb,
and the leopard will lie down with the young goat,
the calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together;
and a little child will lead them.

The cow and the bear will graze.
Their young ones will lie down together.
The lion will eat straw like the ox.

The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole,
and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den.
It will happen in that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse, who stands as a banner of the peoples; and his resting place will be glorious.

read.why: Read Isaiah's vision whole. Before the animals comes the king, and look at what makes him different: he doesn't judge by appearances or hearsay, and he takes the side of the poor. The peace of the animals grows out of his justice.

no-room.title: No room
no-room.line: There is no space for them in the house, so the baby is laid in a feeding trough.

story.retell: Bethlehem was crowded with people who had come to be counted. When Mary's time came, there was no space for them where travellers stayed. She gave birth to her first son, wrapped him in strips of cloth as every mother did, and laid him in the only place there was: a trough where animals were fed.
story.verse: She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.

no-room.artLink: Sandro Botticelli painted the moment after the birth, in a round panel, in about 1480–90.
no-room.see: Mary kneels with her arms crossed over her chest and her eyes nearly closed, looking down at her son. The baby lies on a pillow against a pile of hay, stretching both arms up to her, his head tipped right back to see her face, one foot kicking. They are on a patch of grass on top of rough grey stone blocks, under a thatched roof. Behind, in an enclosure, stand a donkey and an ox. Beyond is open country, hills and a river.
no-room.meaning: Luke tells the birth of the Son of God in two plain sentences, and the detail he chooses is that there was no room. God arrives in the leftover space, among the animals, because nowhere better had been kept for him. It is the shape of his whole life: born where there was no room, with nowhere to lay his head as a man, and buried in a borrowed tomb. Today is the Fourth Sunday of Advent. The question it leaves is simple: is there room?

echo.text: When Odysseus finally returns to Ithaca, disguised as a ragged beggar, the first person he meets is his old swineherd, Eumaeus. Eumaeus has almost nothing, but he takes the stranger in, makes him a bed of brushwood and goatskins, and roasts pork for him, saying that all strangers and beggars come from Zeus.
echo.link: In Homer the king comes home in disguise, and only a poor man in a hut makes room for him. In Bethlehem the king of heaven came in disguise too, and the busy house had no room. The poor would be the first to find him.

no-room.question: Where in your life is there “no room”: a full diary, a crowded mind, a heart with no space left? What could you clear this week to make room for someone?
no-room.prayer: Lord Jesus, you were born where there was no room, and you didn't wait for a better place. Come into the crowded, untidy places of my life, and make room in me for you and for the people you send. Amen.
no-room.midday: This morning: no room in the house, so a baby in a feeding trough. Is there someone you could make a little room for this afternoon?
no-room.evening: Today's story was “no room”. Was your day too full for anyone or anything? What could you set aside to make space before Christmas?

music.why: The old Christmas text Lauridsen sets marvels at exactly this: that animals were the first to see the newborn Lord, lying in a manger.

paras: Now in those days, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be enrolled.
This was the first enrollment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
All went to enroll themselves, everyone to his own city.
Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David;
to enroll himself with Mary, who was pledged to be married to him as wife, being pregnant.
While they were there, the day had come for her to give birth.
She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.

read.why: Read Luke's account of the birth from the beginning. In seven verses it moves from the emperor in Rome to a feeding trough in Bethlehem. The whole of Christmas turns on that move from the top of the world to the bottom.

keeping-watch.title: Keeping watch
keeping-watch.line: Shepherds on the night shift are the first to hear the news.

story.retell: On the hills outside Bethlehem, shepherds were out in the fields through the night, guarding their sheep. Shepherds were poor working men, low on everyone's list. Suddenly an angel stood among them and they were dazzled by light and terrified. The angel told them not to be afraid: a Saviour had been born that very day, and they would find him lying in a feeding trough.
story.verse: There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock. Behold, an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.

keeping-watch.artLink: Jacopo Bassano painted the angel appearing to the shepherds in about 1555–60, as an ordinary night on an Italian farm.
keeping-watch.see: In the dark, a group of country people sit among cows, sheep, a goat and a dog at the bottom of a steep hill. A man smoking a long pipe lies back on an orange cloth; a woman bends to milk a cow; a boy looks down at the animal. Above them, in a burst of gold light breaking through navy-blue night clouds, an angel kneels on a cloud, pointing one hand down at a shepherd and the other up to heaven. The shepherd in pink looks up, shielding his face from the light.
keeping-watch.meaning: Today is the shortest day of the year, and the longest night. The shepherds were the people who worked that night: awake when others slept, keeping watch in the cold. The news came first to them, not to the temple or the palace. If you are awake tonight because of work, worry, a baby or grief, this story is for you. Light comes to those keeping watch in the dark. And the first words it speaks are the ones we most need: don't be afraid.

echo.text: In one of the Iliad's most beautiful pictures, Homer describes a still night when the moon is bright and all the stars shine out, so that every hilltop and valley can be seen, and the shepherd watching below is glad in his heart.
echo.link: Homer's shepherd is glad at the stars on a clear night. Luke's shepherds see the sky itself open, and the glory of God shine around them. The oldest picture of a happy shepherd is a man looking up in the dark.

keeping-watch.question: Who is keeping watch in the dark at the moment: a night worker, a carer, someone grieving, someone who can't sleep? Could you send them a word of light today?
keeping-watch.prayer: O Morning Star, come and shine on those who sit in darkness. Be with everyone keeping watch tonight: those at work, those caring, those who can't sleep. Speak to them, and to me, the words the shepherds heard: don't be afraid. Amen.
keeping-watch.midday: This morning: the shepherds on the night shift. Think of one person keeping watch in the dark, and do something for them this afternoon.
keeping-watch.evening: Tonight is the longest night. Today's story was the shepherds keeping watch. Where did you see a little light today? Who was keeping watch for you?

music.why: MacMillan sets the ancient Advent prayer to Christ the dawn, which is sung on 21 December, the longest night of the year.

paras: There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock.
Behold, an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
The angel said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people.
For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
This is the sign to you: you will find a baby wrapped in strips of cloth, lying in a feeding trough.”
Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God, and saying,

“Glory to God in the highest,
on earth peace, good will toward men.”

read.why: Read the angel's message to the shepherds. Notice the sign they are given: not a palace or a crown, but a baby in a feeding trough. It is the kind of sign a shepherd would know how to find.

glory-in-the-highest.title: Heaven sings
glory-in-the-highest.line: The night sky fills with angels singing of glory to God and peace on earth.

story.retell: As soon as the angel had told the shepherds the news, the whole sky filled. A vast army of angels appeared, but they had not come to fight. They were singing. Their song joined heaven and earth in one line: glory to God above, and peace to people below.
story.verse: Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God, and saying, “Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men.”

glory-in-the-highest.artLink: Juan de Flandes painted the Nativity with the angels' song in the sky for the church of San Lázaro in Palencia, Spain, between about 1508 and 1519.
glory-in-the-highest.see: In the ruins of a stone building, Mary, her fair hair loose, kneels in prayer over her newborn son, with an ox and a donkey looking over a stone trough. Joseph, behind her in a red robe and green cap, leans on his staff and looks up. Out on the hills to the right, two shepherds lie among their sheep: one sleeps, the other throws up both hands and stares at the sky. In the top corner, out of a star-strewn blue sky, an angel in rose pink holds a scroll with the words of the song: “Gloria in excelsis Deo.” An owl watches from the ruined wall.
glory-in-the-highest.meaning: An army appears in the sky, and it sings about peace. That is the reversal at the heart of Christmas. The angels' song holds two things together that we usually keep apart: glory to God, and peace on earth. Worship that doesn't make us more peaceful is missing something; peace that has no room for God tends not to last. Look at the painting again: one shepherd is still asleep. Heaven is singing, and he hasn't noticed yet.

echo.text: At the end of the Republic, Plato tells the story of Er, a soldier who saw the afterlife. Er saw the circling heavens, and on each circle sat a Siren singing a single note, so that all of them together made one harmony.
echo.link: Plato imagined the heavens full of a music too high for human ears. On the hills of Bethlehem, ordinary men heard heaven sing, and the song was not about the stars but about peace for people on earth.

glory-in-the-highest.question: Where could you bring a little of the angels' song today: glory to God in a moment of thanks, and peace on earth in a conversation that needs it?
glory-in-the-highest.prayer: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace. Lord, wake me up to the song I keep sleeping through. Let my thanks go up to you, and let your peace come down through me to someone today. Amen.
glory-in-the-highest.midday: This morning: heaven singing over sleeping shepherds. Stop for a moment this afternoon and give thanks for one thing.
