glory-in-the-highest.evening: Today's story was the angels' song. Did you give glory to God for anything today? Did you make peace with anyone?

music.why: Every “Gloria” begins with the angels' words from this night. Vivaldi set them for the girls' choir of a Venice orphanage, bursting with joy.

paras:
Praise Yah!
Praise Yahweh from the heavens!
Praise him in the heights!

Praise him, all his angels!
Praise him, all his army!

Praise him, sun and moon!
Praise him, all you shining stars!

Praise him, you heavens of heavens,
you waters that are above the heavens.

Let them praise Yahweh’s name,
for he commanded, and they were created.

He has also established them forever and ever.
He has made a decree which will not pass away.

Praise Yahweh from the earth,
you great sea creatures, and all depths;

lightning and hail, snow and clouds;
stormy wind, fulfilling his word;

mountains and all hills;
fruit trees and all cedars;

wild animals and all livestock;
small creatures and flying birds;

kings of the earth and all peoples;
princes and all judges of the earth;

both young men and maidens;
old men and children:

He has lifted up the horn of his people,
the praise of all his saints,
even of the children of Israel, a people near to him.
Praise Yah!

read.why: The angels' song is one line long. This psalm is the long version: angels, sun, moon and stars, sea creatures, snow and wind, mountains, animals, kings and children, all called to praise together. Read it as the song that filled the sky over Bethlehem.

the-shepherds-go.title: Let's go and see
the-shepherds-go.line: The shepherds don't argue about the news. They go and look.

story.retell: When the angels had gone and the night was dark again, the shepherds could have talked themselves out of it. Instead they said to each other, let's go to Bethlehem now and see. They hurried into town, found Mary and Joseph, and saw the baby lying in the feeding trough, just as they had been told. Then they told everyone about it.
story.verse: When the angels went away from them into the sky, the shepherds said to one another, “Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” They came with haste, and found both Mary and Joseph, and the baby was lying in the feeding trough.

the-shepherds-go.artLink: Adriaen Isenbrant painted the shepherds arriving in Bruges in about 1520–40.
the-shepherds-go.see: Mary leans forward from the left with her hands stretched out towards the tiny baby, who lies on an upturned basket beside a bundle of wheat. Joseph kneels opposite, grey-bearded in red and charcoal grey, and two small angels kneel between them. They are in the tiled ruins of an old building, ivy growing along the broken walls, an ox and a donkey in a corner. From the left, three men in burgundy and black come in through the ruins, one of them playing an instrument. Two more kneel on the right. Far behind, tiny figures dance around a fire.
the-shepherds-go.meaning: The shepherds had the most astonishing experience of their lives, and their response was practical: let's go and see. They didn't stay on the hill discussing what it meant. Faith often starts like that, not with being certain but with being curious enough to go and look. They found exactly what they had been told: something very ordinary, a baby in a feeding trough. And they couldn't stop talking about it.

echo.text: When the prophet Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint a king from Jesse's sons, seven of them were brought before him and all were passed over. Was there no one else? Only the youngest, Jesse said, out keeping the sheep. They sent for David, and he was the one.
echo.link: A thousand years earlier, on the same hills, God chose a shepherd boy nobody had thought to invite. Now the shepherds of Bethlehem are invited first, to see David's descendant in a feeding trough.

the-shepherds-go.question: Is there something about faith you've been discussing from a distance for a long time? What would it mean to “go and see” this week: a carol service, a church door, a conversation, a chapter of a Gospel?
the-shepherds-go.prayer: Lord, the shepherds heard, and went, and found you just as they had been told. Give me their haste and their curiosity. When I am tempted only to talk about you, let me go and see. Amen.
the-shepherds-go.midday: This morning: the shepherds hurrying into Bethlehem. Is there something you've been meaning to go and see for yourself?
the-shepherds-go.evening: Today's story was the shepherds going to Bethlehem. Did you go and see anything for yourself today, instead of just hearing about it? What might you go and see over Christmas?

music.why: Rossetti's carol asks what a poor person could bring to the manger, and imagines a shepherd bringing a lamb. The shepherds came with nothing but themselves.

paras: When the angels went away from them into the sky, the shepherds said to one another, “Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
They came with haste, and found both Mary and Joseph, and the baby was lying in the feeding trough.
When they saw it, they publicized widely the saying which was spoken to them about this child.
All who heard it wondered at the things which were spoken to them by the shepherds.
But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as it was told them.

read.why: Read what happens after the angels leave. Watch the order: hearing, going, finding, telling, and going back to work still praising. The shepherds return to their sheep, but they are not the same.

mary-ponders.title: Kept in her heart
mary-ponders.line: While everyone else talks, Mary quietly keeps all of it in her heart.

story.retell: The shepherds burst into the stable and told Mary and Joseph everything: the angel, the light, the singing in the sky. Everyone who heard them was amazed. Mary had just given birth after a long journey, far from home, with strangers crowding in at night. She didn't say much. She held on to every word.
story.verse: But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.

mary-ponders.artLink: Anton Raphael Mengs painted the shepherds' visit in about 1764–65, as the altarpiece for the private chapel of King Charles III of Spain.
mary-ponders.see: In a shadowy wooden stable, every face is lit by the light coming from the baby, who lies swaddled in white in Mary's arms, smiling slightly. Mary turns her head and looks past us, and if you look closely there are tears about to spill from her eyes. Joseph leans in from the shadows, his brow furrowed. On the right, shepherds bow, kneel and point; one bows his head right down to the floor between his hands, and a small boy beside Mary lifts his hands as if about to clap. Angels float in the clouds above.
mary-ponders.meaning: Tonight is Christmas Eve, and everyone is talking, singing and rushing. Mary is the still point in the middle of it. Luke says she “kept” these things, which means guarded them like treasure, and “pondered” them, which means turned them over to see how they fitted. She didn't understand it all yet. She would carry these memories for thirty years, through confusion and grief, and they would hold. Some things are not to be explained tonight, only kept.

echo.text: Augustine marvelled at the human memory. He called it a vast palace with fields and storehouses, holding countless images, and was astonished that he could carry something so huge inside himself and still not fully understand it.
echo.link: Later in the same book, Augustine looks into the great house of memory and finds God waiting there. Mary was the first to use it this way: keeping what she had seen tonight, so she could turn it over for the rest of her life.

mary-ponders.question: Amid all the noise of Christmas, what is one moment from this year you want to keep and ponder, not rush past? Could you find ten quiet minutes tonight to hold it?
mary-ponders.prayer: Lord Jesus, born tonight, let me be still enough to receive you. Like Mary, help me keep what is precious and turn it over in my heart, even when I don't understand. Be born again in quiet places. Amen.
mary-ponders.midday: This afternoon, in the rush before Christmas, remember Mary, holding everything quietly in her heart. Find one still minute.
mary-ponders.evening: It is Christmas Eve. Today's story was Mary keeping these things in her heart. What from today, or this year, do you want to keep? Hold it for a moment before you sleep.

music.why: First sung on Christmas Eve 1818 in a village church in Austria, to a guitar: the stillness Mary kept, set to music.

paras: Now in those days, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be enrolled.
This was the first enrollment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
All went to enroll themselves, everyone to his own city.
Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David;
to enroll himself with Mary, who was pledged to be married to him as wife, being pregnant.
While they were there, the day had come for her to give birth.
She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.
There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock.
Behold, an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
The angel said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people.
For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
This is the sign to you: you will find a baby wrapped in strips of cloth, lying in a feeding trough.”
Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God, and saying,

“Glory to God in the highest,
on earth peace, good will toward men.”
When the angels went away from them into the sky, the shepherds said to one another, “Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
They came with haste, and found both Mary and Joseph, and the baby was lying in the feeding trough.
When they saw it, they publicized widely the saying which was spoken to them about this child.
All who heard it wondered at the things which were spoken to them by the shepherds.
But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as it was told them.

read.why: On Christmas Eve, read the whole of Luke's story of the birth, from the emperor's decree to the shepherds going home. You know it already. Read it as Mary did: slowly, keeping it, letting it fit together.

the-word-became-flesh.title: The Word became flesh
the-word-became-flesh.line: The meaning behind everything is born as a baby, lying on the bare ground.

story.retell: John tells the Christmas story without a stable or a single shepherd. He begins before time: in the beginning was the Word, the reason and meaning through which everything was made, and the Word was God. That Word was the light of every person, shining in the darkness. And then, in one sentence, it came close enough to touch.
story.verse: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

the-word-became-flesh.artLink: Petrus Christus painted the Nativity in Bruges in about 1450, framing it in a carved stone arch.
the-word-became-flesh.see: The baby lies naked on the ground, on the very hem of his mother's blue robe. Mary kneels on the left; Joseph, old and balding, kneels on the right, leaning on his stick, with his hat in his hands; four small angels kneel and pray around them. Behind, under a wooden shelter by a crumbling wall, a cow and a donkey stand in their pen, and two pairs of men, shepherds, lean over the wall to look. Now look at the stone arch framing it all: on its columns stand a naked man and woman, Adam and Eve, with tiny carved scenes climbing the arch above them. The whole human story frames one small baby.
the-word-became-flesh.meaning: Christians believe something astonishing today: not just that a good man was born, but that the meaning behind the whole universe became a human being. The Word became flesh: skin, hunger, cold, a body that could be held and hurt. God did not send advice from a distance; he came to live among us, in a particular town, in a particular family. Petrus Christus puts him on the bare ground, framed by Adam and Eve, because this is where the human story starts again. Happy Christmas.

echo.text: The Greek philosopher Heraclitus taught that everything is held together by a Logos, a word or reason running through the whole world, and complained that people go through life without understanding it, as if asleep.
echo.link: John, remembered as having lived in Heraclitus's city of Ephesus, took the philosophers' word, Logos, and made the most daring claim in the history of ideas: the reason behind everything has a face, and was born in Bethlehem.

the-word-became-flesh.question: If God came close enough to touch, who is close enough for you to touch today: someone to hold, to visit, to sit beside? Who will you be fully present to this Christmas Day?
the-word-became-flesh.prayer: Word of the Father, now in flesh appearing, we welcome you. You came close enough to hold. Be born in us today, and make our love as real as yours: present, touchable, here. Glory to God in the highest. Amen.
the-word-became-flesh.midday: Happy Christmas. This morning: the Word became flesh and lived among us. Be fully present to the people at your table today.
the-word-became-flesh.evening: Today's story was the Word made flesh. Where did you see God's love made real today, in a person, a meal, a gift? Give thanks for it before you sleep.

music.why: Its Christmas Day verse is a paraphrase of today's reading: “Word of the Father, now in flesh appearing.” Traditionally that verse is kept back for this morning.

paras: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The same was in the beginning with God.
All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
In him was life, and the life was the light of men.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
There came a man, sent from God, whose name was John.
The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him.
He was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light.
The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world.
He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him.
He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.
But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:
who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

read.why: The Christmas story told from eternity. John's opening is read at Christmas services all over the world. Read it slowly, aloud if you can, and stop at verse 14: the whole of Christmas in one sentence.

the-servants-prayer.title: Before he had finished
the-servants-prayer.line: An old servant at a well asks God for one small, specific sign, and the answer arrives while he is still speaking.

story.retell: Abraham sent his oldest servant on a long journey back to the family's homeland to find a wife for his son Isaac. Arriving at a well outside the town at evening, when the women came out to draw water, the servant prayed a plain, specific prayer: let the young woman who offers water to me, and to my camels too, be the one. Before he had finished speaking, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder, gave him a drink and ran back and forth until all ten camels had drunk. He gave her a gold ring and two bracelets, and then he bowed his head and thanked God.
story.verse: Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, with her pitcher on her shoulder.

the-servants-prayer.artLink: Veronese and his workshop painted this meeting at the well in Venice in about 1582–88, near the end of his life.
the-servants-prayer.see: Three men, a young woman and a crowd of camels gather round the stone ledge of a well in open country. The woman, her blond hair braided and coiled, wears a full pink skirt and a sheer gold bodice; she stands beside a copper water pot, touching one wrist, and there are bracelets on both her arms. In front of her a man in a striped tunic kneels and holds up a handful of gold. Just beyond him an older, balding man with a trimmed grey beard leans on a tall stick, looks at her and gestures to the gold. One camel drinks from a copper vessel in the corner; another pokes its head in from the edge. A white town lines the horizon under a sky streaked with grey, tan and mauve pink.
the-servants-prayer.meaning: Prayer does not have to be grand. The servant makes no speech. He tells God exactly where he is, by a well at evening, and asks for something small enough to recognise. What he asks for is telling: not a rich girl or a beautiful one, but a kind one, someone who will notice a tired stranger's thirsty animals. And when the answer comes, he does the thing people most often forget. He stops, bows his head and says thank you. Ask plainly, watch carefully, and give thanks out loud.

echo.text: Xenophon remembers how his teacher Socrates prayed. He asked the gods simply for good things, trusting that they knew best what was good. To pray for gold, or silver, or power, Socrates thought, was like praying for a lucky throw of the dice: you could not know whether it would do you any good.
echo.link: Socrates and the servant both passed over the obvious prizes. The servant did not ask for wealth or beauty, only for kindness, and trusted God with the rest.

the-servants-prayer.question: What would you ask God for today if you made it small and specific, like the servant at the well? And whose kindness this week could you notice, and thank them for?
the-servants-prayer.prayer: Lord, the servant asked you for something small, and you answered before he had finished. Teach me to ask you plainly for what I need today, to notice your answer when it comes as an ordinary kindness, and not to forget to say thank you. Amen.
the-servants-prayer.midday: This morning: a servant at a well, praying for one small sign. Watch this afternoon for an ordinary kindness, and name it.
the-servants-prayer.evening: Today's story was the prayer at the well. What did you ask for today, and was anything given? Did you stop to say thank you?

music.why: Dylan's song is a quiet confession about seeing God's hand in the smallest things, as the servant did in a stranger offering to water his camels.

paras: Abraham was old, and well advanced in age. Yahweh had blessed Abraham in all things.
Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had, “Please put your hand under my thigh.
I will make you swear by Yahweh, the God of heaven and the God of the earth, that you shall not take a wife for my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I live.
But you shall go to my country, and to my relatives, and take a wife for my son Isaac.”
The servant said to him, “What if the woman isn’t willing to follow me to this land? Must I bring your son again to the land you came from?”
Abraham said to him, “Beware that you don’t bring my son there again.

Yahweh, the God of heaven—who took me from my father’s house, and from the land of my birth, who spoke to me, and who swore to me, saying, ‘I will give this land to your offspring—he will send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.
If the woman isn’t willing to follow you, then you shall be clear from this oath to me. Only you shall not bring my son there again.”
The servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and swore to him concerning this matter.
The servant took ten of his master’s camels, and departed, having a variety of good things of his master’s with him. He arose, and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.
He made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time that women go out to draw water.
He said, “Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, please give me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham.
Behold, I am standing by the spring of water. The daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.

Let it happen, that the young lady to whom I will say, ‘Please let down your pitcher, that I may drink,’ then she says, ‘Drink, and I will also give your camels a drink,’—let her be the one you have appointed for your servant Isaac. By this I will know that you have shown kindness to my master.”
Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, with her pitcher on her shoulder.
The young lady was very beautiful to look at, a virgin. No man had known her. She went down to the spring, filled her pitcher, and came up.
The servant ran to meet her, and said, “Please give me a drink, a little water from your pitcher.”
She said, “Drink, my lord.” She hurried, and let down her pitcher on her hand, and gave him a drink.
When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, “I will also draw for your camels, until they have finished drinking.”
She hurried, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again to the well to draw, and drew for all his camels.
The man looked steadfastly at her, remaining silent, to know whether Yahweh had made his journey prosperous or not.
As the camels had done drinking, the man took a golden ring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold,
and said, “Whose daughter are you? Please tell me. Is there room in your father’s house for us to stay?”
She said to him, “I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor.”
She said moreover to him, “We have both straw and feed enough, and room to lodge in.”
The man bowed his head, and worshiped Yahweh.

He said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his loving kindness and his truth toward my master. As for me, Yahweh has led me on the way to the house of my master’s relatives.”

read.why: Read the whole of the servant's errand, from Abraham's charge to the prayer at the well. It is one of the first prayers for guidance in the Bible, made in a few plain words, and the answer comes as a young woman with a water jar.

cana-they-have-no-wine.title: They have no wine
cana-they-have-no-wine.line: At a village wedding the wine runs out, and Mary says four words to her son.

story.retell: Jesus, his mother and his first followers were guests at a wedding in Cana, a village in Galilee. Before the celebrations were over, the wine ran out, an embarrassment for the family giving the feast. Mary did not make a plan or a speech. She told Jesus simply that they had no wine, and then told the servants to do whatever he said. He had them fill six great stone water jars to the brim, and what they drew out was the best wine of the feast.
story.verse: When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.”

cana-they-have-no-wine.artLink: A Spanish painter known only as the Master of the Catholic Kings painted this wedding in about 1495–97; his name comes from Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic Monarchs of Spain.
cana-they-have-no-wine.see: The guests sit behind a long table spread with a white cloth. At the left, Mary, in teal blue with a white head scarf, holds her hands together in prayer and looks down at the table. Beside her Jesus, in an eggplant-purple robe, raises two fingers in blessing, and an old man in a blue cap holds a bowl of red wine out towards him. At the right end sit the young couple, the bride in green and gold brocade with rings on her fingers. On our side of the table a server in teal points down at six tall jugs on the patterned floor, a brown dog at his feet. Woven along the bottom of the tablecloth are the Latin words of the angel's greeting to Mary.
cana-they-have-no-wine.meaning: Mary's prayer is four words long. She does not tell Jesus what to do, or how, or when. She simply tells him what is missing, and then tells the servants to listen to him. That is a whole school of prayer: name the need, and be ready to do whatever comes next, even if it is only filling jars with water. Notice too whose need it was. The wine was not hers. Some of the best praying begins with noticing what other people have run out of.

echo.text: A Roman widow named Proba wrote to Augustine to ask him how to pray. He answered that God does not need us to tell him what we want, since he knows it already. We pray, Augustine said, so that our own desire is stretched and made ready to receive what God is preparing to give.
echo.link: Jesus knew the wine had run out before his mother spoke. She told him anyway. That is Augustine's point: prayer does not inform God, it changes the one who prays, and makes room for the gift.

cana-they-have-no-wine.question: Whose “wine” is running out at the moment: a friend, a neighbour, someone at work? Could you tell God about it in one plain sentence today, and then do one small thing for them?
cana-they-have-no-wine.prayer: Lord, Mary told you what was missing and trusted you with the rest. I bring you the people I know who have run out of what they need. Do what only you can do, and show me the jar I can fill. Amen.
cana-they-have-no-wine.midday: This morning: four words at a wedding, “They have no wine.” Who near you has run out of something this afternoon?
cana-they-have-no-wine.evening: Today's story was the wedding at Cana. Whose need did you notice today? Did you tell God about it, and did you fill any jars?

music.why: Bach's chorale begins, in German, “Jesus bleibet meine Freude”, Jesus remains my joy: the note of Cana, joy that does not run out.

paras: On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, of the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?”
Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!”
Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?”
Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!”
Jesus answered him, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you underneath the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these!”
He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
The third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there.
Jesus also was invited, with his disciples, to the wedding.
When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.”
His mother said to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.”
Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece.
Jesus said to them, “Fill the water pots with water.” So they filled them up to the brim.
He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it.
When the ruler of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom
and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!”
This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.

read.why: Read from the calling of Philip and Nathanael to the wedding. Jesus promises Nathanael that he will see greater things; on the third day, at a village party, the first of them happens, because his mother noticed what was missing.

clare-blessed-be-you.title: Thank you for making me
clare-blessed-be-you.line: As she dies, Clare of Assisi thanks God for creating her.

story.ref: The Legend of Saint Clare, Assisi, 1253
story.retell: Clare was the young noblewoman of Assisi who, inspired by Francis, slipped away from her family in 1212 to live in poverty, and spent the next forty years in the little convent of San Damiano outside the town. For much of that time she was ill. As she lay dying in August 1253, with her sisters round her bed, she was heard speaking to her own soul: go in peace, for the one who made you has watched over you as a mother watches over the child she loves. Then she said: blessed are you, Lord, for creating me. One of the sisters said she saw a company of women in white, crowned with gold, come to the bed, and the most beautiful of them bend over Clare.
story.verse: I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

clare-blessed-be-you.artLink: An Austrian painter known as the Master of Heiligenkreuz painted Clare's death on a gold ground in about 1400–10.
clare-blessed-be-you.see: Clare lies back on pillows in a bed hung with red curtains, eyes closed, hands crossed on her chest. Two sisters in black habits stand at the head of the bed. Along the far side stand five young women with crowns and halos, in vivid blue, green, white and burgundy, each holding something different: one a model of a tower, another a little basket of flowers. The one nearest Clare holds her face in her hands. Two more kneel on our side of the bed, one with a tiny dragon and one with a small sheep, and two little nuns in grey read their books. Above, angels swing censers, and at the top a bearded, haloed figure holds a tiny crowned person, probably her soul, received into heaven.
clare-blessed-be-you.meaning: Clare had given up almost everything: family, money, comfort, and in the end her health. You might expect her last words to count the cost. Instead she thanks God for making her. Her death is not a defeat to put a brave face on; it is a going home, in good company. Few of us get to choose our last words. But we can practise them. A life that keeps saying thank you for being made is learning, day by day, how to die well, and how to live.

echo.text: The emperor reminds himself how short a life is, and how to leave it: gently and contentedly, like a ripe olive that falls, praising the earth that bore it and thanking the tree on which it grew.
echo.link: Marcus hoped to go like a ripe olive, grateful to the tree. Clare did, and she knew whom to thank: not nature, but the one who had made her and loved her like a mother.

clare-blessed-be-you.question: If you said thank you for your life today, what would you name first? Is there someone ill or near the end whom you could visit, write to or pray for this week?
clare-blessed-be-you.prayer: Blessed are you, Lord, for creating me. Thank you for my life, for the people in it and for the days still to come. When my time comes, let me go in peace, in good company, into your keeping. Amen.
clare-blessed-be-you.midday: This morning: Clare of Assisi, thanking God for making her as she died. Say a quiet thank you for one ordinary thing this afternoon.
clare-blessed-be-you.evening: Today's story was the death of Clare. What in today are you thankful to have been alive for? Who would you want near you at the end?

music.why: Tavener's song, from words of the Orthodox funeral service, ends not in fear but in welcome: “Come, enjoy rewards and crowns I have prepared for you.”

paras:
Yahweh, you have searched me,
and you know me.

You know my sitting down and my rising up.
You perceive my thoughts from afar.

You search out my path and my lying down,
and are acquainted with all my ways.

For there is not a word on my tongue,
but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.

You hem me in behind and before.
You laid your hand on me.

This knowledge is beyond me.
It’s lofty.
I can’t attain it.

Where could I go from your Spirit?
Or where could I flee from your presence?

If I ascend up into heaven, you are there.
If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, you are there!

If I take the wings of the dawn,
and settle in the uttermost parts of the sea,

even there your hand will lead me,
and your right hand will hold me.

If I say, “Surely the darkness will overwhelm me.
The light around me will be night,”

even the darkness doesn’t hide from you,
but the night shines as the day.
The darkness is like light to you.

For you formed my inmost being.
You knit me together in my mother’s womb.

I will give thanks to you,
for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
Your works are wonderful.
My soul knows that very well.

My frame wasn’t hidden from you,
when I was made in secret,
woven together in the depths of the earth.

Your eyes saw my body.
In your book they were all written,
the days that were ordained for me,
when as yet there were none of them.

How precious to me are your thoughts, God!
How vast is their sum!

If I would count them, they are more in number than the sand.
When I wake up, I am still with you.

read.why: This part of the road faces death honestly. Read the psalm that Clare's last words echo: a poem about being known and made by God before birth, and never out of his reach, even in the dark.

cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.title: Too quick to judge
cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.line: Two brothers heal the sick for nothing, until one accepts a small gift and the other cannot forgive him.

story.ref: The life of Saints Cosmas and Damian, from The Golden Legend
story.retell: Cosmas and Damian were twin brothers, Christian doctors in Cilicia, in what is now southern Turkey, remembered for healing everyone without taking a penny. A woman named Palladia, who had spent everything she had on doctors, was healed by them, and afterwards pressed a small gift on Damian. He refused it, but when she begged him in God's name, he took it rather than shame her. Cosmas was so angry that he said he would not even be buried beside his brother. That night, the story goes, Christ appeared to Cosmas and explained why Damian had accepted, and in the end the brothers were buried side by side.
story.verse: Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.

cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.artLink: Fra Angelico painted this healing in about 1438–40, as one of the small scenes beneath the high altarpiece of San Marco in Florence; Cosmas and Damian were the patron saints of the Medici, who paid for it.
cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.see: Fra Angelico shows two moments side by side. Through an arch on the left, two haloed men in pink and white cloaks and red caps offer a vessel to a woman sitting up in bed under a red blanket, while two more faces peer over the headboard. Through the doorway on the right, a woman in lilac with a white head covering holds out a straw-coloured box to a third haloed man in the same red cap and cloaks. He holds one hand up in front of his chest and reaches for the box with the other. Above the door, a pot of dark green plants sits against a strip of blue sky.
cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.meaning: Cosmas was not wrong to care about honesty. His mistake was to judge his brother from the outside, in a hurry, without asking why. Damian had taken the gift for the woman's sake, to let someone who had been helped give something back with dignity. Many of our quarrels with the people closest to us are like this: we see what they did and supply the worst motive. Justice needs the facts. Mercy asks the question before it reaches a verdict.

echo.text: Plutarch, who was devoted to his own brother Timon, wrote an essay on how brothers can keep the peace. He held up the followers of Pythagoras as an example. They were not even related, he says, but if anger ever drove them to hard words, they never let the sun go down before they had taken each other's right hands, embraced and made peace.
echo.link: The Pythagoreans made peace before sunset. Cosmas needed a dream in the night, but he got there in the end. Both stories say: do not let a quarrel with a brother go to sleep with you.

cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.question: Is there someone close to you whose motives you have judged without asking? Could you ask them, kindly, this week, why they did what they did?
cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.prayer: Lord, you know why people do what they do, and usually I do not. Slow me down before I judge. Give me the humility to ask, the grace to forgive, and the courage to make peace before the sun goes down. Amen.
cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.midday: This morning: Cosmas, too quick to judge his brother. Before you judge anyone this afternoon, ask one question first.
cosmas-and-damian-quick-to-judge.evening: Today's story was the two doctor brothers. Did you judge anyone today without knowing why they acted? Is there a peace to make before you sleep?

music.why: “Where charity and love are, God is there”: the old chant behind Duruflé's motet was sung as people washed one another's feet, and its fuller verses ask for quarrels and strife to cease.

paras: Now accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions.
One man has faith to eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables.
Don’t let him who eats despise him who doesn’t eat. Don’t let him who doesn’t eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him.
Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.
One man esteems one day as more important. Another esteems every day alike. Let each man be fully assured in his own mind.

He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives God thanks. He who doesn’t eat, to the Lord he doesn’t eat, and gives God thanks.
For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself.
For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.
For to this end Christ died, rose, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
For it is written,

“ ‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘to me every knee will bow.
Every tongue will confess to God.’ ”
So then each one of us will give account of himself to God.
Therefore let’s not judge one another any more, but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother’s way, or an occasion for falling.

read.why: Paul wrote to a church divided over food and holy days, each side sure the other was wrong. His question is the one Cosmas had to hear: who are you to judge another's servant? Read on to the end, where he asks them to stop judging one another and start making life easier for each other.

david-without-the-armour.title: Without the armour
david-without-the-armour.line: A shepherd boy takes off the king's armour and goes out to face a giant with a sling and five stones.

story.retell: For forty days the Philistine champion Goliath, a giant in bronze armour, had mocked the army of Israel, and no one dared to fight him. David, the youngest son of a family from Bethlehem, came to the camp with food for his brothers and offered to go. King Saul dressed him in his own clothes, with a bronze helmet and a coat of mail, but David could hardly move in them and took them off. He went out with his shepherd's staff, his sling and five smooth stones from the brook, and the first stone brought the giant down.
story.verse: and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.”

david-without-the-armour.artLink: Andrea del Castagno painted David on a leather parade shield in Florence in about 1450–55.
david-without-the-armour.see: The painting is shaped like a shield, wide at the top and tapering towards the base. David, a young man with curling brown hair, stands barefoot in a short rust-red tunic over a white shirt. He holds the end of a long red sling, weighted with a stone, which swings out behind him. At his feet lies the giant's severed head, ashen and bloodied, with a palm-sized stone sunk in its forehead. Behind him are grey boulders, a winding river and palm-like trees under an azure sky with frothy white clouds. Castagno shows the throw and its result at once.
david-without-the-armour.meaning: Saul did what kings do: he tried to make David look like a soldier. It did not fit. David won as what he was, a shepherd with a shepherd's tools, trusting that the battle belonged to God. The Bible keeps telling this story: the youngest son, the smallest nation, a king born among animals in Bethlehem. God's kingdom does not advance by bigger armour. Most of us are tempted to face our giants in borrowed armour, pretending to be someone stronger. The invitation is to take it off and go as yourself.

echo.from: Livy, The History of Rome, Book 7
echo.text: In 361 BC, Livy says, a Gaul of enormous size stood on a bridge over the river Anio and challenged any Roman to single combat. A young soldier of ordinary height, Titus Manlius, went out with a foot soldier's shield and a short Spanish sword, got in under the giant's guard and killed him. He took the gold collar from the dead man's neck, and was called Torquatus, the man with the collar, ever after.
echo.link: Both young men beat a giant by refusing to fight on the giant's terms. But Manlius trusted his sword and won himself a famous name. David put the sword aside and said the battle was the Lord's.

david-without-the-armour.question: What “armour” do you put on to face hard things: a manner, a title, a front? Is there one situation this week you could face simply as yourself?
david-without-the-armour.prayer: Lord, David went out without the king's armour, trusting you. Take from me the borrowed strength I hide behind. Let me face what is in front of me as myself, with what you have already put in my hands. The battle is yours. Amen.
david-without-the-armour.midday: This morning: David taking off the king's armour. What could you put down this afternoon, and simply be yourself?
david-without-the-armour.evening: Today's story was David and the giant. Where did you try to look stronger than you are today? Where were you simply yourself?

music.why: Leonard Cohen's song is full of King David, the shepherd boy who became a king and a musician; not a worship song, but it is where many people first meet him.

paras: When the words were heard which David spoke, they rehearsed them before Saul; and he sent for him.
David said to Saul, “Let no man’s heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine.”
Saul said to David, “You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him; for you are but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth.”
David said to Saul, “Your servant was keeping his father’s sheep; and when a lion or a bear came, and took a lamb out of the flock,
I went out after him, and struck him, and rescued it out of his mouth. When he arose against me, I caught him by his beard, and struck him, and killed him.
Your servant struck both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God.”
David said, “Yahweh who delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.”
Saul said to David, “Go! Yahweh will be with you.”
Saul dressed David with his clothing. He put a helmet of bronze on his head, and he clad him with a coat of mail.
David strapped his sword on his clothing, and he tried to move; for he had not tested it. David said to Saul, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them.” Then David took them off.

He took his staff in his hand, and chose for himself five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag which he had. His sling was in his hand; and he came near to the Philistine.
The Philistine walked and came near to David; and the man who bore the shield went before him.
When the Philistine looked around, and saw David, he disdained him; for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and had a good looking face.
The Philistine said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?” The Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky, and to the animals of the field.”

Then David said to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

Today, Yahweh will deliver you into my hand. I will strike you, and take your head from off you. I will give the dead bodies of the army of the Philistines today to the birds of the sky, and to the wild animals of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,
and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.”
When the Philistine arose, and walked and came near to meet David, David hurried, and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine.
David put his hand in his bag, took a stone, and slung it, and struck the Philistine in his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the earth.
So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine, and killed him; but there was no sword in the hand of David.

read.why: This part of the road is about a different kind of king. Read David's conversation with Saul before the fight: the king sees only a boy, and David talks about the lion and the bear, and the God who rescued him from them.

luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.title: All night and nothing
luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.line: Fishermen come in after a night of catching nothing, and a teacher asks them to try once more.

story.retell: Simon and his partners had fished all night on the Lake of Gennesaret, the Sea of Galilee, and caught nothing, and were washing their nets. Jesus borrowed Simon's boat to teach the crowd from the water, and afterwards told him to put out into the deep and let down the nets. Simon said they had worked all night for nothing, but at his word he would. The nets filled until they began to break, and both boats were so full they began to sink. Simon fell at Jesus' knees, and Jesus told him not to be afraid.
story.verse: Simon answered him, “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”

luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.artLink: Jacopo Bassano, a painter from a small town near Venice, painted this catch in 1545.
luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.see: Two small wooden boats fill the width of the painting, one overlapping the other. In the stern on the left sits Jesus in rose pink and marine blue, three rays of gold light around his head, one hand raised. Before him a bearded, balding man in marigold orange kneels with his hands pressed together; a younger man with flowing hair steps towards Jesus with his arms flung wide. In the other boat two bare-chested men lean over the side, hauling in the net, while an old man with a white beard holds an oar half in the water and looks back over his shoulder. Behind them the lake stretches away to a distant mountain and a winding shore.
luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.meaning: The miracle came at the end of a wasted night. Simon had done everything he knew, in the place he knew best, and caught nothing. Then, tired and washing up, he was asked to try again, on the word of a teacher from Nazareth. That is often how a long wait ends: not when we have finally got it right, but when we are willing to let the nets down once more because someone we trust has asked. The night was not wasted. It was what brought Simon to his knees.

echo.text: After a storm has scattered his fleet, Aeneas lands on the coast of Africa with his exhausted men. He hunts, shares out food and wine, and tells them to hold on and keep themselves for better days: perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even this. Virgil adds that Aeneas hid his own grief and put on a look of hope.
echo.link: Aeneas could only promise better days some time. On the shore of Galilee the better day came that same morning, out of a night of nothing. Both stories ask the tired to try once more.

luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.question: Where have you worked all night, so to speak, and caught nothing? What would it mean to let the nets down once more this week, on someone else's word?
luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.prayer: Lord, I have worked hard at things that came to nothing. At your word, I will let down the nets again. Give me patience in the empty nights and courage to try once more, and when the nets fill, keep me humble. Amen.
luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.midday: This morning: a night of empty nets, then one more try. What could you try again this afternoon?
luke-5-all-night-and-nothing.evening: Today's story was the empty night and the full net. What felt fruitless today? Is there something you could try once more tomorrow?

music.why: Farjeon's hymn is about a morning that comes new each day, whatever happened in the night: the kind of morning on which Simon's nets came up full.

paras: He rose up from the synagogue, and entered into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was afflicted with a great fever, and they begged him for her.
He stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her. Immediately she rose up and served them.
When the sun was setting, all those who had any sick with various diseases brought them to him; and he laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them.
Demons also came out of many, crying out, and saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of God!” Rebuking them, he didn’t allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
When it was day, he departed and went into an uninhabited place, and the multitudes looked for him, and came to him, and held on to him, so that he wouldn’t go away from them.
But he said to them, “I must preach the good news of God’s Kingdom to the other cities also. For this reason I have been sent.”
He was preaching in the synagogues of Galilee.
Now while the multitude pressed on him and heard the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret.
He saw two boats standing by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them, and were washing their nets.
He entered into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. He sat down and taught the multitudes from the boat.
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.”
Simon answered him, “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”
When they had done this, they caught a great multitude of fish, and their net was breaking.
They beckoned to their partners in the other boat, that they should come and help them. They came, and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.
But Simon Peter, when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.”
For he was amazed, and all who were with him, at the catch of fish which they had caught;
and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon.
Jesus said to Simon, “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”
When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything, and followed him.

read.why: These last days before Advent are about waiting. Read from the evening when Jesus heals Simon's mother-in-law and the sick crowd round the door at sunset, to the day on the lake. Simon had already seen what Jesus could do; it still took a night of nothing to bring him to his knees.

flight-until-i-tell-you.title: Until I tell you
flight-until-i-tell-you.line: Joseph is told to take the child and his mother to Egypt, and to wait there for word to come home.

story.retell: After the wise men had gone home, an angel warned Joseph in a dream that King Herod was searching for the child to kill him. Joseph was to take Jesus and Mary to Egypt and stay there until he was told. He got up in the night and went. They lived as refugees in a foreign country, with no date to go back, until another dream told Joseph that Herod was dead and they could return.
story.verse: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, “Arise and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.”

flight-until-i-tell-you.artLink: Vittore Carpaccio painted the family on the road in Venice in about 1515.
flight-until-i-tell-you.see: A grey-bearded, balding man in a royal-blue tunic and a ruby-red robe leads a donkey along a path, leaning on his walking stick and looking back. On the donkey sits a woman wrapped in a blue and gold cloak, her eyes on the baby she holds close. The child, in white, reaches for her face with one hand and turns to look over his shoulder, straight at us. Grasses and plants are painted one by one along the path; a river runs alongside, and beyond it are green trees, blue mountains and a few buildings under a wide sky with wisps of cloud.
flight-until-i-tell-you.meaning: Joseph was given a direction but no date: go, and stay until I tell you. That is a hard kind of waiting, in a strange place, among strangers, not knowing how long. But it was not empty. The child grew, the family was safe, and the word did come. Many people wait like this: refugees, the long-term ill, people in a long, dark season of life. The promise is not that the wait will be short. It is that they are not forgotten, and that the one who sent them will also call them home.

echo.text: Driven out of Rome by his enemies in 58 BC, Cicero spent a year and a half in exile, mostly in Thessalonica, waiting for a vote that might bring him home. His letters to his friend Atticus from that time are some of the saddest he wrote: he blames himself, weeps, and wishes he had died. In the end the recall came, and in 57 BC he returned to Rome to crowds who came out to welcome him.
echo.link: Cicero waited in exile for Rome to remember him, and nearly despaired. Joseph waited in Egypt for a word from God, and Matthew records no complaint. Both were called home.

flight-until-i-tell-you.question: What are you waiting for without a date: news, a result, a way home? Is there someone far from home near you whom you could welcome this week?
flight-until-i-tell-you.prayer: Lord, you sent Joseph into a strange land with no date to return, and then you called him home. I am waiting for things I cannot time. Keep me faithful where I am, keep safe the people I love, and when your word comes, let me hear it. Amen.
flight-until-i-tell-you.midday: This morning: a family on the road to Egypt, told to wait for word. Can you be faithful this afternoon in the place you are?
flight-until-i-tell-you.evening: Today's story was the flight into Egypt. What are you waiting to hear? Did you meet anyone today who is far from home?

music.why: Dorsey's song asks to be taken by the hand and led on through the storm and the night: the prayer of anyone on a dark road to an unknown place.

paras: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, “Arise and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.”
He arose and took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt,
and was there until the death of Herod; that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked by the wise men, was exceedingly angry, and sent out, and killed all the male children who were in Bethlehem and in all the surrounding countryside, from two years old and under, according to the exact time which he had learned from the wise men.
Then that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying,

“A voice was heard in Ramah,
lamentation, weeping and great mourning,
Rachel weeping for her children;
she wouldn’t be comforted,
because they are no more.”
But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying,
“Arise and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel, for those who sought the young child’s life are dead.”
He arose and took the young child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.
But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in the place of his father, Herod, he was afraid to go there. Being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the region of Galilee,
and came and lived in a city called Nazareth; that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophets that he will be called a Nazarene.

read.why: Read the whole of the flight and the return. It is a hard passage, with Herod's cruelty at its centre, but notice how the waiting is held between two dreams: go and stay, and then, at last, go home.

golden-calf-moses-delayed.title: Tired of waiting
golden-calf-moses-delayed.line: While Moses is on the mountain, the people grow tired of waiting and make a god they can see.

story.retell: Moses had gone up Mount Sinai to meet God and had been gone for forty days. Down below, the people grew restless. They told Aaron they did not know what had become of Moses and asked him to make them gods to lead them. Aaron collected their gold earrings and made a calf, and the next day they held a feast to it, eating, drinking and dancing, while up on the mountain God was giving Moses the law.
story.verse: When the people saw that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron, and said to him, “Come, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.”

golden-calf-moses-delayed.artLink: Jacopo Tintoretto's workshop in Venice painted the feast of the calf in about 1594, the year Tintoretto died.
golden-calf-moses-delayed.see: In the foreground, groups of people rest in the shade of dark rocks: an old man in a white turban looks over his shoulder, a woman holds a baby to her cheek, another offers a child an orange fruit. Beyond a stream, a tall man in a red robe and a crescent-shaped headdress stands while another bends to add a gold dish to a heap of gold on the ground. Further back, a crowd circles a tall stand with a golden calf on top, and four women kneel before it playing instruments. Others feast under canopies on the hillside. And high in the top right corner, half out of the picture, someone in rose pink kneels on the rocks with golden flames flickering all around: most likely Moses on the mountain, where the glory of God looked like fire.
golden-calf-moses-delayed.meaning: The people were not wicked to begin with. They were waiting, the wait went on too long, and the leader they trusted had disappeared into the cloud. So they made something they could see and touch, out of the gold they were wearing. That is what impatience often does: it fills the empty space with something of our own making. The painting shows it at a glance: the feast in the valley, and in the corner, almost out of sight, the fire on the mountain, where the real thing was happening all along.

echo.text: The wind god Aeolus gives Odysseus a leather bag with all the storm winds tied up inside, so that a gentle west wind can carry his ships home. For nine days they sail, and on the tenth they can see the fires on their own island. Odysseus, worn out from steering, falls asleep. His men, sure the bag is full of gold he is keeping from them, untie it, and the winds blow them all the way back.
echo.link: In both stories the leader is out of sight for a while, the end is nearly in view, and the people cannot bear not knowing. Waiting badly is rarely plain wickedness. It is suspicion and haste, a moment before the answer comes.

golden-calf-moses-delayed.question: What “golden calf” do you reach for when a wait goes on too long: something you can see and control? What could you leave in God's hands instead this week?
golden-calf-moses-delayed.prayer: Lord, when you seem far away and the wait goes on, I am tempted to make something of my own to hold on to. Keep me from filling the silence with false gods. Give me patience to wait for you, even when I cannot see what you are doing. Amen.
golden-calf-moses-delayed.midday: This morning: the golden calf, made out of impatience at the foot of the mountain. What are you tempted to grab hold of this afternoon?
golden-calf-moses-delayed.evening: Today's story was the golden calf. Where did impatience get the better of you today? What might God have been doing out of sight?

music.why: Heber's hymn admits that darkness hides God and that sinful eyes cannot see his glory, which is exactly what the people at Sinai could not bear.

paras: When the people saw that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron, and said to him, “Come, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.”
Aaron said to them, “Take off the golden rings, which are in the ears of your wives, of your sons, and of your daughters, and bring them to me.”
All the people took off the golden rings which were in their ears, and brought them to Aaron.
He received what they handed him, fashioned it with an engraving tool, and made it a molded calf. Then they said, “These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt.”
When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it; and Aaron made a proclamation, and said, “Tomorrow shall be a feast to Yahweh.”
They rose up early on the next day, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.
Yahweh spoke to Moses, “Go, get down; for your people, who you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves!

They have turned away quickly out of the way which I commanded them. They have made themselves a molded calf, and have worshiped it, and have sacrificed to it, and said, ‘These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt.’ ”
Yahweh said to Moses, “I have seen these people, and behold, they are a stiff-necked people.
Now therefore leave me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them, and that I may consume them; and I will make of you a great nation.”
Moses begged Yahweh his God, and said, “Yahweh, why does your wrath burn hot against your people, that you have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?

Why should the Egyptians talk, saying, ‘He brought them out for evil, to kill them in the mountains, and to consume them from the surface of the earth?’ Turn from your fierce wrath, and turn away from this evil against your people.

Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self, and said to them, ‘I will multiply your offspring as the stars of the sky, and all this land that I have spoken of I will give to your offspring, and they shall inherit it forever.’ ”
So Yahweh turned away from the evil which he said he would do to his people.
Moses turned, and went down from the mountain, with the two tablets of the covenant in his hand; tablets that were written on both their sides. They were written on one side and on the other.
The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.
When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, “There is the noise of war in the camp.”
He said, “It isn’t the voice of those who shout for victory. It is not the voice of those who cry for being overcome; but the noise of those who sing that I hear.”
As soon as he came near to the camp, he saw the calf and the dancing. Then Moses’ anger grew hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands, and broke them beneath the mountain.
He took the calf which they had made, and burned it with fire, ground it to powder, and scattered it on the water, and made the children of Israel drink it.

read.why: Read on past the feast to Moses coming down the mountain with the tablets in his hands. Before he goes down, notice what he does on the mountain: he pleads for the people, and God relents. A story of impatience is also a story of mercy.

ascension-wait-for-the-promise.title: Wait for the promise
ascension-wait-for-the-promise.line: Before he is taken from their sight, Jesus tells his friends not to rush off, but to wait.

story.retell: For forty days after Easter, Luke says, the risen Jesus appeared to his friends. On the last day he told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the gift his Father had promised, the Holy Spirit. Then, as they watched, he was taken up and a cloud hid him from their sight. Two men in white asked them why they stood looking into the sky. So they went back into the city, to an upstairs room, and waited together in prayer.
story.verse: Being assembled together with them, he commanded them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me.

ascension-wait-for-the-promise.artLink: Johann Koerbecke painted the Ascension in 1456–57 for the high altar of the monastery church at Marienfeld in Westphalia.
ascension-wait-for-the-promise.see: Jesus sits on a dark cloud at the top of the panel in a red robe, the wounds still in his hands and side, one hand raised in blessing and the other holding a staff with a red-cross banner. On bands of black cloud either side are bearded figures holding a palm, a book, two stone tablets, a harp, a sword. Below, the apostles kneel on either side of a smooth green rock, gazing and gesturing upward; on top of the rock are two footprints. Closest to us, Mary in a deep blue mantle looks up with her hands together and a slight smile, and a young blond man in green puts an arm round her. Gold rays shine down from Jesus and up from the heads of those below.
ascension-wait-for-the-promise.meaning: The disciples had followed Jesus for three years and had just seen him alive after death. Now he was gone from sight, and the instruction was not to do something but to wait. They did not know how long; it turned out to be about ten days. And they waited in the right way: together, in a room in the city, praying, with Mary among them. Waiting is not the same as doing nothing. It is staying where you have been put, with the people you have been given, ready. On Sunday Advent begins, the Church's season of waiting. This is how it is done.

echo.text: Ovid tells how Romulus, the founder of Rome, left the earth. As he sat giving judgements to his people, the war god Mars came down in his chariot and carried him off, and his mortal body melted away in the air, like a lead shot flung from a sling. He became the god Quirinus, and the Romans worshipped him.
echo.link: The Romans told of a king taken up and turned into a god with a temple. The disciples watched their Lord taken up and were told something else: wait, the gift is coming, and he will come back. Their story goes on not in a shrine but in a room full of people praying.

ascension-wait-for-the-promise.question: What are you waiting for that you cannot hurry? Who could you wait alongside this week, so that neither of you waits alone?
ascension-wait-for-the-promise.prayer: Lord Jesus, you told your friends to wait for the promise, and they waited together. As Advent comes, teach me to wait well: not alone, not idle, not staring at the sky, but ready, and praying with the people you have given me. Amen.
ascension-wait-for-the-promise.midday: This morning: the disciples watching Jesus go, and told to wait. Is there someone you could wait with this afternoon?
ascension-wait-for-the-promise.evening: Today's story was the Ascension. What did you wait for today? Who kept you company, or whom did you keep company?

music.why: The disciples were told to wait for the Spirit; “Come, Creator Spirit” has been the Church's prayer for that gift for over a thousand years, and is still sung at Pentecost.

paras: The first book I wrote, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began both to do and to teach,
until the day in which he was received up, after he had given commandment through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
To these he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days, and speaking about God’s Kingdom.
Being assembled together with them, he commanded them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me.
For John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”
Therefore when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?”
He said to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”
When he had said these things, as they were looking, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.
While they were looking steadfastly into the sky as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white clothing,
who also said, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.”
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

When they had come in, they went up into the upper room where they were staying; that is Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James.
All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.

read.why: In two days Advent begins. Read the opening of Acts, where Luke takes up his story again: forty days, a promise, a cloud, and a room full of people praying. The last verse names Mary among them, whose waiting Advent remembers.

anthony-makes-room.title: Making room
anthony-makes-room.line: A young man hears a Gospel reading in church and goes straight out to give his inheritance away.

story.ref: Athanasius, The Life of Antony, chapters 2–3, about AD 360
story.retell: Anthony was about eighteen when his parents died in Egypt, leaving him their farmland and a younger sister to look after. A few months later, walking to church, he was thinking about how the apostles had left everything to follow Jesus. As he went in, the Gospel being read was Jesus' word to a rich young man: go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me. Anthony felt it had been spoken to him. He went straight out, gave the family's land to the people of his village, sold everything else and gave the money to the poor, keeping a little back for his sister.
story.verse: Jesus said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”
story.verseRef: Matthew 19:21, the Gospel Anthony heard that day

anthony-makes-room.artLink: The Sienese painter known as the Master of the Osservanza painted Anthony giving away his wealth in about 1430–35, in the same series as his walk to find Paul the hermit.
anthony-makes-room.see: In a pale peach courtyard, a young man with short blond hair and a gold halo, in a gold-trimmed burgundy cloak and pale green hose, holds a white purse by its strings and drops coins into a boy's bowl. Waiting in line are a woman in a patched brown dress holding a baby, a stooped old woman, a man in a frayed black robe with a hole in his sleeve, an old man with his eyes closed led by a little black-and-white dog on a rope, and a traveller with a staff. Through an open doorway behind, Anthony appears again, going down a staircase, purse in hand, towards a heavy wooden door with gold coins heaped beyond it.
anthony-makes-room.meaning: Advent is about preparing the way, and preparing usually means clearing space. Anthony did not hear a vague call to be a bit more generous. He heard one sentence, took it at its word and acted on it the same morning. Most of us will not sell everything. But the question in the story is one anyone can ask: what is taking up the room where Christ might come? It might be money or things, a crowded diary, or a grudge. Making room is the oldest way of getting ready for a guest.

echo.from: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, Book 6
echo.when: Greece, written in the 3rd century AD
echo.text: Crates of Thebes, Diogenes Laertius tells us, came from a wealthy family. He turned his property into money, gave it away to the people of his city and took up the poor, free life of the Cynic philosophers, who owned little more than a cloak and a bag.
echo.link: Crates and Anthony both gave away a fortune. Crates did it to be free of things. Anthony did it to follow someone. Both found that having less left room for more.

anthony-makes-room.question: What is taking up the room in your life where something better could come: a possession, a habit, a full diary? What is one thing you could give away this week?
anthony-makes-room.prayer: Lord, Anthony heard your word and made room for you that same day. Show me what fills the space I should be keeping for you. Give me the freedom to let it go, and the joy of giving it to someone who needs it. Amen.
anthony-makes-room.midday: This morning: Anthony giving away his inheritance to follow Christ. What could you clear away this afternoon to make room?
anthony-makes-room.evening: Today's story was Anthony making room. What did you hold on to today that you could have let go? What could you give away tomorrow?

music.why: One verse of the old Irish prayer, in Eleanor Hull's version, begins “Riches I heed not”: the choice Anthony made in a single morning.

paras: Behold, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”
He said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”
He said to him, “Which ones?”
Jesus said, “ ‘You shall not murder.’ ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ ‘You shall not steal.’ ‘You shall not offer false testimony.’
‘Honor your father and your mother.’ And, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ ”
The young man said to him, “All these things I have observed from my youth. What do I still lack?”
Jesus said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”
But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.
Jesus said to his disciples, “Most certainly I say to you, a rich man will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven with difficulty.
Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye, than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom.”
When the disciples heard it, they were exceedingly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?”
Looking at them, Jesus said, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
Then Peter answered, “Behold, we have left everything, and followed you. What then will we have?”

Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive one hundred times, and will inherit eternal life.
But many will be last who are first; and first who are last.

read.why: Read the Gospel Anthony heard that morning. The rich young man went away sad, because he had great possessions; Anthony, who also had them, went the other way. Peter's question at the end is honest: what will we have? Jesus' answer is about receiving far more than was left behind.

joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.title: Giving in the dark
joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.line: An old couple who have waited twenty years for a child keep giving to the poor and to the temple.

story.ref: The Protevangelium of James, 2nd century, and The Golden Legend · the Conception of Mary
story.retell: The Bible says nothing about Mary's parents, but a second-century story, the Protevangelium of James, gives them names: Joachim and Anna. They were devout and well off, and for many years they had no child. The Golden Legend says that for twenty years they divided all they had into three: a third for the temple, a third for the poor and for pilgrims, and a third for themselves. When at last Joachim's offering was turned away at the temple because he was childless, he went off in shame to his shepherds in the hills, and Anna mourned at home. Then an angel came to each of them with the news that they would have a child, and the child was Mary. Today Catholics keep the feast of her Immaculate Conception; the Orthodox keep the Conception of Mary by St Anna tomorrow.
story.verse: He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother of children. Praise Yah!

joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.artLink: Andrea di Bartolo of Siena painted this scene in about 1400–05, as one of a series on the life of Mary.
