joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.see: Against a gold background, under two tall, tower-like buildings, a grey-bearded old man with a halo, Joachim, in a royal-blue robe, has a basket of bread rolls over one arm and holds a roll out to a group of poor people in torn and patched clothes: a man and a woman stooped over sticks, another kneeling beside a crutch. Just behind him, Anna, haloed, in a white head covering and an emerald-green dress, holds out a spouted vessel towards the other side. There, under a ceiling painted blue with gold stars, a priest in a crimson cloak and a tall pointed white cap holds out his hand to three boys carrying tall white sacks.
joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.meaning: For twenty years Joachim and Anna prayed for something that did not come, and they did not stop giving. Their own hope stayed in the dark, and they kept handing out bread. That is a kind of light too: not the light of an answered prayer, but the light a person gives off while still waiting for one. The story says the answer, when it came, was far bigger than anything they had asked. But the painting catches them before that, on an ordinary day, being generous with an ache in their hearts. Advent is full of people like them.

echo.text: Seneca says that if we want to be like the gods, we should give even to the ungrateful. The sun rises on wicked people too, he points out, and the seas lie open even to pirates. The gods go on giving without waiting to be thanked or repaid.
echo.link: Seneca's gods give because giving is their nature, like sunlight. Joachim and Anna gave while their own prayers went unanswered, and in the end the light rose for them too.

joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.question: Is there a prayer of yours that has gone unanswered for a long time? While you wait, who could you be generous to this week, as Joachim and Anna were?
joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.prayer: Lord, Joachim and Anna kept giving while they waited in the dark. When my own hopes are slow to be answered, keep my hands open to others. Let me give light while I wait for it, and trust you with the rest. Amen.
joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.midday: This morning: Joachim and Anna, giving to the poor through twenty years of waiting. Who could you give to this afternoon?
joachim-and-anna-giving-in-the-dark.evening: Today's story was Joachim and Anna. Did you give anything today, even while something in you was still waiting? Where did you see light?

music.why: Rachmaninoff's sixth movement, “Rejoice, O Virgin Mother of God”, greets the child Joachim and Anna waited for; it rises from a whisper to a great cry of joy before falling quiet again.

paras: Now there was a certain man of Ramathaim Zophim, of the hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
This man went up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice to Yahweh of Armies in Shiloh. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests to Yahweh, were there.
When the day came that Elkanah sacrificed, he gave to Peninnah his wife, and to all her sons and her daughters, portions;
but to Hannah he gave a double portion, for he loved Hannah, but Yahweh had shut up her womb.
Her rival provoked her severely, to irritate her, because Yahweh had shut up her womb.
So year by year, when she went up to Yahweh’s house, her rival provoked her. Therefore she wept, and didn’t eat.
Elkanah her husband said to her, “Hannah, why do you weep? Why don’t you eat? Why is your heart grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
So Hannah rose up after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh. Now Eli the priest was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of Yahweh’s temple.
She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed to Yahweh, weeping bitterly.

She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look at the affliction of your servant and remember me, and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”
As she continued praying before Yahweh, Eli saw her mouth.
Now Hannah spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, “How long will you be drunk? Get rid of your wine!”
Hannah answered, “No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit. I have not been drinking wine or strong drink, but I poured out my soul before Yahweh.
Don’t consider your servant a wicked woman; for I have been speaking out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation.”
Then Eli answered, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”
She said, “Let your servant find favor in your sight.” So the woman went her way and ate; and her facial expression wasn’t sad any more.
They rose up in the morning early and worshiped Yahweh, then returned and came to their house to Ramah. Then Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and Yahweh remembered her.
When the time had come, Hannah conceived, and bore a son; and she named him Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked him of Yahweh.”

read.why: The story of Joachim and Anna is modelled on a much older one in the Bible. Read Hannah's: a childless woman, a yearly festival at the house of God, tears, a priest who misunderstands, and at last a child. Light comes into the dark slowly here, and through prayer.

last-supper-on-the-night.title: On the night
last-supper-on-the-night.line: On the night he is betrayed, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks and gives himself to his friends.

story.retell: On the evening of the Passover, Jesus sat at table with his twelve closest friends. He told them that one of them would betray him, and one by one they asked him whether it was them. Judas had already been paid thirty pieces of silver. Then, as they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them as his body, and passed round a cup of wine as his blood, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
story.verse: As they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks for it, and broke it. He gave to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.”

last-supper-on-the-night.artLink: William Blake painted the supper in 1799, one of a series of small Bible paintings he made for his friend and patron Thomas Butts.
last-supper-on-the-night.see: Against an almost black background, thirteen figures recline round a long table, all painted in a glowing golden yellow. At the centre a radiant gold starburst surrounds Jesus, who looks out towards us with his hands raised, palms open, at his chest. Beside him a young, long-haired figure in teal mirrors his pose, wrists crossed, turning to look at him. Some of the others bend low over the table in prayer. And in the lower right corner one man in brick red has turned his back on the table and is counting coins in a sack.
last-supper-on-the-night.meaning: Christians have remembered this meal for two thousand years as the meal on the night Jesus was betrayed. It is the darkest night in the story: one friend has sold him, the rest will run away, and tomorrow he will die. And in the middle of it, Jesus gives thanks. Blake paints exactly that: darkness all round, light at the centre, and one man turning away towards his money. The light does not wait for the darkness to clear. It shines in it, and gives itself away.

echo.text: In AD 65 the emperor Nero ordered Seneca, the philosopher who had been his tutor, to take his own life. Tacitus says Seneca asked for writing tablets to make his will and was refused. So he turned to the friends around him and said that, since he could not repay their kindness any other way, he would leave them the one thing he still had, and the finest: the pattern of his life.
echo.link: Seneca, facing death among his friends, left them his example. Jesus, on the night before he died, left his friends more than that: himself, given in bread and wine, to be shared again and again.

last-supper-on-the-night.question: Where is it dark for you, or for someone you love, at the moment? Could you give thanks for one thing in the middle of it today, and give something of yourself to someone else?
last-supper-on-the-night.prayer: Lord Jesus, on the darkest night you gave thanks and gave yourself. Be the light at the centre of my table and my troubles. Keep me from turning away, and teach me to give myself to others as you gave yourself to me. Amen.
last-supper-on-the-night.midday: This morning: the last supper, light at the centre of the darkest night. Give thanks for one thing this afternoon, whatever else is going on.
last-supper-on-the-night.evening: Today's story was the last supper. What did you give thanks for today? Was there a moment you turned away, or a moment you gave yourself?

music.why: Mozart wrote this short motet, “Hail, true body”, a few months before his own death; it is a prayer to the body given at this table.

paras: Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests,
and said, “What are you willing to give me, that I should deliver him to you?” They weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver.
From that time he sought opportunity to betray him.
Now on the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
He said, “Go into the city to a certain person, and tell him, ‘The Teacher says, “My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.” ’ ”
The disciples did as Jesus commanded them, and they prepared the Passover.
Now when evening had come, he was reclining at the table with the twelve disciples.
As they were eating, he said, “Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.”
They were exceedingly sorrowful, and each began to ask him, “It isn’t me, is it, Lord?”
He answered, “He who dipped his hand with me in the dish will betray me.
The Son of Man goes, even as it is written of him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”
Judas, who betrayed him, answered, “It isn’t me, is it, Rabbi?”
He said to him, “You said it.”
As they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks for it, and broke it. He gave to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.”
He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave to them, saying, “All of you drink it,
for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.
But I tell you that I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father’s Kingdom.”
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

read.why: Read from Judas striking his bargain to the hymn they sang before going out to the Mount of Olives. These are the longest nights of the year, and this is the night the Church has never stopped remembering.

lucy-would-not-be-moved.title: A light that would not move
lucy-would-not-be-moved.line: On the eve of her feast: a young woman of Syracuse who gave her dowry to the poor and could not be dragged away.

story.ref: The life of St Lucy, from The Golden Legend · the eve of St Lucy's Day
story.retell: Lucy was a young Christian woman of Syracuse in Sicily, put to death in about 304 under the emperor Diocletian. The Golden Legend says that after her mother was healed of a long illness, Lucy persuaded her to give the money saved for Lucy's dowry to the poor. The man she had been promised to was furious and denounced her as a Christian to the governor. When the governor ordered her to be dragged away, the story says, no number of men or oxen could move her, and even after she was struck with a sword she did not die until a priest had brought her communion. Tomorrow is her feast; her name comes from the Latin for light.
story.verse: Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lucy-would-not-be-moved.artLink: Veronese painted Lucy's death and last communion in Venice in about 1585–86, a few years before his own death.
lucy-would-not-be-moved.see: In front of a town square, Lucy kneels in a shimmering thistle-purple gown, turning away from us towards an old, white-bearded priest in a white robe and gold stole, who holds a gold cup and offers her a small white wafer. Her lips are parted. Behind her, a man in butterscotch yellow, his face in shadow, leans over her shoulder and drives a dagger into her chest, and a thin line of blood runs down. A man in celestial blue kneels between us and the priest, holding a thick candle. Beyond, in the square, people and oxen gather round a woman in pink on a platform, under a dark blue sky veiled with cloud.
lucy-would-not-be-moved.meaning: Lucy's story is told in the bright colours of legend, but its heart is simple: a young woman who gave away what had been saved for her own future, and who could not be moved from what she believed. In the old calendar her feast fell close to the shortest day of the year, and in Sweden and elsewhere children still walk in procession on her day with candles in their hair. Light in darkness is not always a blaze. Sometimes it is one person who will not be moved, kneeling, steady, while everything round her goes wrong.

echo.text: Epictetus, a former slave who became a teacher, imagined a tyrant threatening a philosopher. I will put you in chains. My leg, perhaps; but not even Zeus can overpower my will. I will throw you into prison. My poor body, you mean. What is truly yours, he taught, no one can take from you.
echo.link: The Stoic said no one could move his will. Lucy's story says the same in a picture: men and oxen could not shift her. Her strength, the Christians said, was not only her own, but came from the one who had lit her lamp.

lucy-would-not-be-moved.question: Is there something good you have been keeping back for yourself that you could give away this Advent? Where do you need to stand firm this week, quietly and kindly?
lucy-would-not-be-moved.prayer: Lord, you made Lucy a light in a dark time. Make me steady where I need to stand firm, generous with what I have been keeping for myself, and a small light for someone in the dark this week. Amen.
lucy-would-not-be-moved.midday: This morning: Lucy, whose name means light, who could not be moved. Where could you be a small, steady light this afternoon?
lucy-would-not-be-moved.evening: Today's story was St Lucy, and tomorrow is her feast. Where did you stand firm today? Whose darkness could you lighten a little tomorrow?

music.why: Lucy's name comes from the Latin for light, and Haydn's Creation has the most famous burst of light in music: at “and there was light” the whole choir and orchestra blaze out in C major.

paras: Seeing the multitudes, he went up onto the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him.
He opened his mouth and taught them, saying,

“Blessed are the poor in spirit,
for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.

Blessed are those who mourn,
for they shall be comforted.

Blessed are the gentle,
for they shall inherit the earth.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness,
for they shall be filled.

Blessed are the merciful,
for they shall obtain mercy.

Blessed are the pure in heart,
for they shall see God.

Blessed are the peacemakers,
for they shall be called children of God.

Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake,
for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
“Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
“You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.
You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

read.why: Read the opening of the Sermon on the Mount, with its blessings on the poor, the merciful and the persecuted, ending with the words Lucy lived: you are the light of the world. A lamp, Jesus says, is meant to be seen.
